review.purpose: Approved implementation: apply all 129 reviewed chapter updates in all 13 languages, English first, followed by a translation audit.
review.scope: All 1189 English chapter takeaways in 39 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books reviewed; existing notes and references inspected for flagged chapters.
review.policy: State explicit narrative and attributed speech in the summary. Label inference, textual variants, and disputed interpretation in notes. Proposed cross-references are contextual selections, not proof that every interpretation is established.
review.approval: User approved all 129 rows and implementation in all 13 languages on 2026-10-16; existing Verse of the Day fixes remain included.
review.address_validation: All proposed cross-reference addresses resolve in the bundled English Bible; this check does not establish interpretive agreement.
review.display_punctuation: English review prose uses ASCII punctuation. The structured review retains the exact current summary and existing notes/references for comparison.
review.cross_reference_format: Every proposed cross-reference and direct-reference entry includes its citation followed by passage-specific context, matching the app format.
review.implementation_status: All 129 approved chapters implemented in all 13 languages; independent translation review and final preservation checks passed.

rows.current_summary: God rests on the seventh day after completing creation, then forms Adam from dust, places him in the Garden of Eden with instructions not to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil, and creates a woman from Adam's rib as his helper. Adam names all the animals, names the woman, and they live together naked without shame.
rows.current_summary_original: God rests on the seventh day after completing creation, then forms Adam from dust, places him in the Garden of Eden with instructions not to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil, and creates a woman from Adam's rib as his helper. Adam names all the animals, names the woman, and they live together naked without shame.
rows.concern: "God rests ... then forms Adam" can make the creation of humans occur after the seventh-day rest.
rows.scripture_says: Verses 1-3 conclude the creation account; verse 4 introduces the account focused on the garden and humanity.
rows.proposed_summary: After describing God's seventh-day rest, the chapter recounts how the LORD God formed the man from dust, placed him in Eden, gave him a command, and made the woman as his corresponding helper. The man and woman live together without shame.
cross_references: Genesis 1:26-31: God creates humanity male and female before the sixth day ends, placing human creation before the seventh-day rest described in Genesis 2.
Matthew 19:4-6: Jesus joins the creation of male and female with the one-flesh statement, reading the creation and marriage passages together.
rows.translation_context_note: The current detailed wordplay notes do not address this chronological wording. Existing cross-references are about creation by the word and miss the immediately relevant Genesis 1 sequence.
rows.proposed_note: Genesis 1 already places humanity within the completed creation. Genesis 2 first describes the seventh-day rest, then turns to the garden account; its chapter order does not require humans to have been created on an eighth day. Verse 23 calls her woman; the name Eve appears in 3:20.
existing_cross_references: Psalm 33:6: By the *word* of the LORD the heavens were made.
John 1:1-3: In the beginning was the *word* (logos); all things came to be through the *word*.
Hebrews 11:3: By faith we understand the universe was formed by the *word* of God.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: שָׁבַת / שַׁבָּת (shavat / shabbat) - Greek: σάββατον (sabbaton) - Aramaic: שבתא (shabta)
existing_translation_notes.note: To cease; the seventh day is set apart as a gift and marker in time.

2:7 forms ha-adam, the man, out of the dust of ha-adamah, the ground, and the two words are the same root. English cannot show it, so a reader misses that the name is the material. The same pairing returns as the sentence at 3:19, back to the adamah, because out of it you were taken.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים (nishmath chayyim) - נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה (nephesh chayyah)
existing_translation_notes.note: Neshamah is breath drawn through the nose, and 2:7 has it breathed into the nostrils. Nephesh chayyah, what the man then becomes, is rendered living soul or living being, and it is the same phrase already used of the animals at 1:20-21 and 1:24. What separates the man in 2:7 is not the phrase at the end but the breathing at the start.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פִּישׁוֹן (Pishon) - גִּיחוֹן (Gichon) - חִדֶּקֶל (Chiddeqel, Tigris) - פְּרָת (Perath, Euphrates)
existing_translation_notes.note: 2:10-14 names four and locates each one. Two are still on the map: the Chiddeqel is the Tigris, which the text places east of Asshur, and the Perath is the Euphrates. The Pishon runs around Havilah, where the text notes gold, bdellium and onyx, and the Gihon around Cush; neither of those two courses can be traced on the ground today. Bdellium is a pale aromatic gum, named again at Numbers 11:7 for the colour of manna.

existing_translation_notes.term: To work it and keep it
existing_translation_notes.note: Avad is to work or to serve, and shamar is to guard or keep watch over. The two verbs appear as a pair again at Numbers 3:7-8 and 18:5-6, where they are the Levites' duty toward the tabernacle: serve it and guard it. 2:15 gives the man a job with the same two words before anything has gone wrong.

English helper suggests an assistant, and the Hebrew does not carry that. Ezer is used about twenty times in the Old Testament and most of those are of God Himself: my help and my shield (Psalm 33:20), the God of your father who helps you (Genesis 49:25), our help is in the name of the LORD (Psalm 124:8). Kenegdo means corresponding to him, standing opposite. 2:18 and 2:20 pair a word of strength with a word of match.

2:23 is a sentence built on sound: she shall be called ishshah because she was taken out of ish. The two Hebrew words differ by one ending, so the naming and the reason are audible in a way no English pair reproduces. 2:24 then draws the conclusion about leaving and holding fast, which Jesus quotes at Matthew 19:5 and Paul at Ephesians 5:31.

The last word of 2:25 and one of the first words of 3:1 are near twins in Hebrew. The couple are arummim, naked, and the serpent is arum, crafty. The chapter break falls between them, but in a scroll they sit side by side, and the pun is the hinge English readers never see.

existing_translation_notes.note: A large box-like vessel; term also used for the basket of baby Moses.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה אַמָּה (chamesh esreh ammah)
existing_translation_notes.note: A cubit runs about 18 inches, so fifteen cubits is roughly 22 feet or 6.8 meters. Genesis 6:15 gives the ark a height of 30 cubits, exactly twice that figure. Verse 20 is measuring how far the water stood above the high ground, not the total depth of the flood.

existing_translation_notes.term: The seventeenth day of the second month
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בְּשִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִי (be-shivah asar yom la-chodesh ha-sheni)
existing_translation_notes.note: Genesis dates the flood by month and day, and the numbers are internally consistent. The water rises on the second month, day seventeen (7:11) and the ark grounds on the seventh month, day seventeen (8:4). That is five months, and 7:24 and 8:3 both call the same span 150 days, which gives months of exactly 30 days. The year is counted from Noah's birthday, not from a national calendar.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: שִׁנְעָר (Shinar), the plain of southern Mesopotamia
existing_translation_notes.note: Genesis 10:10-12 is a list of real cities that have all been dug up. Babel is Babylon on the Euphrates; Erech is Uruk, one of the oldest cities in the world; Akkad gave its name to the Akkadian language that the whole Near East later used for diplomacy. Nineveh and Calah, both on the Tigris, became the capitals of Assyria, and the palace at Nineveh is where Sennacherib's wall reliefs were found. The verse traces the movement from the southern plain of Shinar northward to Assyria.

Genesis 10:14 places the Philistines in the line of the Casluhites and names the Caphtorites in the same breath; Amos 9:7 says the LORD brought the Philistines from Caphtor, and Jeremiah 47:4 calls them the remnant from the coasts of Caphtor. Caphtor is a place across the sea, not another Canaanite hill town, which is why the Philistines in Judges and Samuel look and fight differently from Israel's other neighbors: five confederated cities on the coastal plain, iron working they kept to themselves (1 Samuel 13:19-22), and uncircumcised, which is the standing insult used against them.

2 Samuel 8:11: Spoils set apart to the LORD in later narratives.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֵן (kohen) - Greek: ἱερεύς (hiereus) - Aramaic: ܟܗܢܐ (kahana)
existing_translation_notes.note: An authorized minister/officiant of worship and blessing.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿaser) - Greek: δεκάτη (dekatē) - Aramaic: ܥܣܝܪܬܐ (ʿasirta)
existing_translation_notes.note: A tenth portion of goods; here given by Abram to Melchizedek.

The word appears only here in the Hebrew Bible and means men trained or tried in service. These 318 are not hired soldiers but retainers born in Abram's own household, which tells you the scale of his establishment: a private force large enough to chase a coalition army more than 150 miles north, from Mamre near Hebron to beyond Damascus, and break it in a night attack.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בֶּאֱרֹת חֵמָר (be'erot chemar, 'wells of bitumen')
existing_translation_notes.note: Natural asphalt seeps, real geology at the southern end of the Dead Sea, where lumps of bitumen still surface after earthquakes. Bitumen was a traded commodity and a waterproof glue. The same substance mortars the bricks at Babel (Genesis 11:3), seals Noah's ark (Genesis 6:14), and coats the basket that carries the infant Moses (Exodus 2:3).

rows.current_summary: Jacob meets Rachel at a well near Harran, works seven years to marry her, but Laban tricks him into marrying Leah first; Jacob then works another seven years for Rachel, and Leah bears him four sons while Rachel remains childless.
rows.current_summary_original: Jacob meets Rachel at a well near Harran, works seven years to marry her, but Laban tricks him into marrying Leah first; Jacob then works another seven years for Rachel, and Leah bears him four sons while Rachel remains childless.
rows.concern: The sequence can imply that Jacob waited fourteen years before marrying Rachel.
rows.scripture_says: Jacob marries Rachel after Leah's wedding week, then serves seven additional years.
rows.proposed_summary: Jacob meets Rachel at a well near Harran, works seven years to marry her, but Laban tricks him into marrying Leah first; Jacob marries Rachel after Leah's wedding week and then works another seven years for her, and Leah bears him four sons while Rachel remains childless.
cross_references: Hosea 12:12: Hosea recalls Jacob tending sheep to obtain a wife, supplying a later biblical reference to his marriage-by-service arrangement.
rows.translation_context_note: Existing references confirm service for a wife but do not clarify when the second marriage occurred.
rows.proposed_note: Jacob served seven years before Leah's wedding. After that wedding week he also married Rachel, then served another seven years; Rachel's wedding did not wait until the end of those years.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 24:11-20: Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at a well outside the town, and she waters his camels.
Hosea 12:12: Jacob fled to the land of Aram and worked for a wife; for a wife he tended sheep.
Exodus 2:15-21: Moses meets the daughters of the priest of Midian at a well, waters their flock, and is given Zipporah.
Deuteronomy 21:15-17: A man with a loved and an unloved wife may not pass over the unloved wife's firstborn son.
Genesis 49:3-4: Reuben, the firstborn born here, loses his rank in Jacob's last words.

existing_translation_notes.note: The mohar was paid by the groom to the bride's father, the opposite direction from a dowry. Exodus 22:16-17 treats it as a fixed going rate for a virgin, and Saul demanded a hundred Philistine foreskins in place of it (1 Samuel 18:25). Jacob reached Haran with nothing to weigh out, so he paid in labor instead: seven years, then seven more, fourteen years of a herdsman's work as the purchase price of two wives.

The wedding feast ran seven days. Samson's ran the same seven (Judges 14:12). Laban tells Jacob to finish out Leah's week before Rachel is given, so the second marriage came about seven days after the first, and the second seven years of service were worked afterward rather than in advance.

Zilpah and Bilhah are handed over with the brides (29:24, 29:29) as the father's contribution to his daughter's new household. The maid stayed the wife's own property, which is why each sister could give her own maid to Jacob and reckon the resulting sons to herself (30:3-4, 30:9). Sarai had used the same arrangement with Hagar (16:1-4).

Each name puns on the sentence Leah speaks as she gives it, and English keeps the name but drops the play. Reuven sounds like ra'ah ben, 'look, a son', and she says the LORD has looked on her affliction. Shimon comes from shama, to hear. Levi comes from lavah, to attach or join. Yehudah comes from yadah, to praise.

rows.current_summary: Rachel gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob to bear children for her, then Leah does the same with her servant Zilpah; eventually Rachel conceives and bears Joseph. After Joseph's birth, Jacob negotiates with Laban to claim spotted and speckled animals as wages, then uses peeled branches at watering troughs to breed animals that match his agreed-upon colors, growing wealthy in the process.
rows.current_summary_original: Rachel gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob to bear children for her, then Leah does the same with her servant Zilpah; eventually Rachel conceives and bears Joseph. After Joseph's birth, Jacob negotiates with Laban to claim spotted and speckled animals as wages, then uses peeled branches at watering troughs to breed animals that match his agreed-upon colors, growing wealthy in the process.
rows.concern: The summary can present the branches as an effective breeding mechanism while omitting Jacob's later attribution to God.
rows.scripture_says: Jacob puts peeled branches before the mating flocks; in chapter 31 he credits God with taking the livestock from Laban and giving it to him.
rows.proposed_summary: Rachel and Leah build their households through their servants, and God enables Rachel to bear Joseph. Jacob agrees to receive marked animals as wages and places peeled branches before the breeding flocks. His flocks grow; in the following chapter he credits God with giving him Laban's livestock.
cross_references: Genesis 31:8-12: Jacob tells his wives that God gave him Laban's livestock despite changing wage terms, identifying whom he credits for the increase.
rows.translation_context_note: The essential Genesis 31 cross-reference is already present and explicitly rejects branches as the source of the transfer. The summary needs the same restraint about causality.
rows.proposed_note: The account records Jacob's use of peeled branches; it does not explain a biological mechanism. In Genesis 31:8-12 Jacob tells his wives that God gave him the livestock despite Laban's changing wage terms.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 16:1-4: Sarai gives her maidservant Hagar to Abram so that she may build a family through her.
Song of Songs 7:13: The mandrakes give their fragrance, the only other mention of the plant in Scripture.
Genesis 31:8-12: Jacob tells his wives it was God, not the branches, that moved Laban's flocks into his hands.
Genesis 35:23-26: The full roll of Jacob's twelve sons by Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah.
Genesis 35:16-19: Rachel bears the second son she asks for here, Benjamin, and dies giving birth to him.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: זָכַר (zakhar) - Greek: μιμνῄσκομαι (mimnēiskomai) - Aramaic: ܕܟܪ (dakar)
existing_translation_notes.note: To call to mind with action; used for God regarding Rachel.

Mandragora officinarum, a low Mediterranean plant with a thick forked root and a small yellow fruit that ripens in late spring, which is why Reuben finds them during the wheat harvest (30:14). The fruit carried a long reputation across the ancient world as an aid to love and conception. The Hebrew name shares its consonants with dod, 'love', and the only other occurrence is Song of Songs 7:13, where it stands beside the lovers' door.

existing_translation_notes.term: That she may bear children for me
existing_translation_notes.note: Rachel's words in 30:3 read literally 'she shall bear on my knees'. Setting a newborn on someone's knees was the act that made the child theirs. Joseph does the same with Machir's sons at the end of the book (50:23). The maid bore the child, the mistress received it on her knees, and the child counted in the mistress's line.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: יוֹסֵף (Yosef) - from אָסַף (asaph, 'take away') and יָסַף (yasaph, 'add')
existing_translation_notes.note: The name carries two puns at once, and the text supplies both. Rachel says God has taken away (asaph) her disgrace, then asks the LORD to add (yasaph) another son (30:23-24). English can carry one of the two, never both.

rows.current_summary: Joseph's brothers, jealous of their father's favoritism and Joseph's dreams of dominion, strip him of his robe and sell him to Ishmaelites heading to Egypt; they deceive their father Jacob with the bloodied robe, leading him to believe Joseph is dead.
rows.current_summary_original: Joseph's brothers, jealous of their father's favoritism and Joseph's dreams of dominion, strip him of his robe and sell him to Ishmaelites heading to Egypt; they deceive their father Jacob with the bloodied robe, leading him to believe Joseph is dead.
rows.concern: Note-focused: notes for Tamar and Potiphar's wife belong to later chapters; the price note treats sanctuary valuation as a demonstrated market rate.
rows.scripture_says: This chapter gives Joseph's price as twenty shekels. Leviticus 27:5 independently gives twenty shekels as a sanctuary valuation for a male aged five to twenty.
rows.proposed_summary: Joseph's brothers, jealous of their father's favoritism and Joseph's dreams of dominion, strip him of his robe and sell him to Ishmaelites heading to Egypt; they deceive their father Jacob with the bloodied robe, leading him to believe Joseph is dead.
cross_references: Leviticus 27:5: The law assigns twenty shekels to a male aged five to twenty for a vow valuation, the figure compared with Joseph's sale price.
Genesis 38:14-19: Tamar disguises herself and sleeps with Judah, locating the incident described by the misplaced prostitute note in Genesis 38.
Genesis 39:7-12: Potiphar's wife repeatedly solicits Joseph and seizes his cloak as he flees, locating those incidents in Genesis 39.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Prostitute, Lie with, and Flee notes describe events absent from chapter 37. The existing valuation cross-reference is useful, but its current note turns numerical similarity into an unsupported market-price explanation.
rows.proposed_note: Joseph was seventeen and was sold for twenty shekels. Leviticus 27:5 gives the same number for the sanctuary valuation of a male aged five to twenty; that is a comparison, not proof of a slave-market price schedule. Tamar appears in Genesis 38, and Potiphar's wife in Genesis 39.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 42:6-9: The brothers bow to the ground before Joseph in Egypt, and he remembers the dreams told here.
Leviticus 27:5: Twenty shekels is the sanctuary valuation of a male between five and twenty years old.
2 Samuel 13:18: The robe of many colors is what the king's virgin daughters wore, the only other use of the phrase.
Acts 7:9-10: Stephen says the patriarchs sold Joseph out of jealousy, but God was with him.
Genesis 44:30-34: Judah offers himself as a slave rather than watch his father lose a second son.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מָכַר (makhar) - Greek: πιπράσκω (pipraskō) - Aramaic: זבן (zavan)
existing_translation_notes.note: To exchange for money; Joseph was sold for twenty shekels of silver.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: זוֹנָה (zonah) - Greek: πόρνη (pornē) - Aramaic: ܙܢܝܬܐ (zanita)
existing_translation_notes.note: A woman offering sex for payment; Tamar disguised herself this way.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: שָׁכַב (shakav) - Greek: κοιμάομαι (koimaomai) - Aramaic: ܫܟܒ (shakab)
existing_translation_notes.note: To lie down sexually; Potiphar’s wife demanded Joseph lie with her.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נוּס (nus) - Greek: φεύγω (pheugō) - Aramaic: ܥܪܩ (ʿraq)
existing_translation_notes.note: To escape or run away; Joseph fled when seized by Potiphar’s wife.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

A fragrant gum resin from the Commiphora tree of Arabia and East Africa. Used as a holy anointing-oil ingredient (Exodus 30:23), as perfume, as an embalming spice (John 19:39), and, mixed with wine, as a pain-dulling drink (Mark 15:23). One of the magi's gifts.

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

Genesis 37:28 gives the price paid for Joseph, and Leviticus 27:5 sets exactly twenty shekels as the valuation of a male between five and twenty years old. Joseph was seventeen (37:2). The figure is not arbitrary; it is the going rate for a boy of that age. Exodus 21:32 later prices a slave gored by an ox at thirty shekels, the valuation of an adult woman in Leviticus 27:4, and the same thirty pieces appear in Zechariah 11:12-13 and Matthew 26:15.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נְכֹאת וּצְרִי וָלֹט (nekhot uts'ri valot), gum, balm, and resin
existing_translation_notes.note: Genesis 37:25 puts a loaded caravan on the road at Dothan, and that is where the road was. Dothan sits at the north end of the hill country where the route from Gilead crosses toward the coastal plain and turns south for Egypt; the whole eastern trade in aromatic resins moved along it. Balm of Gilead was a medicinal resin famous enough to be used as a figure for healing in Jeremiah 8:22 and 46:11, and myrrh appears again as a burial spice at John 19:39.

Joseph was seventeen and was sold for twenty shekels. Leviticus 27:5 gives the same number for the sanctuary valuation of a male aged five to twenty; that is a comparison, not proof of a slave-market price schedule. Tamar appears in Genesis 38, and Potiphar's wife in Genesis 39.

implemented_reference_changes: Leviticus 27:5: The law assigns twenty shekels to a male aged five to twenty for a vow valuation, the figure compared with Joseph's sale price.

Genesis 39:7-12: Potiphar's wife repeatedly solicits Joseph and seizes his cloak as he flees, locating those incidents in Genesis 39.

rows.current_summary: The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh; Aaron's staff becomes a snake and swallows the staffs of Pharaoh's magicians, but Pharaoh's heart hardens. Moses then strikes the Nile with his staff and turns all the water to blood throughout Egypt, yet Pharaoh's magicians replicate the act and Pharaoh refuses to listen.

Moses then strikes the Nile with his staff and turns all the water to blood throughout Egypt, yet Pharaoh's magicians replicate the act and Pharaoh refuses to listen.
rows.concern: The summary gives Aaron's action to Moses.
rows.scripture_says: Aaron raises the staff and strikes the Nile in Pharaoh's presence.
rows.proposed_summary: The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh; Aaron's staff becomes a snake and swallows the staffs of Pharaoh's magicians, but Pharaoh's heart hardens. Aaron then strikes the Nile with his staff and turns all the water to blood throughout Egypt, yet Pharaoh's magicians replicate the act and Pharaoh refuses to listen.
rows.translation_context_note: The Nile note discusses Egypt's river worship but does not clarify the actor. Exodus 4 describes a related sign given to Moses and can contribute to the confusion.
rows.proposed_note: Moses receives the command to instruct Aaron. Verse 20 identifies Aaron as the one who raises the staff and strikes the Nile.
existing_cross_references: Exodus 4:2-9: The staff, the leprous hand, and Nile water turned to blood given to Moses as signs.
2 Timothy 3:8-9: Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, and their folly became plain to everyone.
Psalm 105:29: He turned their waters into blood and caused their fish to die.
Isaiah 19:5-8: The Nile dries up, the canals stink, and the fishermen of Egypt mourn.
Revelation 16:3-4: Bowls of wrath turn the sea and the rivers to blood.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: קָשָׁה (qashah), to make hard - חָזַק (chazaq), to make strong - כָּבֵד (kaved), to be heavy
existing_translation_notes.note: Three different Hebrew verbs arrive in English as one word. At 7:3 God says He will make Pharaoh's heart qasheh, hard; at 7:13 it is chazaq, strong or firm; at 7:14 it is kaved, heavy, the same root as the 'heavy' labour of 5:9 and the 'heavy' mouth Moses complained of at 4:10. The text distributes the action as well as the vocabulary: Pharaoh hardens his own heart at 8:15, 8:32 and 9:34, and the LORD is named as the one hardening it from 9:12 on.

A loanword from Egyptian, describing the lector priests who read the ritual books and were credited with power over nature. They are court professionals, not stage entertainers. 2 Timothy 3:8 names two of them, Jannes and Jambres.

Exodus 4:3 turns the staff into a nachash, an ordinary snake. Before Pharaoh in Exodus 7:9 the word changes to tannin, the term for the great creatures of Genesis 1:21, and the word Ezekiel 29:3 uses for Pharaoh himself, the monster lying in his own streams. English prints 'snake' and 'serpent' and the change disappears.

The Hebrew uses an Egyptian loanword for the river, not the usual word for a stream. Egypt's whole food supply depended on the Nile flood, and the inundation was worshipped as the god Hapi. Exodus 12:12 states that the LORD executed judgment against all the gods of Egypt, and the first blow lands on the river.

Verse 7:7 dates the confrontation precisely: Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they walk into the throne room. Acts 7:23 and 7:30 divide his life into forty in Egypt and forty in Midian, and Deuteronomy 34:7 puts him at a hundred and twenty when he dies, which makes the wilderness the last forty.

rows.current_summary: God sends a plague killing all Egyptian livestock while sparing Israel's, then a plague of boils on people and animals; when Pharaoh still refuses to release Israel, God sends a devastating hailstorm that destroys crops and kills anyone caught outside, though it avoids Goshen. Pharaoh temporarily agrees to let Israel go after the hail stops, but immediately hardens his heart again and refuses.

Pharaoh temporarily agrees to let Israel go after the hail stops, but immediately hardens his heart again and refuses.
rows.concern: Pharaoh's promise is placed after the hail stops; "all Egyptian livestock" also loses the stated field restriction.
rows.scripture_says: The livestock warning concerns animals in the field. Pharaoh promises release during the hail, then refuses after it stops.
rows.proposed_summary: God sends a plague killing Egyptian livestock in the field while sparing Israel's, then a plague of boils on people and animals; when Pharaoh still refuses to release Israel, God sends a devastating hailstorm that destroys crops and kills anyone caught outside, though it avoids Goshen. During the hail, Pharaoh promises to let Israel go, but after it stops he hardens his heart again and refuses.
cross_references: Exodus 8:15: Pharaoh hardens his heart after relief from a plague, establishing the earlier pattern repeated after the hail stops.
rows.translation_context_note: The current notes do not explain either qualification. The chapter itself records surviving livestock and the correct order.
rows.proposed_note: The livestock warning in verse 3 specifies animals in the field. Later animals are brought under shelter before the hail. Pharaoh promises release while asking for the hail to stop, then hardens his heart after it stops.
existing_cross_references: Psalm 78:47-48: He destroyed their vines with hail and their herds with lightning bolts.
Psalm 105:32-33: He gave them hail for rain, with lightning throughout their land, and shattered their trees.
Romans 9:17: Paul quotes the word spoken to Pharaoh, I raised you up to display My power in you.
Deuteronomy 28:27: The boils of Egypt are listed among the curses for covenant breaking.
Revelation 16:21: Enormous hailstones fall from heaven on men, and they curse God.

existing_translation_notes.note: The word covers herds and flocks as property and wealth. Egypt kept sacred bulls, Apis at Memphis and Mnevis at Heliopolis, and the cow goddess Hathor was among the most widely worshipped deities in the land. Exodus 9:4 records that the plague drew a line between Israel's animals and Egypt's.

Ash from a brick kiln, the very furnace Israel had been forced to work. Thrown into the air it became festering boils on man and beast. The lector priests could not even stand before Moses because the boils were on them too (Exodus 9:11).

existing_translation_notes.term: flax and barley, wheat and spelt
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פִּשְׁתָּה וּשְׂעֹרָה (pishtah u-seorah) - חִטָּה וְכֻסֶּמֶת (chittah u-khussemet)
existing_translation_notes.note: This is a dated agricultural note dropped into the narrative. Barley ripens about a month ahead of wheat, and flax is pulled while in flower. Exodus 9:31-32 says the barley was already in the ear and the flax in bloom while the wheat and spelt were still green, which places the hail a few weeks before the Exodus in the month of Abib.

Dever is the standard word for an epidemic, used of both animals and people, and it turns up in the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:21 and in David's choice at 2 Samuel 24:13-15. Here at 9:3 it falls on horses, donkeys, camels, cattle and flocks, which is to say on Egypt's transport, its ploughing, and its meat and milk at once.

existing_translation_notes.term: the officials who feared the word
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: הַיָּרֵא אֶת־דְּבַר יְהוָה (hayyare et-devar YHWH)
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 9:20-21 split Pharaoh's own court in two. Some officials believed the warning and brought their slaves and animals under cover before the hail; others left them in the field and lost them. It is the first sign in the account that the warnings were landing on Egyptians, and 12:38 records that a mixed crowd left the country with Israel.

rows.current_summary: Moses warns Pharaoh of a locust plague; when it devastates Egypt, Pharaoh asks forgiveness, but after the locusts are blown away he hardens his heart again. The LORD then brings three days of darkness over Egypt, and when Pharaoh offers to let the Israelites go but retain their livestock, Moses refuses and Pharaoh orders him never to return.
rows.current_summary_original: Moses warns Pharaoh of a locust plague; when it devastates Egypt, Pharaoh asks forgiveness, but after the locusts are blown away he hardens his heart again. The LORD then brings three days of darkness over Egypt, and when Pharaoh offers to let the Israelites go but retain their livestock, Moses refuses and Pharaoh orders him never to return.
rows.concern: The summary attributes this chapter's hardening to Pharaoh himself.
rows.scripture_says: Verses 20 and 27 explicitly say that the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart.
rows.proposed_summary: Moses warns Pharaoh of a locust plague; when it devastates Egypt, Pharaoh asks forgiveness, but after the locusts are blown away the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart again. The LORD then brings three days of darkness over Egypt, and when Pharaoh offers to let the Israelites go but retain their livestock, Moses refuses and Pharaoh orders him never to return.
cross_references: Exodus 9:34: Pharaoh and his officials harden their hearts after the hail stops, supplying the self-hardening attribution alongside chapter 10's divine attribution.
Romans 9:17-18: Paul cites God's words to Pharaoh and speaks of God showing mercy and hardening, giving the later apostolic discussion of divine agency.
rows.translation_context_note: The existing darkness note addresses Egyptian religion, not the passage's explicit attribution. This preserves both forms of agency without replacing either one.
rows.proposed_note: This chapter names the LORD as the one who hardens Pharaoh's heart. Other passages describe Pharaoh hardening his own heart; the narrative uses both descriptions.
existing_cross_references: Joel 1:4-7: A locust swarm strips the land, leaving the fig trees bare and the branches white.
Psalm 105:34-35: He spoke, and locusts came without number and devoured every plant in the land.
Joel 2:1-2: A day of darkness and gloom, like blackness spread over the mountains.
Deuteronomy 6:20-25: When your son asks what these statutes mean, you are to tell him you were slaves in Egypt.
Revelation 16:10: The fifth bowl plunges the kingdom of the beast into darkness.

existing_translation_notes.note: The desert locust, which swarms and migrates on the wind; Exodus 10:13 brings them on an east wind and Exodus 10:19 clears them on a west one. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization reckons a swarm covering one square kilometer holds about 40 million insects and eats in a day what 35,000 people would eat. The text says nothing green was left in Egypt.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: וְיָמֵשׁ חֹשֶׁךְ (ve-yamesh choshekh), 'darkness that may be felt'
existing_translation_notes.note: The verb means to grope or to feel with the hand. Egypt's chief deity was the sun god Ra, and Pharaoh held his throne as Ra's son, so the sun going out for three days struck at the crown as well as the temple. Exodus 10:23 notes that Israel had light where they lived.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אָבְדָה מִצְרָיִם (avedah Mitsrayim), 'Egypt is destroyed'
existing_translation_notes.note: At 10:7 Pharaoh's own officials tell him the country is finished and ask him to let the people go, before the locusts have even arrived. The plagues have already taken the river, the livestock, and the barley and flax harvest (9:31), and the court can read a ledger. It is the second time in the book that Egyptians break with their king, after 9:20.

Pharaoh negotiates three times and each offer keeps a hostage. Sacrifice inside Egypt (8:25); go, but not far (8:28); only the men, leaving wives and children behind (10:11); and finally everyone but the flocks and herds (10:24). Moses refuses each in turn, and answers the last one at 10:26 with 'not a hoof will be left behind,' because the animals are what the sacrifices are made of.

The locusts arrive on an east wind (10:13) and leave on a west one (10:19), which is how desert locust swarms actually travel: they ride the prevailing wind rather than steering. The same east wind drives back the sea at 14:21. Hebrew uses one word, ruach, for wind, breath and spirit, so the reader of the original hears the same word in all three places.

rows.current_summary: God commands Moses to consecrate all firstborn males and establish an annual Feast of Unleavened Bread to commemorate the exodus; he then leads Israel away from Egypt by the desert road toward the Red Sea, guiding them by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, while Moses carries Joseph's bones as promised.
rows.current_summary_original: God commands Moses to consecrate all firstborn males and establish an annual Feast of Unleavened Bread to commemorate the exodus; he then leads Israel away from Egypt by the desert road toward the Red Sea, guiding them by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, while Moses carries Joseph's bones as promised.
rows.concern: The consecration summary omits the explicit redemption of human firstborn, a material distinction beside the Jephthah discussion.
rows.scripture_says: Firstborn sons must be redeemed; the firstborn consecration command does not require sacrificing them.
rows.proposed_summary: God commands Israel to consecrate the firstborn, redeem every firstborn son, and remember the exodus through the Feast of Unleavened Bread. He leads the people by cloud and fire, while Moses carries Joseph's bones as promised.
cross_references: Numbers 18:15-16: Firstborn sons must be redeemed for five shekels at one month old, explicitly distinguishing their consecration from sacrifice.
Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.
Luke 2:22-24: Jesus' parents present Him to the Lord and bring the prescribed birds, showing firstborn consecration within a family's observance of the law.
rows.translation_context_note: The current redemption note and Numbers 18 reference already state this correctly. The proposal carries that essential distinction into the summary.
rows.proposed_note: Every firstborn son must be redeemed, not sacrificed. The chapter distinguishes human redemption from the treatment of sacrificial animals, so consecration to the LORD cannot be read as permission for human sacrifice.
existing_cross_references: Numbers 3:11-13: The Levites taken by God in place of every firstborn male of Israel.
Numbers 18:15-16: Every firstborn son redeemed at one month old for five shekels of the sanctuary.
Luke 2:22-24: Joseph and Mary bring the firstborn Jesus to the temple with the offering the law required.
Genesis 50:24-26: Joseph makes the sons of Israel swear to carry his bones up out of Egypt.
Joshua 24:32: Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem in the plot of ground Jacob bought.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עַמּוּד עָנָן (ammud anan), pillar of cloud - עַמּוּד אֵשׁ (ammud esh), pillar of fire
existing_translation_notes.note: An ammud is an upright column, the same word used for the posts holding up the tabernacle curtains (26:32). Verses 13:21-22 say neither pillar ever left its place in front of the people, so the column functions as a marching guide that can be seen from anywhere in a camp of that size, by day as a cloud and by night as fire. Numbers 9:15-23 makes the rule explicit: the camp moved when it lifted and stayed when it settled.

To buy back by paying a set price. Every firstborn male belonged to God, so a firstborn son and a firstborn donkey had to be bought back rather than sacrificed; Numbers 18:16 fixes the price for a son at five shekels of the sanctuary, about 57 grams of silver. Luke 2:22-24 shows the rite still being kept.

existing_translation_notes.term: a sign on your hand and a reminder on your forehead
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: לְאוֹת עַל־יָדְכָה וּלְטוֹטָפֹת בֵּין עֵינֶיךָ (le-ot al-yadkhah u-le-totafot bein einekha)
existing_translation_notes.note: The Hebrew totafot appears only in this command and in Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18. It is the line behind the leather boxes of scripture, tefillin, called phylacteries in Matthew 23:5, worn on the arm and the head.

existing_translation_notes.term: the road through the land of the Philistines
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים (derekh erets Pelishtim)
existing_translation_notes.note: The coastal highway from the eastern Delta to Gaza, the shortest way into Canaan at roughly 150 miles, and the route Egypt used for its armies. It was garrisoned with forts and wells at intervals, which is exactly why Exodus 13:17 says God did not lead Israel that way.

Succoth is the first stop out of Egypt (12:37, 13:20) and its name means booths, the temporary branch shelters people threw up when they camped. The Feast of Booths in Leviticus 23:42-43 is named for the same thing and given the same reason: so Israel would remember living in shelters on the way out of Egypt. Etham is described as on the edge of the wilderness, which means the party had reached the point where cultivated Delta land stops.

Joseph made Israel swear to carry his bones out (Genesis 50:25), and 13:19 records Moses collecting on that oath while the country is in chaos behind him. Egyptians embalmed and Genesis 50:26 says Joseph was embalmed and put in a coffin, so there was something to carry. Joshua 24:32 finishes the account: they buried him at Shechem, in the plot of ground Jacob had bought.

rows.current_summary: Laws govern theft and restitution, with penalties ranging from double repayment to death depending on the offense; additional rules address property damage, borrowed animals, seduction, sorcery, idolatry, treatment of foreigners and the poor, lending practices, and offerings to God.
rows.current_summary_original: Laws govern theft and restitution, with penalties ranging from double repayment to death depending on the offense; additional rules address property damage, borrowed animals, seduction, sorcery, idolatry, treatment of foreigners and the poor, lending practices, and offerings to God.
rows.concern: The opening makes death sound like a judicial punishment for ordinary property theft.
rows.scripture_says: Theft requires restitution; verses 2-3 separately address bloodguilt when a householder kills a burglar, distinguishing night from daylight.
rows.proposed_summary: The chapter sets restitution for theft and property loss, and distinguishes bloodguilt in the killing of a burglar by night or after sunrise. It also gives laws on sexual conduct, sorcery, idolatry, loans, offerings, and protection of foreigners, widows, orphans, and the poor.
cross_references: Job 24:16: Job describes thieves digging through houses in darkness, supplying the physical break-in setting relevant to the burglary law.
Leviticus 6:1-5: A person guilty of theft or deception must restore the property and add a fifth, providing a parallel law of restitution.
rows.translation_context_note: The current notes address related laws but do not separate burglary bloodguilt from theft penalties. Job 24 supplies the same breaking-through-a-house context.
rows.proposed_note: Verses 1-4 prescribe restitution for theft. The death in verses 2-3 is a burglar killed during a break-in, with different bloodguilt rules before and after sunrise; it is not a court's death sentence for stealing property.
existing_cross_references: Leviticus 6:1-5: Property taken by deceit must be restored in full with a fifth added on the day of the guilt offering.
Deuteronomy 24:10-13: Do not keep a poor man's cloak overnight; return it by sunset so he can sleep in it.
Deuteronomy 23:19-20: Do not charge your brother interest on money, food, or anything that can be lent.
Leviticus 19:33-34: The foreigner among you is to be treated as one born among you, and loved as yourself.
James 1:27: Pure religion is to look after orphans and widows in their distress.

existing_translation_notes.note: The outer garment doubled as a blanket, so seizing it overnight left a poor man without bedding; Exodus 22:26-27 orders it returned by sunset. An ostracon from Mesad Hashavyahu near Yavneh-Yam, written in the late seventh century BC, is a field worker's petition complaining that exactly this happened to him.

The word is built on the verb 'to bite.' The law does not regulate a rate; Exodus 22:25 forbids acting as a creditor toward a poor Israelite at all, and Deuteronomy 23:19-20 restates it. The prohibition is about lending inside the covenant community.

To devote something irrevocably to God, so that it can never be redeemed, sold, or put to ordinary use. Leviticus 27:28-29 defines the term, and Joshua 6:17-19 applies it to Jericho. In Exodus 22:20 it is the sentence on anyone who sacrifices to another god.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פָּתָה (pathah), to entice or persuade; at 22:16 יְפַתֶּה (yephatteh)
existing_translation_notes.note: This verb is the third of three that English versions blur together. Exodus 22:16-17 covers a man who talks an unbetrothed woman into it: he must pay the bride price and marry her, but 22:17 lets her father refuse the marriage outright, and the man pays the silver anyway. Deuteronomy 22:28-29 handles the parallel case with taphas, to take hold of, and Deuteronomy 22:25-27 handles force with chazaq, where the man is executed and the woman is declared guiltless. In Hebrew Bibles these two verses are numbered 22:15-16.

The mohar was paid by the groom to the bride's father, the opposite direction from a dowry, and it is what Exodus 22:16-17 requires whether or not the marriage goes ahead. Shechem offers to pay any mohar Jacob's sons name (Genesis 34:12). Saul asks David for one made of a hundred Philistine foreskins instead of silver, intending David to die collecting it (1 Samuel 18:25). Deuteronomy 22:29 fixes the sum for its case at fifty shekels.

existing_translation_notes.term: The foreigner, the widow, and the orphan
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: גֵּר (ger), a resident foreigner - אַלְמָנָה (almanah), widow - יָתוֹם (yatom), orphan
existing_translation_notes.note: These three had no clan to stand up for them, which in a society run on family claims meant no one to press a case at the gate. Exodus 22:21-24 forbids wronging any of them and gives the reason for the first: you were foreigners in Egypt. Then it does something unusual for a law code and names the enforcement, saying that if they cry out He will hear the cry Himself. Deuteronomy 24:17-21 attaches the harvest gleanings to the same three.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מְכַשֵּׁפָה (mekhashephah), a woman practicing kishuph
existing_translation_notes.note: The word covers paid ritual work: spells and binding formulas, potions, and figures made to act on a person at a distance. Exodus 7:11 uses the masculine form of the same root for the specialists Pharaoh calls in against Moses. Deuteronomy 18:10-11 gives the full list of trades Israel was to have none of, and 2 Kings 9:22 charges Jezebel with these practices by name. Exodus 22:18 puts the practitioner under a death sentence.

implemented_note_changes.note: Verses 1-4 prescribe restitution for theft. The death in verses 2-3 is a burglar killed during a break-in, with different bloodguilt rules before and after sunrise; it is not a court's death sentence for stealing property.

implemented_reference_changes: Leviticus 6:1-5: A person guilty of theft or deception must restore the property and add a fifth, providing a parallel law of restitution.
Job 24:16: Job describes thieves digging through houses in darkness, supplying the physical break-in setting relevant to the burglary law.

rows.current_summary: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD, and fire from his presence consumes them; Moses forbids Aaron and his remaining sons to mourn or leave the tent of meeting. The LORD himself commands Aaron not to drink wine or strong drink when entering the tent and to distinguish holy from common; Moses directs the eating of the priests' portions, and when he finds the sin-offering goat burned rather than eaten, Aaron's explanation satisfies him.
rows.current_summary_original: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD, and fire from his presence consumes them; Moses forbids Aaron and his remaining sons to mourn or leave the tent of meeting. The LORD himself commands Aaron not to drink wine or strong drink when entering the tent and to distinguish holy from common; Moses directs the eating of the priests’ portions, and when he finds the sin-offering goat burned rather than eaten, Aaron’s explanation satisfies him.
rows.concern: "Forbids ... to mourn" turns restrictions on priestly mourning rites into a ban on grief itself.
rows.scripture_says: Moses forbids disheveled hair, torn garments, and leaving the tent; the rest of Israel may mourn. Aaron's response later acknowledges his loss.
rows.proposed_summary: Nadab and Abihu die after offering unauthorized fire. Moses forbids Aaron and his remaining sons to perform the stated mourning rites or leave the tent, while Israel may mourn. The chapter gives priestly duties and records Moses accepting Aaron's explanation about the uneaten sin offering.
cross_references: Leviticus 21:1-12: Priests have specified family exceptions to corpse defilement, while the high priest faces stricter mourning and sanctuary restrictions, clarifying the ritual limits.
rows.translation_context_note: No current mourning note supplies this distinction. The priestly mourning laws in chapter 21 provide direct legal context.
rows.proposed_note: The restrictions name particular public mourning acts and departure from the tent. They do not say that Aaron felt no grief or was forbidden to grieve inwardly; verses 19-20 record his loss being taken seriously.
existing_cross_references: Numbers 3:2-4: Nadab and Abihu die before the LORD and leave no sons.
Numbers 26:61: The second census records again that they died offering unauthorized fire.
Exodus 30:9: The standing prohibition against offering unauthorized incense on the golden altar.
Ezekiel 44:21: No priest is to drink wine before entering the inner court.
Ezekiel 44:23: The priests are to teach the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֵשׁ זָרָה (esh zarah), literally 'strange fire'
existing_translation_notes.note: Zar means foreign or belonging to someone else, the same word used of an outsider who may not eat holy food (22:10). The coals for the incense were to be taken from the altar itself (16:12), so fire brought from anywhere else broke the one rule governing the whole procedure. Leviticus 10:1 says plainly that they offered fire He had not commanded them, and 10:9 follows immediately with a ban on priests drinking wine before entering the tent.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה (miḥūts la-maḥaneh), Greek: ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς (exō tēs parembolēs), Aramaic: לבר מן מדברא (lebar men midbara)
existing_translation_notes.note: Place for burning sacrificial remains and carrying out bodies; symbolizes removal of impurity from the holy camp.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

A metal pan for carrying live coals from the altar, with incense laid on top. Numbers 16:6-7 has Korah's company each take one, and Numbers 16:39 has the bronze ones hammered into altar plating afterward. It was a priest's tool, and Nadab and Abihu used theirs with fire the LORD had not commanded.

existing_translation_notes.term: holy and common, clean and unclean
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: קֹדֶשׁ / חֹל (qodesh / chol) - טָמֵא / טָהוֹר (tame / tahor)
existing_translation_notes.note: Two separate pairs, not one sliding scale, and Leviticus 10:10 makes teaching the difference part of the priest's job. Holy and common describe what is set apart to God and what is not. Clean and unclean describe ritual status. A thing can be common and clean at the same time, which is the ordinary condition of most of life.

Yayin is grape wine; shekhar covers other fermented drink, including that made from grain or dates. The ban applies to priests on duty in the tent (10:9), and the Nazirite vow in Numbers 6:3 extends it further. Ezekiel 44:21 repeats it for the priests of the restored temple.

rows.current_summary: God instructs Moses and Aaron on which animals the Israelites may eat: land animals with divided hooves that chew cud, water creatures with fins and scales, and certain insects; all others are unclean, and touching their carcasses causes ceremonial uncleanness until evening.
rows.current_summary_original: God instructs Moses and Aaron on which animals the Israelites may eat: land animals with divided hooves that chew cud, water creatures with fins and scales, and certain insects; all others are unclean, and touching their carcasses causes ceremonial uncleanness until evening.
rows.concern: The exhaustive food list omits permitted birds and then declares all other animals unclean.
rows.scripture_says: The chapter lists forbidden birds; Deuteronomy explicitly permits clean birds.
rows.proposed_summary: God instructs Moses and Aaron on which animals the Israelites may eat: land animals with divided hooves that chew cud, water creatures with fins and scales, permitted birds, and certain insects; all others are unclean, and touching their carcasses causes ceremonial uncleanness until evening.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 14:11-20: The law expressly permits clean birds while listing prohibited birds, confirming that the dietary rules do not exclude every bird.
rows.translation_context_note: The current bird-list note already describes a list of forbidden species, and Deuteronomy 14 is already linked. The summary contradicts that distinction.
rows.proposed_note: The bird list names prohibited birds; it does not prohibit every bird. Deuteronomy 14:11 and 14:20 explicitly allow clean birds.
existing_cross_references: Deuteronomy 14:3-21: The same list of clean and unclean creatures, with some differences of order and detail.
Genesis 7:2-3: Noah takes clean animals by sevens and unclean by twos, long before Sinai.
Acts 10:9-16: Peter's vision of the sheet, and the voice telling him not to call unclean what God has cleansed.
Ezekiel 4:14: Ezekiel protests that he has never eaten anything unclean in his life.
Daniel 1:8-16: Daniel refuses the king's food and asks for vegetables and water instead.

existing_translation_notes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

These are ritual categories, not verdicts about hygiene, health, or sin. Being unclean is a status that bars a person from the sanctuary until it lapses or is washed off; most cases end at sunset (11:24-25). Ordinary life produced it constantly, and nothing in Leviticus calls an unclean person guilty for being unclean.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מַפְרֶסֶת פַּרְסָה וּמַעֲלַת גֵּרָה (mafreset parsah u-maalat gerah)
existing_translation_notes.note: The text gives observable tests, not reasons. A land animal must have a fully split hoof and bring up the cud, and both are required, which is why the camel and the pig each fail on one count (11:4-7). Water creatures need fins and scales (11:9); insects need jointed legs for hopping (11:21).

Leviticus 11 uses sheqets, a word reserved for these creatures and what touches them. The stronger term toevah, usually rendered abomination, is the one used for moral offenses in Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. English blurs two different Hebrew words into one.

Leviticus 11:13-19 never gives a rule for birds, only a list of about twenty. Nearly all of them are birds of prey, carrion eaters, or waders, and the bat is counted with them. Several of the Hebrew names cannot now be matched to a species with certainty, which is why English versions differ from one another in this list.

Leviticus 11:7 gives the pig its own line because it is the near miss: the hoof is split clean through, but it brings up no cud. Pigs were farmed and eaten all around Israel, and Isaiah 65:4 and 66:17 place the eating of pig flesh inside pagan rites, among the graves and in the sacred groves. Refusing pork became the most visible thing that marked a Jew off from his neighbors in the ancient world.

existing_translation_notes.term: why the clay pot is smashed
existing_translation_notes.note: Leviticus 11:32-36 treats a vessel by what it is made of. Ancient earthenware is porous and cannot be scoured out, so a clay pot or a clay oven that takes uncleanness is broken and thrown away. Wood, cloth, leather, and sackcloth are only rinsed and are clean at sunset, and a spring or a cistern stays clean because running and stored water is not a container. The rule follows the material, not the price of the object.

rows.current_summary: The LORD establishes rules for various bodily discharges; anyone or anything touched by someone with a discharge becomes unclean and requires washing and waiting until evening, with purification offerings required after seven days of cleansing.
rows.current_summary_original: The LORD establishes rules for various bodily discharges; anyone or anything touched by someone with a discharge becomes unclean and requires washing and waiting until evening, with purification offerings required after seven days of cleansing.
rows.concern: One washing, waiting, and offering rule is applied to every discharge and every contact.
rows.scripture_says: Abnormal discharges, semen, and menstruation have distinct rules; the seven-day count and bird offerings apply to specified abnormal discharges.
rows.proposed_summary: The LORD gives distinct purification rules for abnormal discharges, emissions of semen, and menstruation. These include washing, periods of uncleanness, and, for specified abnormal discharges, offerings after seven clean days.
cross_references: Mark 5:25-34: Jesus heals a woman who has bled for twelve years, supplying a specific prolonged-bleeding case alongside Leviticus' distinct discharge rules.
rows.translation_context_note: The current discharge notes already explain this distinction, and Mark 5 is already linked. The summary needs to agree with those notes.
rows.proposed_note: The chapter distinguishes ordinary semen emissions and menstruation from abnormal or prolonged discharges. The offerings after seven clean days belong to the specified abnormal discharges, not every bodily emission.
existing_cross_references: Leviticus 12:1-8: The related law for a woman after childbirth, closing with the same offering.
Numbers 5:1-4: Anyone with a discharge or a skin disease is sent outside the camp.
Leviticus 22:4-7: A priest with a discharge may not eat the sacred offerings until sunset and a washing.
Mark 5:25-34: A woman with a flow of blood for twelve years reaches through the crowd to touch His cloak.
2 Samuel 11:4: Bathsheba is described as purifying herself from her uncleanness.

existing_translation_notes.note: A general term for an abnormal bodily flow, not a named disease. The chapter distinguishes it from ordinary emissions and from menstruation, and prescribes washing, waiting until evening, and for the chronic case a seven-day count and two birds (15:13-15). Mark 5:25 describes a woman under exactly this chapter's long-term condition.

The most common ruling in the chapter, and the one that shows the scale of the system: most uncleanness ended at sundown with a wash. The Hebrew day turns at evening, so the status lapsed the same night. Leviticus 22:6-7 applies the same limit to priests.

existing_translation_notes.term: lest they die by defiling My tabernacle
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: וְלֹא יָמֻתוּ בְּטֻמְאָתָם (ve-lo yamutu betumatam)
existing_translation_notes.note: Leviticus 15:31 gives the reason for the whole chapter: the danger is uncleanness carried into the sanctuary, not uncleanness itself. Numbers 5:1-4 acts on the same principle by moving affected people outside the camp while the tent stands in the middle of it.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁכָּב (mishkav), a bed - מוֹשָׁב (moshav), a seat
existing_translation_notes.note: The rules at 15:4-12 and 15:19-27 work outward by contact: the bed, the seat, the saddle, anyone who touches them, anyone the man spits on, and any clay pot he handles, which is broken. The remedy in almost every case is the same and it is small, wash your clothes, bathe, and be clean at sunset. What the chapter builds is a traceable chain of contact, not a scale of guilt.

existing_translation_notes.term: a discharge of blood for many days
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 15:25-30 cover bleeding outside the monthly cycle or continuing past it, and rule the woman unclean for as long as it lasts, with everything she lies or sits on unclean too. That is the standing of the woman in Matthew 9:20-22, Mark 5:25-34 and Luke 8:43-48, who had bled for twelve years: twelve years in which touching anyone passed the uncleanness on, which is why she comes up behind Him and says nothing.

rows.proposed_note: Verse 6 addresses the person who turns to mediums and says God will cut that person off. Verse 27 addresses the medium or spiritist and commands stoning. The chapter distinguishes the offenses and their stated penalties.
existing_cross_references: Leviticus 18:6-30: The same prohibitions set out without penalties attached.
Deuteronomy 18:9-14: The list of forbidden practices Israel is not to learn from the nations of Canaan.
2 Kings 23:10: Josiah defiles Topheth so no one can make a son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech.
Jeremiah 32:35: High places of Baal in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, where children were offered to Molech.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אוֹב (ʾov) / יִדְּעֹנִי (yiddeʿoni), Greek: ἐγγαστρίμυθος (engastrimythos) / μάντις (mantis), Aramaic: אובא (ʾova) / ידעונא (yidʿona)
existing_translation_notes.note: Spiritist or consulter of the dead; strictly forbidden under penalty of death.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כָּרֵת (karēt), Greek: ἐξολοθρεύω (exolothreuō), Aramaic: כרת (karat)
existing_translation_notes.note: To be removed from the people, sometimes by death, sometimes by exclusion; the text does not always specify which.

existing_translation_notes.term: pass through the fire to Molech
existing_translation_notes.note: Leviticus 20:2-5 sets the death penalty on giving a child to Molech and adds a second penalty for a community that looks the other way. 2 Kings 23:10 has Josiah wrecking the site in the Valley of Ben Hinnom to stop it, and Jeremiah 32:35 names the same place. The practice is treated as importable, not theoretical.

existing_translation_notes.term: I will set My face against
existing_translation_notes.note: A judicial formula, the opposite of the blessing in Numbers 6:25 where the LORD makes His face shine on a person. It appears at 17:10, 20:3, 20:5, and 20:6, always where the community itself might fail to act. Ezekiel 14:8 uses the same phrase.

A legal declaration that the executed person, not the court, bears responsibility for the death. It runs through Leviticus 20 as the closing formula on capital cases. 2 Samuel 1:16 and Matthew 27:25 both use the same idiom.

Leviticus 20:2 and 20:27 assign stoning, and Deuteronomy 17:5-7 gives the procedure. The condemned was taken outside the town gate, at least two witnesses were required, and those witnesses threw first, before the rest of the people, so that a false accuser had to kill with his own hands. Jesus points at that rule at John 8:7. Acts 7:58 shows the witnesses laying their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul so they could throw freely.

Leviticus 20:4-5 anticipates a community that hides its eyes rather than act, and Israel's own record shows it happening at the top. Ahaz sacrificed his son in the fire (2 Kings 16:3) and Manasseh did the same and added sorcery, divination, and mediums (2 Kings 21:6). Josiah finally wrecked the site itself, defiling the Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom so no one could use it again (2 Kings 23:10).

existing_translation_notes.term: If a man lies with a male
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־זָכָר מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה (ve-ish asher yishkav et zakhar mishkevei ishah) - דְּמֵיהֶם בָּם (demeihem bam)
existing_translation_notes.note: Leviticus 20:13 repeats the wording of 18:22 and adds the sentence: both are put to death, and the chapter's closing formula follows, 'their blood is upon them,' which places responsibility for the death on the condemned rather than on the court. Leviticus 20 is the penalty chapter for the practices listed in chapter 18, and it runs the same way through the other cases it takes up. The Greek Old Testament of this verse is the source of the compound Paul uses at 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10.

existing_translation_notes.term: Where Paul's word arsenokoitai comes from
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek (LXX) Leviticus 18:22: μετὰ ἄρσενος οὐ κοιμηθήσῃ κοίτην γυναικός - Greek (LXX) Leviticus 20:13: ὃς ἂν κοιμηθῇ μετὰ ἄρσενος κοίτην γυναικός - Greek: ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai), singular ἀρσενοκοίτης (arsenokoites)
existing_translation_notes.note: Paul's word arsenokoitai, at 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10, means men who lie with males. Literally it is male-bedders: men who engage in sexual acts with other males. Koite is the ordinary Greek word for a bed and the standard term for sexual intercourse, which is how the New Testament itself uses it at Romans 13:13 and Hebrews 13:4. The word is a rare compound, and its two halves stand side by side in the Greek Old Testament of these two verses: Leviticus 18:22 reads meta arsenos ou koimethese koiten gynaikos, and Leviticus 20:13 reads hos an koimethe meta arsenos koiten gynaikos, where arsenos and koiten are adjacent.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: חָלַל (ḥālal), Greek: βεβηλόω (bebēloō), Aramaic: חלל (ḥll)
existing_translation_notes.note: To treat something holy as common or ordinary.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מוּם (mum), a defect - תָּמִים (tamim), whole or sound
existing_translation_notes.note: Leviticus 22:20-25 lists what rules an animal out of an offering: blind, injured, maimed, with a wart, a festering sore or a running sore, and anything with bruised, crushed, torn or cut parts. The same word bars a priest from serving at the altar in 21:17-23, though 21:22 lets him eat the holy food. Malachi 1:8 charges Israel with breaking exactly this rule by bringing the blind and lame animals to the altar.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: קָדַשׁ (qadash), Greek: ἁγιάζω (hagiazō), Aramaic: קדש (qdsh)
existing_translation_notes.note: To set apart as holy; God sanctifies priests and offerings.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: וּבָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְטָהֵר (u-va ha-shemesh ve-taher)
existing_translation_notes.note: A priest made unclean bathes and waits for sundown, and then may eat the holy food again (22:6-7). The Hebrew day begins at evening, so sunset both ends the uncleanness and starts the new day. This is the rhythm behind Mark 1:32, where the crowds come to Jesus after sunset on the Sabbath.

A neder is a promise already made and now owed; a nedavah is given with no obligation behind it. Leviticus 22:23 lets a slightly deformed animal serve as a freewill offering but not in payment of a vow, because a vow names what will be brought. Deuteronomy 23:21-23 warns against making one lightly.

existing_translation_notes.term: not on the same day as its young
existing_translation_notes.note: Leviticus 22:28 forbids slaughtering a parent animal and its offspring on one day, and 22:27 requires a newborn to stay with its mother seven days first. Deuteronomy 22:6-7 gives the matching rule for a bird's nest, releasing the mother before taking the young.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿaser), Greek: δεκάτη (dekatē), Aramaic: מעשר (maʿasar)
existing_translation_notes.note: A tenth part dedicated to God, from crops or herds.
The smallest Hebrew weight unit; twenty gerahs equal one shekel (Exodus 30:13). Approximately half a gram in modern measure.

Every 50th year, after seven sabbatical-year cycles (Leviticus 25). Land returned to original families, Hebrew slaves were freed, and debts cancelled; a structural reset of social and economic inequality. The 'year of the Lord's favor' Jesus proclaims in Luke 4:19 draws directly on jubilee language from Isaiah 61.

Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages. The temple tax was half a shekel (Exodus 30:13); in New Testament reckoning that equaled two denarii / two days' wages.

A fixed price list for redeeming a person vowed to the LORD: fifty shekels for a man aged twenty to sixty, thirty for a woman, twenty and ten for those aged five to twenty, five and three for infants, fifteen and ten for the elderly (27:3-7). At about 11.4 grams a shekel, fifty shekels is roughly 570 grams of silver. Verse 8 lets the priest set a lower figure for anyone who cannot pay.

The largest dry measure, ten ephahs, about 220 liters or a little over six bushels; the word shares its consonants with chamor, a donkey, and a homer is reckoned as a donkey's load. Ezekiel 45:11 fixes the ephah and the bath each at a tenth of it. Leviticus 27:16 prices land by the seed it takes to sow, fifty shekels of silver per homer of barley.

The flock was counted out through a narrow gate while the shepherd touched every tenth animal with his staff to mark it for the tithe (27:32). The owner is forbidden to look them over and pick, or to swap a marked animal for a worse one. Jeremiah 33:13 and Ezekiel 20:37 both use the same picture.

existing_translation_notes.note: The same Hebrew word means a staff and a tribe, and the whole chapter turns on that. Twelve matteh are collected, one per matteh, with each leader's name written on it. English has to choose one word and the pun disappears completely. A leader's staff was his badge of office, cut and carried personally, which is what makes each one identifiable in verse 9.

The almond is the first tree in the land to flower, blossoming in late January or February while everything else is bare, and its name puns with shoqed, watching or being awake. Jeremiah 1:11-12 uses that pun outright. A staff that goes from bare wood to bud, blossom and ripe fruit overnight compresses a whole season of the earliest-waking tree into one night.

The staff is put back in front of the Testimony and stored permanently, in the same place as the jar of manna (Exodus 16:33-34). Hebrews 9:4 lists all three items together: the jar of manna, Aaron's budded staff and the tablets. These were the physical archive of the disputes God had already settled, kept where the disputes had been settled.

The people's reaction in verses 12 and 13 is not repentance but panic about proximity: anyone who comes near the tabernacle dies, so are we all going to die? Chapter 18 opens as the direct answer to that question, assigning the Levites as the buffer who bear the risk on everyone else's behalf. The chapter division cuts a single exchange in half.

existing_translation_notes.note: The second count comes to 601,730 against the first count's 603,550, a drop of 1,820 across thirty-eight years, and it counts an entirely different set of men: every one from the first census except Caleb and Joshua has died (26:64-65). Simeon falls hardest, from 59,300 to 22,200, and Manasseh rises most, from 32,200 to 52,700. The purpose is stated in verses 52 to 56: this roll, not the old one, is what the land will be divided by.

The allotment worked in two steps. The size of each tribe's share was fixed by its number in this census, larger tribes getting more land, and then the lot decided which piece of country each tribe got (26:54-56). Lots were physical objects, stones or marked pieces, drawn or shaken out of a container; Proverbs 16:33 says the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

existing_translation_notes.term: The line of Korah did not die out
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 11 is a single sentence with long consequences. Korah's sons were not swallowed up with him, and their descendants became temple singers and gatekeepers: Heman the singer is traced back through Korah in 1 Chronicles 6:33-37, and eleven psalms carry the heading of the sons of Korah, among them Psalms 42, 44 to 49 and 84.

The chapter is not a list of individuals but of clans, each named for a founding ancestor, and the counts are given by clan. This was the working unit of Israelite society between the household and the tribe: it held land together, supplied the kinsman-redeemer, and provided the men who answered a muster. Achan is identified through exactly this ladder, tribe then clan then household then man (Joshua 7:16-18).

rows.concern: "Always stand" can make a personal vow appear to override prohibitions such as child sacrifice.
rows.scripture_says: The chapter makes vows binding and defines when a father or husband may annul them. Other Torah laws provide atonement for rash oaths and forbid child sacrifice.
rows.proposed_summary: Moses gives laws on binding vows and the circumstances in which a father or husband may annul a woman's vow. The chapter also states that the vows of widows and divorced women are binding.

rows.proposed_note: These rules address whether a vow is binding or can be annulled within a household. They do not turn a forbidden act into a lawful one. Leviticus 5:4-6 provides confession and atonement for rash oaths, and Deuteronomy 12:31 condemns child sacrifice.

existing_translation_notes.note: Two different undertakings. A neder is a positive promise to give or do something, usually an offering. An issar is a binding restriction a person puts on themselves, going without something, which is why verse 13 links it to denying oneself. The Nazirite vow of chapter 6 is both at once. Both were legally enforceable, which is why this chapter exists.

existing_translation_notes.term: He must not break his word
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ (lo yachel devaro), he shall not profane his word
existing_translation_notes.note: The Hebrew verb is the one used for profaning something holy. A man's spoken undertaking is treated as a sacred object he can desecrate, which is a stronger idea than breaking a promise. In a world with almost no written contracts, an oath was the enforcement mechanism, and that is why Scripture takes false swearing so seriously.

existing_translation_notes.term: On the day he hears of it
existing_translation_notes.note: The window for a father or husband to cancel a vow is a single day, the day he learns of it (30:5,8,12). Silence past that day confirms it permanently. And if he cancels it late, after having already let it stand, verse 15 puts the liability on him: he bears her guilt. The rule protects the woman from being bound to something the household cannot honour, and it stops a man from using the power casually.

Verse 9 states the exception without qualification: whatever a widow or a divorced woman binds herself to stands. She is answerable to no father and no husband and her word is her own. Anna in Luke 2:36-37 is a widow living permanently at the temple in fasting and prayer, which is the kind of standing commitment this verse leaves open to her.

existing_translation_notes.note: An aron is a chest or box, the same word used for Joseph's coffin in Genesis 50:26. Exodus 25:10-16 gives its size as two and a half cubits by one and a half by one and a half, roughly three and three quarter feet long by two and a quarter high and deep, made of acacia, overlaid inside and out with gold, and carried on poles that stayed in its rings. Acacia is the hard desert timber available in Sinai.

existing_translation_notes.term: Levi has no portion or inheritance
existing_translation_notes.note: Every other tribe received a block of land. Levi received none, and lived instead on the tithe of the other tribes (Numbers 18:21-24) and in forty-eight towns with their surrounding pasture, scattered through everyone else's territory (Numbers 35:1-8; Joshua 21). Verse 9 states the trade plainly: the LORD is his inheritance.

Literally the foreskin of your heart. Circumcision on the eighth day was the physical sign of the covenant cut with Abraham, and an uncircumcised male was to be cut off from his people (Genesis 17:10-14). Verse 16 applies the same operation to the inner man, as Deuteronomy 30:6 and Jeremiah 4:4 and 9:25-26 do.

A ger is a resident alien, someone living permanently in Israel who holds no clan land and therefore has no family to fall back on, which is why the law names him alongside the widow and the fatherless. He gleans the corners and the fallen fruit (Leviticus 19:9-10), rests on the sabbath (Exodus 20:10), stands under one law with the native-born (Leviticus 24:22), and may eat the Passover if circumcised (Exodus 12:48).

The figure comes from the household list in Genesis 46:8-27, repeated in Exodus 1:5. The Greek Septuagint reads seventy-five in both places, and that is the number Stephen gives when he retells the story in Acts 7:14.
