existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מוֹת יוּמָת (mot yumat), 'he shall surely be put to death'
existing_translation_notes.note: The chapter attaches this sentence to one crime, persuading Israel to serve other gods, and it applies it three ways: to a prophet whose sign comes true (13:5), to a family member who does it in private (13:9-10), and to a whole town (13:15). The procedure is not a lynching. Verse 13:14 requires that you inquire, investigate and interrogate thoroughly, and 17:6 fixes the evidence standard at two or three witnesses with never a conviction on one.

existing_translation_notes.term: Purge the evil from your midst
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: וּבִעַרְתָּ הָרָע מִקִּרְבֶּךָ (u-viarta ha-ra miqqirbekha)
existing_translation_notes.note: A fixed closing formula on a completed case, used at 13:5, 17:7, 17:12, 19:19, 21:21, 22:21 and 24:7. The verb baar means to burn away or sweep out. It always follows a verdict and a stated procedure rather than standing on its own as a command to act, and Paul quotes the Greek of it at 1 Corinthians 5:13 when he tells the Corinthians to remove a man from the congregation.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵת (ot o mofet), a sign or a wonder
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 13:1-3 set a test that runs the other way from the one at 18:21-22. There, a prediction that fails marks a false prophet. Here the sign does come about, and the man is still to be rejected, because of what he says next: let us follow other gods. The chapter states the reason plainly at 13:3, that the LORD is testing whether Israel loves Him with all their heart.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת (ir hannidachat), 'the city that is led astray'
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 13:12-18 handle a whole town that has turned to other gods. The plunder is gathered in the public square and burned with the city as a whole burnt offering, nothing is taken, and the site is left a permanent ruin never to be rebuilt (13:16). Joshua 6:17-19 applies the same rule to Jericho, and Joshua 7 records Achan taking from the ban there and what followed.

rows.current_summary: Moses lists who cannot enter the LORD's assembly - including the emasculated, those born of forbidden marriages, Ammonites, and Moabites - while permitting Edomites and Egyptians after certain generations. He then instructs the people on camp purity, treatment of refugees, prohibitions on prostitution and interest-charging, proper vow-keeping, and gleaning rights in neighbors' fields.

He then instructs the people on camp purity, treatment of refugees, prohibitions on prostitution and interest-charging, proper vow-keeping, and gleaning rights in neighbors' fields.
rows.concern: The summary narrows an uncertain birth-status term to "forbidden marriages" and leaves assembly membership undefined.
rows.scripture_says: The app translates the term as illegitimate birth and sets restrictions on entering the LORD's assembly; it does not define a general category of guilt for children.
rows.proposed_summary: Moses gives restrictions on entry to the LORD's assembly, including people of illegitimate birth, Ammonites, and Moabites, and specifies when Edomite and Egyptian descendants may enter. He also gives laws on camp purity, refugees, lending, vows, and neighboring fields.
cross_references: Ruth 4:13-17: Ruth marries Boaz and bears Obed, David's grandfather, supplying a family-history passage to read alongside the descent restrictions.
Isaiah 56:3-7: The LORD promises covenant-keeping eunuchs and foreigners a place in His house and accepted worship, supplying context for assembly restrictions.
Acts 8:26-39: Philip explains the good news about Jesus to an Ethiopian eunuch and baptizes him, providing a later account of a eunuch's reception.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Ruth and Isaiah references are useful and already present, but no note explains the disputed term or the scope of assembly membership. Keep the proposed summary tied to the base translation rather than silently choosing a narrower definition.
rows.proposed_note: The Hebrew birth-status term is rendered differently in English translations, including illegitimate birth or birth from an unlawful union. This legal restriction is not a statement that a child personally committed the parents' sin. Ruth and Isaiah 56 are important context for the chapter's language about descent and belonging.
existing_cross_references: Numbers 22:1-6: Balak of Moab sends for Balaam to curse Israel, the reason given in 23:4.
Nehemiah 13:1-3: This law is read aloud, and everyone of foreign descent is separated from Israel.
Ruth 4:13-17: Ruth the Moabitess bears Obed, the grandfather of David.
Isaiah 56:3-5: The eunuch who keeps the covenant is given a name in God's house better than sons and daughters.
Exodus 22:25: Do not act as a creditor or charge interest to a poor man among My people.

existing_translation_notes.term: Do not hand back a runaway slave
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: לֹא־תַסְגִּיר עֶבֶד אֶל־אֲדֹנָיו (lo tasgir eved el-adonav), 'you shall not hand over a slave to his master'
existing_translation_notes.note: Deuteronomy 23:15-16 forbids returning an escaped slave, orders that he be allowed to settle in whatever town he chooses, and adds 'do not oppress him.' Every other surviving law code of the region runs the opposite way. The laws of Hammurabi of Babylon, carved about 1750 BC and now in the Louvre, make it a capital offence to bring a slave out through the city gates (law 15) or to shelter a runaway and refuse to surrender him when the officer demands it (law 16), and law 17 pays a two-shekel reward to anyone who catches one and brings him back. The Torah offers no reward and orders no return.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: קְהַל יְהוָה (qehal YHWH), the assembly of the LORD
existing_translation_notes.note: The qahal is Israel gathered as a congregation, not the population at large and not the land. Exclusion at 23:1-8 removed a man from that standing; it did not put him outside Israel. The same passage admits Edomites and Egyptians in the third generation and gives the reasons, Edom is your brother and you lived as a foreigner in Egypt (23:7-8). Isaiah 56:3-5 takes up the eunuch of 23:1 by name and promises him a memorial in God's house better than sons and daughters.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מוֹאָב (Moav) - בֶּן־עַמִּי (Ben-Ammi), 'son of my kin'
existing_translation_notes.note: Both nations descend from Lot by his daughters after Sodom, and Genesis 19:37-38 records the names given to the two sons. They held the plateau and the deep valleys east of the Dead Sea, on Israel's approach route from the wilderness. Deuteronomy 23:4 states the charge against them: they met Israel with no food or water, and they hired Balaam of Pethor to curse them (Numbers 22:1-6). Ruth 4:13-17 then has a Moabite woman become great-grandmother to David.

Both words are built on the root for holy, so these were people formally attached to a sanctuary rather than street traders, and 23:17 forbids Israel to supply either. Genesis 38:21-22 uses qedeshah of the woman Judah's friend goes back to look for. 1 Kings 14:24 reports the qadesh present in the land under Rehoboam, and 15:12 has Asa driving them out. Hosea 4:14 charges the men of Israel with sacrificing alongside such women.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה (etnan zonah), 'the hire of a harlot' - מְחִיר כֶּלֶב (mechir kelev), 'the price of a dog'
existing_translation_notes.note: Where English versions of 23:18 read 'male prostitute,' the Hebrew word is dog. The verse refuses both payments as an offering in the house of the LORD for any vow, and calls both detestable to Him. Micah 1:7 uses etnan the same way, of harlot's wages gathered into an idol and burned back out of it.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נֶשֶׁךְ (neshekh), 'a bite,' from נָשַׁךְ (nashakh), to bite
existing_translation_notes.note: The noun for interest is built on the verb to bite, and 23:19 uses both, closing with 'anything that may be lent for interest' in the verb form. The ban covers money, food, and anything else, and it runs toward a brother Israelite; 23:20 permits interest toward a foreigner. Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:36-37 state the same rule, and Leviticus pairs it with a second word, tarbit, increase.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: קָמָה (qamah), standing grain - חֶרְמֵשׁ (chermesh), a sickle
existing_translation_notes.note: Deuteronomy 23:24-25 lets any passer-by eat his fill of a neighbor's grapes or pull heads of grain by hand, and draws the line at the container and the tool: no basket, no sickle. That marks off a traveler's meal from a harvest. It is the law the disciples are keeping at Matthew 12:1 when they pluck heads of grain crossing the fields, which is why the objection raised against them is about the sabbath and not about theft.

rows.current_summary: Jabin of Hazor rallies multiple northern kings and their armies against Israel; Joshua defeats them at the Waters of Merom, then destroys Hazor and captures all the royal cities, eliminating their kings and populations as the Lord commanded. Joshua conquers the entire region from Mount Halak to Baal Gad, destroys the Anakites, and distributes the land to Israel's tribes.
rows.current_summary_original: Jabin of Hazor rallies multiple northern kings and their armies against Israel; Joshua defeats them at the Waters of Merom, then destroys Hazor and captures all the royal cities, eliminating their kings and populations as the Lord commanded. Joshua conquers the entire region from Mount Halak to Baal Gad, destroys the Anakites, and distributes the land to Israel's tribes.
rows.concern: "Destroys the Anakites" omits the explicit surviving populations and can imply their total extinction.
rows.scripture_says: Joshua removes the Anakim from Israel's hill country; some remain in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod.
rows.proposed_summary: Joshua defeats the northern alliance at Merom, destroys Hazor, and captures its allied cities. He removes the Anakim from Israel's hill country, while some remain in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. The chapter closes with the land allotted to Israel and rest from war.
cross_references: Numbers 13:28-33: The spies report fortified cities and descendants of Anak, identifying the people discussed in Joshua's later conquest account.
1 Samuel 17:4: Goliath comes from Gath, one of the cities named in Joshua 11's qualification about surviving Anakim.
Joshua 13:1-6: The LORD tells the aged Joshua that much territory remains unpossessed, including Philistine cities, qualifying an unrestricted reading of conquest summaries.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Anakim note already names the surviving cities, but the summary drops the qualification. Joshua 13 also prevents an unqualified reading of the whole-land formula.
rows.proposed_note: Verse 22 explicitly leaves Anakim in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. The conquest summary must be read alongside that limit and the later account of territory still remaining, rather than as the extinction of every Anakite.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 15:16: The land is left alone for four generations 'for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete', the stated reason this campaign happens when it does and not earlier.
Deuteronomy 9:4-5: Not for your righteousness, Moses says, but for the wickedness of these nations and to keep the promise sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Deuteronomy 20:16-18: The command 11:12 says Joshua was carrying out, given there with the reason attached: so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods.
Deuteronomy 7:1-2: The seven nations are named and the order to devote them to destruction is given, which is what 11:15 says Joshua left nothing undone of.
Judges 4:1-3: A later Jabin of Hazor with nine hundred iron chariots oppresses Israel for twenty years, in the city 11:10-11 burned to the ground.

existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 5 and 7 put the whole northern coalition in one camp at the waters of Merom, in the uplands of Galilee north-west of the Sea of Galilee. It is one of the few places in that broken country with room to assemble horses and chariots in numbers. Verse 7 says Joshua and his whole army came on them there suddenly.

Verse 10 calls Hazor the head of all those kingdoms, and the site bears it out: Tel Hazor in upper Galilee is the largest ancient mound in Israel, roughly two hundred acres with an upper citadel and a walled lower city, sitting on the trade road from Egypt to Mesopotamia. Yigael Yadin excavated it from 1955 to 1958 and found a violent destruction layer with burned mudbrick and smashed statuary. Verse 11 says Joshua burned Hazor with fire, and only Hazor.

Verses 6 and 9 have Israel cripple the captured horses by cutting the tendon at the back of the hock and burn the chariots rather than keep them. Chariots were the dominant weapon of the coalition and the one thing Israel could have taken over. The order removes the technology from the field instead, which is the same policy Deuteronomy 17:16 sets for Israel's future kings.

Verses 11 to 15 show that the ban was not one blanket rule applied the same way everywhere. Hazor alone is burned. The other towns still standing on their mounds are left standing (verse 13), and verse 14 says Israel took the livestock and the goods of those cities as plunder for themselves. The account insists Joshua left nothing undone of what Moses commanded, and what Moses commanded was this specific about what burns and what is kept.

Verses 21 and 22 clear the Anakim out of Hebron, Debir and Anab in the hill country. These are the tall clans the twelve reported on at Numbers 13:28 and 33, and Deuteronomy 9:2 quotes the proverb about them: who can stand before the sons of Anak? Verse 22 records where the survivors went, to Gaza, Gath and Ashdod, which is the town Goliath of Gath comes from in 1 Samuel 17.

rows.current_summary: The remaining northern tribes receive their allotted territories: Simeon within Judah's borders, followed by Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, with specified town lists and boundaries for each. Joshua is then given Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, completing the land division overseen by Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh.
rows.current_summary_original: The remaining northern tribes receive their allotted territories: Simeon within Judah's borders, followed by Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, with specified town lists and boundaries for each. Joshua is then given Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, completing the land division overseen by Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh.
rows.concern: The remaining tribes are all called northern, although Simeon is inside southern Judah.
rows.scripture_says: Simeon's towns lie within Judah's allotment; the chapter also assigns the other remaining tribes.
rows.proposed_summary: The remaining tribes receive their allotted territories: Simeon within Judah's borders, followed by Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, with specified town lists and boundaries for each. Joshua is then given Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, completing the land division overseen by Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh.
cross_references: Joshua 15:20-32: Judah's southernmost towns are listed in the Negev, establishing the southern geography of the territory within which Simeon receives towns.
rows.translation_context_note: The existing Simeon note explicitly locates it in the south. The summary contradicts that note.
rows.proposed_note: Simeon's inheritance lay inside Judah's territory. The tribes assigned in this chapter were not all in the north.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 49:5-7: Simeon and Levi are to be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel.
Joshua 21:9-16: Towns for the priests are taken out of Judah and Simeon, inside the same southern territory.
Judges 1:34: The Amorites press the people of Dan back into the hill country and will not let them come down to the plain.
Judges 18:1-31: Dan sends out spies, takes Laish in the far north, and renames the town Dan.
Matthew 4:13-16: The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, Galilee of the Gentiles, where the people saw a great light.

existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 1 and 9 give Simeon no block of its own. Its towns sit inside Judah's southern territory because Judah's share had been drawn too large, and the tribe is steadily absorbed; by the time of the kings Simeon has almost stopped appearing as a separate people. Jacob had said of Simeon and Levi that he would divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Genesis 49:7), and both tribes end up living inside other men's land.

Verse 13 puts this village on Zebulun's border in the hills of lower Galilee, a few miles north-east of Nazareth. It is the home town of the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, named as such at 2 Kings 14:25, where he foretells Jeroboam II restoring Israel's northern border. The man sent to Nineveh came from a hill village in Galilee.

Verse 22 sets Tabor on Issachar's border, at the point where Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali meet. It is a bare dome of a hill rising about 1,886 feet straight out of the flat Jezreel plain, steep on every side and visible from a long way off. Barak musters ten thousand men on it and comes down off it into Sisera's chariots (Judges 4:6-14), which is the whole of the tactic: chariots cannot climb it and cannot fight on the slope.

Verses 40 to 46 give Dan a small allotment on the coastal plain, squeezed between Judah, Ephraim and the Philistine towns of Ekron and Timnah, and verse 47 records that the tribe lost it and went north instead. They took Leshem by the sword and renamed it Dan after their ancestor. Judges 18 tells the same migration at length and calls the town Laish; it sits at the far north of the country over the largest spring feeding the Jordan, and from then on the phrase from Dan to Beersheba means the whole land.

Verses 49 and 50 give Joshua his portion last, after every tribe has been served, and he asks for one particular town in the hill country of Ephraim instead of drawing it by lot. Verse 50 says he had to rebuild it before he could live in it. He is buried there at the end of the book (24:30).

rows.current_summary: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bokim for breaking covenant and disobeying his commands; after Joshua's death, a new generation abandons the LORD for foreign gods, prompting him to give them over to raiders and establish a cycle where judges save them temporarily but they return to idolatry after each judge dies.
rows.current_summary_original: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bokim for breaking covenant and disobeying his commands; after Joshua's death, a new generation abandons the LORD for foreign gods, prompting him to give them over to raiders and establish a cycle where judges save them temporarily but they return to idolatry after each judge dies.
rows.concern: The Judge note categorically says a shofet was not a courtroom official, even though the book expressly describes Deborah receiving Israel for judgment.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 2 presents judges as deliverers; Judges 4:4-5 gives Deborah judicial authority and says Israelites came to her for judgment. The role includes more than one function.
rows.proposed_summary: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bokim for breaking covenant and disobeying his commands; after Joshua's death, a new generation abandons the LORD for foreign gods, prompting him to give them over to raiders and establish a cycle where judges save them temporarily but they return to idolatry after each judge dies.
cross_references: Judges 4:4-5: Deborah is both a prophet and a judge, and Israelites come to her for judgment, showing that the judges' role includes judicial decisions.
Deuteronomy 16:18-20: Israel must appoint judges who judge fairly, reject bribes, and pursue justice, establishing the judicial function associated with the title.
rows.translation_context_note: The takeaway can remain. Replace the note's exclusion with: 'In Judges the title can include deliverance, leadership, and judicial decisions; Deborah is both prophet and judge.' Do not turn the military role of some judges into a denial of Deborah's judicial authority.
rows.proposed_note: The Hebrew shofet can describe a ruler or someone who gives judgment. In Judges, God raises deliverers against Israel's oppressors, but their role is not limited to warfare. Deborah is both a prophet and a judge; Israelites come to her for judgment (4:4-5). The title therefore includes judicial authority as well as leadership and deliverance.
existing_cross_references: Joshua 24:29-31: Joshua dies at a hundred and ten and is buried at Timnath-serah, and Israel served the LORD all his days.
Deuteronomy 7:1-5: Devote them to destruction, make no covenant with them, and tear down their altars, pillars, and Asherim.
Exodus 34:12-16: Make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land, or their daughters will draw your sons after their gods.
Numbers 33:55: If you do not drive out the inhabitants, those you let remain will be barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides.
Psalm 106:34-42: They did not destroy the peoples, but mixed with the nations, learned their works, and served their idols.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל (baal), lord or master; plural בְּעָלִים (bealim) - עַשְׁתָּרוֹת (Ashtaroth)
existing_translation_notes.note: Baal means lord or master, and he was the Canaanite storm god, held to send the rain that every harvest depended on; the plural in verse 11, the Baals, reflects the fact that each locality had its own. His worship ran on the farming year, and his prophets on Carmel cut themselves with swords and lances until the blood ran (1 Kings 18:28). Ashtoreth, plural Ashtaroth, was the goddess set beside him, named at 1 Kings 11:5 as the goddess of the Sidonians and served with sexual rites; the Philistines put Saul's armour in her temple (1 Samuel 31:10). Verse 13 says Israel forsook the LORD and served both.

Malakh means one who is sent, a messenger, and the word is used of human couriers as readily as of heavenly ones; the Greek angelos behind the English angel means the same thing. In verse 1 the messenger comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and speaks in the first person as God, saying I brought you up out of Egypt and I will never break My covenant with you. The same figure appears to Gideon (6:11-22) and to Manoah and his wife (13:3-21), and in each case the person addressed reacts as though he has met God Himself.

The place gets its name in verse 5 from what happened there, which is how a great many places in Scripture are named. Israel hears the charge, weeps, and sacrifices, and the site carries the word for weeping from then on. The same pattern names Bethel, Beersheba, Massah, Meribah, and the Valley of Achor.

A shofet was not a courtroom official. The word covers ruling and setting things right, and in this book it names a deliverer raised up for a particular crisis who then led that part of Israel for the rest of his life. None of them was elected, none inherited the office, and none ruled the whole nation. The book covers roughly three centuries between Joshua and Samuel.

existing_translation_notes.term: Played the harlot after other gods
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 17 does not say Israel experimented with other religions; it uses zanah, the ordinary verb for prostitution, and applies it to the nation. The image runs right through the prophets, most of all in Hosea, because the covenant at Sinai was framed as a marriage bond with exclusive claims. The word is chosen to say that this is betrayal of a person, not a change of opinion.

direct_references: Judges 2:16-19: The LORD raises judges to deliver Israel from its enemies, but the people return to other gods after each judge dies, establishing the book's recurring pattern.

rows.current_summary: Gideon appeases angry Ephraimites, pursues and defeats the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, and punishes Sukkoth and Peniel for refusing aid; he refuses kingship but collects gold that becomes an idol in Ophrah. After Gideon dies, Israel abandons the LORD and forgets his deliverance.
rows.current_summary_original: Gideon appeases angry Ephraimites, pursues and defeats the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, and punishes Sukkoth and Peniel for refusing aid; he refuses kingship but collects gold that becomes an idol in Ophrah. After Gideon dies, Israel abandons the LORD and forgets his deliverance.
rows.concern: The summary blurs Gideon with the object he made. The Ephod note also identifies Gideon's artifact too precisely by importing the high-priestly garment's form and the entire captured-gold weight.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 8:26 records 1,700 shekels of earrings; 8:27 says Gideon made an ephod, set it in Ophrah, and Israel went astray after it. The ephod became a snare to Gideon and his household.
rows.proposed_summary: Gideon appeases Ephraim, defeats the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, and punishes Succoth and Penuel for refusing aid. He refuses kingship but makes a gold ephod and places it in Ophrah; Israel worships the ephod, which becomes a snare to Gideon and his household. After his death, Israel turns to the Baals and forgets the LORD's deliverance.
cross_references: Exodus 28:6-30: The prescribed priestly ephod is a woven garment associated with Aaron's breastpiece of judgment, providing the priestly background for the object named in Gideon's story.
Judges 17:5: Micah makes an ephod and household idols for his private shrine and appoints his son as priest, another use of an ephod within the book's accounts of unauthorized worship.
Judges 18:17-20: The Danites take Micah's ephod along with his images, and his priest gladly joins them, continuing the story of religious objects diverted into private and tribal worship.
rows.translation_context_note: Distinguish the priestly garment prescribed in Exodus from Gideon's artifact. Judges names it an ephod and describes its idolatrous use, but does not explain its exact shape, whether it was wearable, or how all the gold was incorporated. Do not make Gideon himself the idol.
rows.proposed_note: Exodus 28 describes the high priest's ephod as a garment associated with the breastpiece of judgment. Judges 8:27 uses the same word for the object Gideon made and placed in Ophrah, but does not describe its exact shape or say whether it was wearable. Verse 26 weighs the collected earrings at 1,700 shekels; the account does not explain how that gold was incorporated. Israel's idolatrous attachment is to the ephod. It becomes a snare to Gideon and his household; Gideon himself is not described as becoming an idol.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 32:22-31: Jacob wrestles until daybreak and names the place Peniel, because he saw God face to face.
Exodus 28:6-30: The ephod of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet, with the breastpiece and the Urim and Thummim set in it.
Deuteronomy 17:14-20: The law of the king, who must not multiply wives, horses, or silver and gold for himself.
Numbers 31:1-12: Israel's earlier war on Midian, in which the five kings of Midian are killed.
Judges 9:1-6: Abimelech, the son born at Shechem, kills his seventy brothers on one stone and is made king there.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עֹלֵלוֹת (olelot), gleanings of the vineyard
existing_translation_notes.note: Gideon answers an armed complaint with a vine-grower's proverb in verse 2. The olelot are the small clusters left on the vines after the main picking, which the law reserved for the poor and the foreigner and forbade the owner to go back for (Leviticus 19:9-10, Deuteronomy 24:21). He is saying that Ephraim's leftovers beat his own whole harvest, and verse 3 says the flattery worked.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: סֻכּוֹת (Sukkot), booths - פְּנוּאֵל (Penuel), the face of God
existing_translation_notes.note: Both towns stand on the Jabbok in the Jordan valley east of the river, and Jacob named both of them: Peniel where he wrestled through the night and said he had seen God face to face, and Succoth where he built shelters for his livestock (Genesis 32:30, 33:17). They refuse bread to three hundred exhausted men because they expect Gideon to lose and do not want Midianite reprisals afterwards. Verses 16 and 17 record what he does to them on the way back.

Verses 21 and 26 have Gideon strip crescent-shaped pendants from the necks of the kings' camels, along with chains and pendants. Saharon means little moon, and the crescent was one of the commonest ornaments and amulets in that world, worn by people and hung on valuable animals. Isaiah 3:18 lists the same item among the finery stripped from the women of Jerusalem.

Verse 26 weighs the earrings alone at 1,700 shekels. A shekel is a weight, not a coin, about two-fifths of an ounce, so this is roughly forty-three pounds of gold, and it does not count the crescents, pendants, purple garments and camel chains listed with it. The purple is worth noting on its own: that dye came from a sea snail harvested on the Phoenician coast and was among the most costly substances anyone traded in.

The ephod of the law is a garment, not an image: a sleeveless vestment of gold, blue, purple and scarlet worn by the high priest over his robe, with two shoulder pieces and a woven band, and the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim fastened to the front of it (Exodus 28:6-30). Because the means of enquiring of God hung on it, bring the ephod came to mean ask God a question (1 Samuel 23:9-12). Verse 27 has Gideon make one out of forty-three pounds of captured gold and set it up in his home town, and Israel prostitutes itself to it there.

direct_references: Judges 8:23-27: Gideon refuses rule, collects gold earrings, and makes an ephod that Israel worships; the object becomes a snare to Gideon and his household.
rows.implementation_status: Implemented and audited in all 13 languages

implemented_note_changes.note: Exodus 28 describes the high priest's ephod as a garment associated with the breastpiece of judgment. Judges 8:27 uses the same word for the object Gideon made and placed in Ophrah, but does not describe its exact shape or say whether it was wearable. Verse 26 weighs the collected earrings at 1,700 shekels; the account does not explain how that gold was incorporated. Israel's idolatrous attachment is to the ephod. It becomes a snare to Gideon and his household; Gideon himself is not described as becoming an idol. The prescribed garment uses gold, blue, purple, and scarlet, with shoulder pieces and a woven band; the breastpiece containing the Urim and Thummim is fastened to it (Exodus 28:6-30). In 1 Samuel 23:9-12, David calls for the ephod when inquiring of the LORD.

Judges 9:1-6: Abimelech massacres his brothers, Jotham escapes, and the men of Shechem make Abimelech king, beginning the aftermath of Gideon's household.

Judges 18:17-20: The Danites take Micah's ephod along with his images, and his priest gladly joins them, continuing the story of religious objects diverted into private and tribal worship.

After three years, conflict erupts between Abimelek and Shechem; Abimelek destroys the city and its tower, then dies when a woman drops a millstone on his head at Thebez.

rows.proposed_note: Jotham escapes the massacre of Gideon's sons (9:5). At Thebez, a woman's millstone crushes Abimelech's skull, and his armor-bearer then kills him with a sword at his request (9:53-54). Both the woman's blow and the armor-bearer's action belong to the account of his death.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Abimelek), my father is king
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 5 is a dynastic massacre: every rival claimant killed together, on one stone, in one act. Abimelech's own name means my father is king, which is what Gideon had refused to be (8:23), and his claim rests on his mother's family at Shechem rather than his father's house at Ophrah. Jehu does the same thing to Ahab's seventy sons at Samaria, and has their heads sent to him in baskets (2 Kings 10:1-8).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל בְּרִית (Baal-berit), lord of the covenant - אֵל בְּרִית (El-berit), god of the covenant
existing_translation_notes.note: The god of Shechem, named at 8:33 and here in verses 4 and 46, where the same shrine is called the temple of El-berith. Two details show what such a temple was for besides worship: verse 4 has Abimelech drawn seventy shekels of silver out of its treasury to hire men, so it held the town's money, and verse 46 has the townspeople take refuge in its stronghold, so it was also the strongest building they had. Shechem is the town where Joshua had made Israel swear its covenant to the LORD (Joshua 24:25).

The fable in verses 8 to 15 is built out of the four plants everyone listening farmed. The olive, the fig and the vine were the crops a hill farm lived on, slow to grow, worth years of care, and all three are made to say they will not leave their own work to sway over the trees. The atad is a scrubby thorn that gives no fruit and no shade and burns fiercely once alight, which is why the last line of the fable is about fire coming out of it.

Shechem sits in the pass between two mountains: Gerizim on the south, about 2,890 feet, and Ebal on the north, about 3,084 feet. Moses assigned the blessings to Gerizim and the curses to Ebal, and Joshua read the whole law between them (Deuteronomy 11:29, Joshua 8:30-35). Jotham climbs the blessing mountain in verse 7 and shouts a curse down into the pass.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פֶּלַח רֶכֶב (pelah rekhev), the rider stone
existing_translation_notes.note: Household grain was ground between two stones, a fixed lower one and a shaped upper one that a woman worked back and forth with both hands. It is a solid block of basalt, and dropped from a tower it is a killing weight. Verse 53 is remembered well enough that Joab quotes it as a caution about approaching walls generations later (2 Samuel 11:21).

rows.current_summary: Tola and Jair each judge Israel for two decades before the people turn to foreign gods, prompting God to let the Philistines and Ammonites oppress them for eighteen years; after Israel repents and removes idols, the Ammonites gather for war and the Gileadites assemble at Mizpah, promising leadership to whoever attacks first.
rows.current_summary_original: Tola and Jair each judge Israel for two decades before the people turn to foreign gods, prompting God to let the Philistines and Ammonites oppress them for eighteen years; after Israel repents and removes idols, the Ammonites gather for war and the Gileadites assemble at Mizpah, promising leadership to whoever attacks first.
rows.concern: The summary rounds two stated reigns to two decades and makes eighteen years sound like the combined duration of all oppression. The first Ammonites note reverses the Gilead/oppression/river-crossing sequence. An existing note also equated Milcom and Molech without labeling that identification; it now states what 1 Kings 11:5,7 and 2 Kings 23:10 actually name.
rows.scripture_says: Tola judges twenty-three years and Jair twenty-two (10:2-3). Verse 8 locates eighteen years of Ammonite oppression among Israelites east of the Jordan in Gilead; verse 9 then describes attacks across the Jordan.
rows.proposed_summary: Tola judges Israel for twenty-three years and Jair for twenty-two. Israel again serves foreign gods, and the LORD gives them over to Philistine and Ammonite oppression; the Ammonites oppress the Israelites in Gilead for eighteen years. Israel repents and removes its idols, and Gilead's leaders promise leadership to whoever begins the fight against Ammon.
rows.translation_context_note: Keep the Philistine and Ammonite enemies distinct and limit the stated eighteen years to the oppression specified in verse 8. Revise the first Ammonites note so it agrees with the Gilead note and the chapter's sequence.
rows.proposed_note: The chapter gives Tola twenty-three years and Jair twenty-two (10:2-3). It names both Philistine and Ammonite oppressors, but the eighteen years in verse 8 refer to the oppression of Israelites east of the Jordan in Gilead. Verse 9 then reports the Ammonites crossing the Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim.
existing_cross_references: Judges 2:11-19: The repeating pattern of forsaking the LORD, being sold to enemies, crying out, and a judge raised up.
Deuteronomy 32:37-38: Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge? Let them rise up and help you.
1 Samuel 12:10: We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.
Genesis 19:36-38: Lot's two daughters bear Moab and Ben-ammi, the fathers of Moab and Ammon.
Jeremiah 2:28: Where are your gods that you made for yourself? As many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.

existing_translation_notes.note: Ammon descended from Lot through his younger daughter, which is what Genesis 19:38 records, so Israel and Ammon were reckoned distant kin. Their country lay east of the Jordan on the desert edge, with its capital at Rabbah, the site of modern Amman, and their god was Milcom, also called Molech, whose worship took children in fire (1 Kings 11:5-7, 2 Kings 23:10). Verses 7 to 9 have them cross the river and press Gilead for eighteen years.

Verse 17 gathers Israel at Mizpah, and the name means lookout or watchpost, from the verb to keep watch. This is the Gileadite Mizpah east of the Jordan, where Jephthah is made head in 11:11 and where he comes home in 11:34, and it is not the Mizpah in Benjamin where Samuel later gathers the nation (1 Samuel 7:5-6). Genesis 31:49 attaches the same name to the heap of stones Jacob and Laban set up as a boundary, for the reason that the LORD would watch between them.

Verse 6 lists them one by one: the Baals and the Ashtaroth of Canaan, the gods of Aram, of Sidon, of Moab, of Ammon, and of the Philistines. Each name is a real cult with its own rites. Baal was the storm god who was believed to give rain, Ashtoreth the goddess served with sexual rites, Chemosh of Moab and Milcom of Ammon both took children in fire, and Dagon of the Philistines was a god of grain. Israel is not described as vaguely drifting; it is described taking up all of them.

The highland east of the Jordan between the Yarmuk and the Arnon, wooded, well watered, and good for flocks; it was known for balm (Jeremiah 8:22). Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled there, which left them outside the Jordan and first in line when Ammon pushed west. Verse 8 has the Ammonite pressure crush Gilead for eighteen years before it crosses the river.

direct_references: Judges 10:2-9: Tola judges for twenty-three years and Jair for twenty-two; the account locates eighteen years of oppression in Gilead and also reports Ammonite attacks across the Jordan.
Judges 10:16-18: Israel removes its foreign gods, and Gilead's leaders promise leadership to whoever begins the attack against Ammon, setting the immediate background for Jephthah's appointment.

rows.current_summary: Gilead's elders recall Jephthah, the outcast son of a prostitute, to command them against Ammon, and he answers the Ammonite king's land claim by recounting how the LORD gave Israel the land of Sihon. He vows to offer up whatever first comes out of his house if the LORD grants victory; the LORD delivers Ammon and his only daughter comes out to meet him, and after two months mourning her virginity he does to her as he vowed, so Israel's daughters go out each year to lament her.
rows.current_summary_original: Gilead’s elders recall Jephthah, the outcast son of a prostitute, to command them against Ammon, and he answers the Ammonite king’s land claim by recounting how the LORD gave Israel the land of Sihon. He vows to offer up whatever first comes out of his house if the LORD grants victory; the LORD delivers Ammon and his only daughter comes out to meet him, and after two months mourning her virginity he does to her as he vowed, so Israel’s daughters go out each year to lament her.
rows.concern: The vow note calls spoken vows absolutely binding, which can imply that a vow requires an unlawful act. The revision should preserve the vow's burnt-offering language and distinguish the narrative's report from divine approval, without giving the dedication reading equal textual weight.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 11:31 pledges an olah, a burnt offering. Verse 39 says Jephthah did to his daughter as he had vowed. Verse 34 identifies her as his only child; verses 37-39 emphasize her virginity. The Spirit comes upon Jephthah before the vow (11:29-30). The Torah condemns child sacrifice.
rows.proposed_summary: Gilead makes Jephthah its leader, and he disputes Ammon's claim to Israel's land. Before fighting, he vows to offer as a burnt offering whatever comes out of his house to meet him if the LORD grants victory. He defeats Ammon, but his only child, his daughter, comes out to greet him. After two months mourning her virginity, she returns, and he does to her as he vowed. The narrator adds that she had never known a man. Israel's daughters lament her for four days each year.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not worship the LORD through practices such as burning sons and daughters as sacrifices, explicitly prohibiting the kind of act a personal vow might be invoked to excuse.
Deuteronomy 18:10: No one in Israel may sacrifice a son or daughter in the fire, establishing a prohibition that Jephthah's vow cannot override.
Leviticus 18:21: Giving children as sacrifices to Molech is forbidden as profaning God's name, another explicit Torah prohibition of child sacrifice.
Leviticus 5:4-6: Guilt from a thoughtless oath calls for confession and a sin offering through which the priest makes atonement, providing the Torah's response to sinful rash sworn speech.

Leviticus 27:1-8: Special vows involving persons carry monetary valuations, and a priest adjusts the amount for someone too poor to pay, distinguishing these rules from instructions to sacrifice a person.

Leviticus 27:28-29: Devoted things cannot be sold or redeemed, and a person devoted to destruction cannot be ransomed but must be put to death; this concerns cherem, a distinct category from the vow recorded in Judges 11.
Genesis 22:1-14: Abraham is stopped before killing Isaac and offers a ram in his place, contrasting God's intervention here with the vow and its reported fulfillment in Judges 11.
Leviticus 1:3-9: A burnt offering from the herd is slaughtered, cut into pieces, and burned on the altar, establishing the sacrificial meaning of the offering named in Jephthah's vow.
rows.translation_context_note: Retain the burnt-offering vow and its reported fulfillment in the summary. Explain in the note that literal sacrifice is the stronger reading; do not imply equal textual support for dedication or infer obedience from the Torah's prohibition. The virginity clause does not establish continued celibate service. Separate Jephthah's act from divine authorization, and keep ordinary vow valuations distinct from cherem.
rows.proposed_note: Olah in verse 31 means a burnt offering. Verse 39 reports that Jephthah did to his daughter as he had vowed; together, these statements strongly support literal sacrifice, although the killing is not separately described. Her virginity is consistent with death before marriage and motherhood; she was his only child. The lifelong-dedication reading is a less direct alternative: some interpreters read the two clauses in verse 31 as dedication or sacrifice, but that distinction is disputed, and verse 39 does not state a subsequent life of celibacy. The Torah condemns child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10; Leviticus 18:21). A vow cannot authorize it, and recording an act does not establish God's approval. The Spirit comes upon Jephthah before his vow (11:29-30). Leviticus 5:4-6 provides confession and atonement for sinful rash oaths. Leviticus 27:1-8 concerns monetary valuations; cherem in 27:28-29 is distinct and does not authorize a father to kill an innocent daughter through a personal vow.
existing_cross_references: Numbers 21:21-31: Israel asks Sihon for passage, is refused and attacked, and takes his land, the history Jephthah recites.
Deuteronomy 2:19: Do not harass the sons of Ammon or contend with them, for I have given their land to the sons of Lot.
Leviticus 27:1-8: The scale of silver payments for redeeming a person who has been vowed to the LORD.
Deuteronomy 12:31: They burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods, which the LORD hates.
Genesis 22:1-14: Abraham is stopped before he strikes, and a ram caught in the thicket is offered instead.

existing_translation_notes.note: A neder is a promise made to God, usually offering something in return for help, and the law treats it as absolutely binding once spoken: Numbers 30:2 says a man shall not break his word, Deuteronomy 23:21-23 says it is no sin not to vow but delay in paying is charged against you, and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 repeats it. The law also provided a way out that Jephthah does not take. Leviticus 27:1-8 sets a fixed scale of silver by which a person vowed to the LORD is redeemed instead of given: fifty shekels for a man between twenty and sixty, thirty for a woman, ten for a girl between five and twenty, with reduced rates for the very young and the old.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה (ishah zonah), a prostitute
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 1 to 3 turn on inheritance law. Jephthah is Gilead's son by a prostitute, and his half-brothers by the wife expel him with the words you shall have no inheritance in our father's house. Land passed to the sons of the household, and a son with no standing in it had nothing to hold and nowhere to go, so he leaves for Tob, north-east of Gilead, and worthless men gather to him. The same elders who let that happen come looking for him to command their army in verse 6.

Verse 24 has Jephthah name Chemosh in his message about disputed land. Chemosh was the national god of Moab; Numbers 21:29 calls the Moabites the people of Chemosh, Solomon built him a high place east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7), and 2 Kings 3:27 records a king of Moab burning his own heir on the wall. King Mesha's inscription, found at Dhiban in 1868, credits Chemosh with his victories over Israel in his own words.

Verses 39 and 40 close with a yearly practice: the daughters of Israel went out four days every year on account of Jephthah's daughter. Israel kept the memory of what a vow cost by setting aside a fixed period for it, the same way the nation kept fasts and feasts. The book records the custom without excusing the vow that caused it.

direct_references: Judges 11:30-40: Jephthah promises a burnt offering for victory; his only child greets him, and after two months mourning her virginity she returns and he fulfills the vow, followed by Israel's annual lament.
Judges 11:29-30: The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah before he makes his vow, placing the divine empowerment before the sworn promise rather than presenting it as a response to that promise.

rows.current_summary: Ephraim confronts Jephthah over not being called to fight the Ammonites; Jephthah defeats them at the Jordan, using the word "Shibboleth" to identify and kill forty-two thousand Ephraimites. Jephthah leads Israel six years before dying, followed by judges Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon.
rows.current_summary_original: Ephraim confronts Jephthah over not being called to fight the Ammonites; Jephthah defeats them at the Jordan, using the word "Shibboleth" to identify and kill forty-two thousand Ephraimites. Jephthah leads Israel six years before dying, followed by judges Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon.
rows.concern: The summary attributes all 42,000 deaths to the pronunciation test. The Shibboleth note repeats the same overstatement and must be revised with the summary.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 12:4 describes the battle; 12:5-6 describes the ford killings and then gives the total killed 'at that time'. The text does not isolate 42,000 as a separate count from the pronunciation test alone.
rows.proposed_summary: Ephraim confronts Jephthah over the Ammonite war, and Gilead defeats Ephraim. At the Jordan fords, Gileadite guards use 'Shibboleth' to identify and kill fleeing Ephraimites; the chapter reports forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed at that time. Jephthah judges Israel for six years, followed by Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon.
cross_references: Judges 8:1-3: An earlier quarrel over exclusion from battle ends when Gideon's reply calms Ephraim, contrasting with the fighting between Ephraim and Gilead in Judges 12.
Proverbs 15:1: A gentle answer turns away anger, while harsh speech stirs it up, providing a wisdom parallel to the contrasting responses to Ephraim in Judges 8 and 12.
rows.translation_context_note: Retain the reported total and the sequence of battle and ford killings without claiming a separately stated count for either stage.
rows.proposed_note: The guards use Shibboleth to identify fleeing Ephraimites at the Jordan crossings. The chapter reports forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed 'at that time' after describing both the battle and the ford killings (12:4-6). It gives no separate battle and ford totals. The summary should retain the reported count without assigning every death to the pronunciation test.
existing_cross_references: Judges 8:1-3: Ephraim quarrels with Gideon in the same terms for not being called to the fight, and he answers them softly.
Proverbs 15:1: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
Joshua 22:10-34: The eastern tribes build an altar by the Jordan and the rest of Israel nearly goes to war over it.
Judges 3:28: Ehud seizes the fords of the Jordan against Moab and lets no one cross over.
Nehemiah 13:23-24: Half the children of the mixed marriages spoke the language of Ashdod and could not speak the language of Judah.

existing_translation_notes.note: The word itself means an ear of grain, or in other passages a flowing stream, and its meaning is beside the point; it was chosen because it starts with the sh sound that the Ephraimite dialect across the river did not use. A man could claim any tribe he liked, but he could not change how his mouth had been trained to speak since childhood. Verse 6 records the toll: forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed at the crossings, on the evidence of one syllable.

The Jordan runs in a deep, thicketed trench and can only be crossed at a handful of shallow places. Whoever holds the fords controls who gets across, which is why they are seized three separate times in this book (Judges 3:28, 7:24, and here in verse 5). An army cut off from the fords is trapped on the wrong side of the river with nowhere to go.

existing_translation_notes.term: Thirty daughters married outside the clan
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 9 says Ibzan sent thirty daughters out of his clan in marriage and brought thirty wives in from outside for his sons. Marriage was a treaty between households, and daughters going out and wives coming in built a network of obligation across a whole region. Sixty such matches is a record of a man who ruled by alliance, which is why the writer counts them the way he counts years in office.

Verse 14 counts Abdon's forty sons and thirty grandsons riding seventy donkeys, and 10:4 does the same for Jair's thirty sons. This is a note about standing, not transport: before horses were common in Israel the donkey was the mount of a man of rank, and a household that could put seventy men on their own animals was wealthy and settled. Zechariah 9:9 draws on the same picture of a king coming on a donkey.

cross_references: Numbers 6:1-21: Nazirite separation includes uncut hair, restrictions on grape products and corpse contact, and offerings and shaving when the period ends, supplying the legal background for Samson's dedication.

rows.translation_context_note: Keep lifelong dedication from the womb distinct from the ordinary time-limited Nazirite vow in Numbers 6. Retain 'begin' rather than presenting full liberation as accomplished by Samson.
rows.proposed_note: The announcement says Samson will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines (13:5); it does not promise that he will complete their liberation. His dedication begins in the womb and lasts for life. Numbers 6 also describes voluntary Nazirite vows that end after a stated period with offerings and the shaving of the head. Samson's lifelong calling is therefore distinct from that ordinary pattern.

existing_translation_notes.term: A Nazirite to God from the womb
existing_translation_notes.note: From nazar, to separate. Numbers 6:1-21 sets out the vow in full: nothing at all from the grapevine, not wine, not vinegar, not fresh or dried grapes, not even the skins or the seeds; no razor on the head for the whole term; and no going near a dead body, not even a father's or mother's. It was normally taken for a set period and ended at the sanctuary with offerings and the shaving of the head, the hair burned under the fellowship sacrifice. Samson's is imposed for life and begins before he is born.

Zorah and Eshtaol are villages in the Sorek valley on the western edge of the hill country, looking straight out onto Philistine territory, which is why this family lives under Philistine rule. Mahaneh-dan means camp of Dan and lies between the two. Dan never took the coastal allotment it was given, because the Amorites forced the tribe back up into the hills (Judges 1:34), and Judges 18:11-12 has six hundred armed Danites camping at this same spot on their way north to take Laish instead.

Malakh means one who is sent, a messenger, and the word is used of human couriers as readily as of heavenly ones. Manoah's wife first reports him as a man of God, the ordinary term for a prophet, and Manoah only draws his conclusion after the figure goes up in the altar flame. His reaction in verse 22, that they will die because they have seen God, rests on the rule stated in Exodus 33:20 and on Jacob's surprise in Genesis 32:30 at surviving the encounter.

existing_translation_notes.term: Why do you ask my name
existing_translation_notes.note: The word rendered beyond comprehension is peli, from pala, to be wonderful or out of reach. The chapter then uses the same root twice more: verse 19 says the LORD acted wondrously, maphli laasot, while Manoah and his wife watched. The same root supplies the first title in Isaiah 9:6, pele yoets, Wonderful Counsellor. The answer and the sign are the same word.

existing_translation_notes.term: A burnt offering and a grain offering on a rock
existing_translation_notes.note: An olah is the whole burnt offering, the one sacrifice burned entirely with no portion eaten by priest or worshipper; the name means that which goes up. A minchah is a grain offering of flour and oil. Manoah uses a bare rock rather than a built altar, exactly as Gideon did when the angel touched the meat and bread with his staff and fire came up out of the rock (Judges 6:19-21).

Judges 13:19-25: Manoah offers to the LORD, the angel ascends in the flame, and Samson is later born and blessed as the Spirit begins to stir him, tracing the promise's fulfillment.

rows.current_summary: Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah, insists on marrying her despite his parents' objections, and tears apart a lion with his bare hands on the way there. At his wedding feast he poses a riddle to thirty Philistine men, but when his wife coerces him into revealing the answer, the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to kill thirty men in Ashkelon and give their clothes to the riddle solvers; his wife is then given to another man.
rows.current_summary_original: Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah, insists on marrying her despite his parents' objections, and tears apart a lion with his bare hands on the way there. At his wedding feast he poses a riddle to thirty Philistine men, but when his wife coerces him into revealing the answer, the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to kill thirty men in Ashkelon and give their clothes to the riddle solvers; his wife is then given to another man.
rows.concern: The summary says Samson's wife coerces him but omits the Philistines' threat to burn her and her father's household. It also omits the narrator's explanation in verse 4.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 14:4 says the LORD was seeking an occasion against Philistine rule. Verse 15 records the death threat against Samson's wife and her family; verses 16-17 then report her pressure on Samson.
rows.proposed_summary: Samson insists on marrying a Philistine woman, while the narrator says the LORD is seeking an occasion against Philistine rule. At the wedding feast, the Philistine companions threaten to burn his wife and her father's household unless she obtains the riddle's answer. Under that threat she presses Samson, and he tells her. After the answer is disclosed, the Spirit of the LORD empowers Samson; he kills thirty men in Ashkelon and takes their clothes to pay the wager. His wife is then given to his companion.
cross_references: Judges 15:6: The Philistines burn Samson's wife and her father to death, showing that the threatened violence in the wedding story later reaches both of them.
rows.translation_context_note: Preserve the wife's coercive situation rather than making her an unqualified deceiver. Verse 4 describes the LORD's larger purpose; it is not blanket moral approval of every character's action. Separately, distinguish the lion-carcass uncleanness rule in Leviticus 11 from the human-corpse language and close-relative examples of Numbers 6:6-7 rather than stating their scope as identical.
rows.proposed_note: The Philistine companions threaten to burn Samson's wife and her father's household unless she obtains the riddle's answer (14:15). Her pressure on Samson occurs under that threat. Verse 4 separately explains the LORD's purpose in creating an occasion against Philistine rule; that larger purpose does not make every character's conduct a command from God. Leviticus 11:24-28 addresses animal-carcass uncleanness. Numbers 6:6-7 addresses corpse contact for Nazirites and specifically mentions parents and siblings; applying that passage directly to the lion requires interpretation.
existing_cross_references: Deuteronomy 7:3-4: Do not intermarry with them, for they will turn your children away from following Me to serve other gods.
Numbers 6:6-8: A Nazirite shall not go near a dead body all the days of his separation to the LORD.
Leviticus 11:27,39: Whoever touches the carcass of an unclean animal is unclean until the evening.
Judges 3:1-4: The Philistines were left in the land to test Israel and to teach war to those who had not known it.
Genesis 29:27: Complete the week of this one, the seven-day wedding feast behind the seven days of the riddle.

existing_translation_notes.note: A chidah is a saying deliberately built to be hard, and posing them was a contest of wit, not a children's game; the queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with them (1 Kings 10:1), and Proverbs 1:6 lists them among the things wisdom teaches a man to read. Samson's, in verse 14, cannot be solved by thinking, because it describes a private incident nobody else saw. The stake in verses 12 and 13 is thirty linen wraps and thirty changes of clothing, a serious wager for thirty village men.

existing_translation_notes.term: The lion's carcass and the Nazirite rule
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 8 and 9 have Samson turn aside to the dead lion, scoop honey out of it with his hands, eat it as he walks, and give some to his parents without telling them where it came from. Numbers 6:6-7 forbids a Nazirite to go near any dead body at all, even a father's or mother's, and touching a carcass makes any Israelite unclean (Leviticus 11:24-28). The chapter reports his silence about it, and expects the reader to know what has been broken.

Verse 1 has Samson go down to Timnah, a Philistine town in the Sorek valley a few miles down from his home at Zorah; down is literal, since it is a drop from the hill country toward the coastal plain. It had been allotted to Judah and then to Dan (Joshua 15:10, 19:43) and neither held it. Deuteronomy 7:3 forbids marriage with the peoples of the land, which is exactly what his parents say to him in verse 3.

A wedding was not a ceremony but a week of eating and drinking at the bride's town, with the groom's side hosting and thirty local men attached to him as companions (verse 11). Jacob's week for Leah works the same way (Genesis 29:27). The riddle and its wager in verses 12 and 13 are entertainment for the feast, thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes being a substantial stake.

direct_references: Judges 14:3-4: Samson's parents object to his Philistine marriage, while the narrator says the LORD is seeking an occasion against Philistine rule, distinguishing their knowledge from the larger purpose.

Judges 14:12-20: The companions threaten Samson's wife and her father's household to obtain the riddle's answer; she presses him under that threat, and the disclosure leads to Samson's violent payment of the wager.

Judah binds him and hands him over to the Philistines, but the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to break free and kill a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone; God provides water when he nearly dies of thirst.
rows.current_summary_original: Samson's wife is given to another man, prompting him to burn the Philistines' crops with foxes; when they retaliate by killing his wife, he slaughters many of them and hides in a cave. Judah binds him and hands him over to the Philistines, but the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to break free and kill a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone; God provides water when he nearly dies of thirst.
rows.concern: The summary says the Philistines kill Samson's wife but omits her father, and it can flatten the escalation into a simple righteous-retaliation chain.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 15:6 says the Philistines burn both the woman and her father. Verses 3, 7, and 11 put competing justifications for revenge in the characters' own words; verses 14 and 19 separately report divine empowerment and provision.
rows.proposed_summary: Samson finds that his wife has been given to his companion and burns the Philistines' crops. The Philistines burn his wife and her father, and Samson retaliates with a great slaughter. Judah binds him and hands him over, but the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to break free and kill a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone. When he cries out in thirst, God provides water.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 32:35: The LORD claims vengeance and repayment as His own, providing a point of comparison for Samson's personal declarations of retaliation.
Exodus 22:6: The person whose fire consumes stacked or standing grain or a field must make restitution, supplying legal background for the destruction of the Philistines' crops.
rows.translation_context_note: Keep the death of the father as well as the wife. Attribute the retaliatory claims to the speakers; divine empowerment in the battle does not turn every preceding act into a divine instruction. The place-name note should also avoid saying all three names originate in this chapter: Lehi is already used in verse 9 before Ramath-lehi and En-hakkore receive their explicit naming explanations.
rows.proposed_note: The Philistines burn both Samson's wife and her father (15:6). Samson and the men of Judah give their own explanations for the cycle of retaliation, while the narrator separately reports the Spirit's empowerment and God's provision of water. The place-name explanations also differ: Lehi is already named in verse 9; Ramath-lehi and En-hakkore receive explicit naming explanations later in the chapter.
existing_cross_references: Judges 14:19-20: Samson's wife is given to the companion who had been his best man, which sets this chapter going.
Deuteronomy 32:35: Vengeance is Mine and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip.
Exodus 22:6: Whoever starts a fire that spreads into standing grain must make full restitution for what is burned.

Genesis 21:19: God opens Hagar's eyes and she sees a well of water, and she gives the boy a drink.

existing_translation_notes.note: One Hebrew word covers both the fox and the jackal, and translators have to choose. Jackals run in packs and scavenge around towns and ruins, which makes taking them in numbers plausible in a way that trapping three hundred solitary foxes is not. Scripture uses the same word for the animals that haunt a ruined city (Lamentations 5:18) and that feed on the bodies of the fallen (Psalm 63:10). Tied tail to tail in pairs, three hundred animals carry a hundred and fifty torches.

existing_translation_notes.term: The standing grain, the vineyards and olive groves
existing_translation_notes.note: This is the destruction of an entire year in one night, at the worst possible moment. Wheat was cut with a hand sickle, bound, and stacked in the field before threshing, so verse 5 names both the cut stacks and the grain still standing. The vines and olives are worse: they are not an annual crop but decades of capital, and a young olive tree takes years to come into full bearing.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: לֶחִי (Lechi) - Hebrew: עֵין הַקּוֹרֵא (Ein ha-Qore)
existing_translation_notes.note: All three names are made in the chapter itself. Lehi means jawbone, Ramath-lehi means the height of the jawbone, and En-hakkore means the spring of the one who called. The pattern of naming a place after what happened there runs through the whole Old Testament, and it is how a landscape kept its history when almost nobody could read.

existing_translation_notes.term: The ropes became like burnt flax
existing_translation_notes.note: Cord was spun from flax fibre or palm fibre and laid up into rope, and the text stresses that these two were new, at full strength. Flax that has been through a fire keeps its shape until it is touched and then falls apart. The verb used of the Spirit here and in Judges 14:6 and 14:19 is tsalach, to rush or break in on someone, not a gentle arrival.

Circumcision on the eighth day was the physical sign of the covenant made with Abraham (Genesis 17:10-14). It was not unique to Israel; Jeremiah 9:25-26 lists Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and the desert peoples alongside Judah as circumcised in the flesh. The Philistines, who had come to the coast from across the sea, did not practise it, which is why the word becomes the standing insult for them specifically, in Judges 14:3 and in David's question at the Valley of Elah in 1 Samuel 17:26.

direct_references: Judges 15:1-8: Samson burns the Philistines' crops after finding his wife given to another man; they burn both her and her father, and he answers with further slaughter.

Judges 15:11-19: Judah hands Samson over, the Spirit empowers him against the Philistines, and God supplies water after his plea, distinguishing the reported divine help from the characters' claims about retaliation.

rows.current_summary: Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza and tears out the city gates; later, Delilah deceives him into revealing that his strength comes from his uncut hair, and after the Philistines shave his head and blind him, he prays for strength one final time and pulls down the temple, killing himself and thousands of Philistines.
rows.current_summary_original: Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza and tears out the city gates; later, Delilah deceives him into revealing that his strength comes from his uncut hair, and after the Philistines shave his head and blind him, he prays for strength one final time and pulls down the temple, killing himself and thousands of Philistines.
rows.concern: The summary makes uncut hair the source of Samson's strength. The Gaza note also turns the Hebron reference into a definite forty-mile journey and exact elevation gain.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 16:17 links uncut hair to Nazirite dedication. Verse 20 explicitly says the LORD had departed from Samson. Verse 3 identifies a hill in relation to Hebron but gives no mileage or elevation.
rows.proposed_summary: Samson carries away Gaza's gates and later tells Delilah that his uncut hair marks his dedication to God as a Nazirite. After his hair is shaved, his strength leaves him; the narrator says the LORD has departed from him. The Philistines blind and imprison him. He later prays for strength and brings down their temple, dying with thousands of Philistines.
cross_references: Judges 13:5: Samson is designated a Nazirite to God from the womb, and no razor is to touch his head, connecting his uncut hair with his consecration.
Numbers 6:5: Uncut hair belongs to a Nazirite's vowed separation to the LORD, supplying the legal background for Samson's explanation of his hair.
rows.translation_context_note: Present the hair as the sign of dedication, with the narrator's explicit statement that the LORD departed. Label the hill's identification and travel distance as geographical interpretation, or remove the precise forty-mile/three-thousand-foot claim; the verse does not supply those figures.
rows.proposed_note: Samson identifies his uncut hair with his dedication to God as a Nazirite (16:17). After the shaving, the narrator explains that the LORD had departed from him (16:20); the account does not present hair as an independent source of power. Verse 3 places the hill in relation to Hebron but gives neither a travel distance nor an elevation gain. Those numerical estimates depend on identifying the hill geographically.
existing_cross_references: Judges 13:5: The child is to be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and no razor is to come on his head.
Numbers 6:5: All the days of his vow no razor shall touch his head; he shall let the locks of his hair grow long.
1 Samuel 5:1-5: The ark is set in Dagon's temple at Ashdod, and the image falls with its head and hands broken off.
Exodus 11:5: The firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, named as the lowest place in a household.
Hebrews 11:32-34: Samson is named among those who through faith were made strong out of weakness.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר הָעִיר (shaar ha-ir), the city gate
existing_translation_notes.note: Gaza was the southernmost of the five Philistine cities, on the coast road running down to Egypt. The gate was the single heaviest and most valuable piece of a town's defence: two leaves of timber plated or braced, hung on posts sunk into the ground, with a bar dropped across at dusk. Verse 3 has Samson pull out the doors, both posts and the bar together and carry them to a hill facing Hebron, which is roughly forty miles away and three thousand feet higher. The town wakes up with no gate.

Verse 23 names the god the Philistines credit with handing Samson over. Dagon had temples at Gaza and at Ashdod, and his name matches the Hebrew word for grain, dagan; two Israelite towns are called Beth-dagon, house of Dagon (Joshua 15:41, 19:27), which shows how far his worship reached. 1 Samuel 5:2-5 records what happened to his image at Ashdod when the captured ark was set beside it: it fell face down twice, and the second time its head and both hands were broken off on the threshold.

existing_translation_notes.term: The two pillars of the house
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 27 puts about three thousand men and women on the roof watching, and verses 26 and 29 have Samson set his hands on the two central pillars the building rested on. Philistine temples of this kind have been dug up: the one excavated at Tell Qasile, on the northern edge of modern Tel Aviv, has two stone bases for wooden roof pillars set close enough together for one man to reach both at once. Pull those and the roof comes down on everyone standing on it.

Verse 21 has the blinded Samson set to grind in the prison. Daily flour was made by hand between two stones, hours of work every morning, and it was the job of women and slaves; Exodus 11:5 uses the slave girl at the mill as the picture of the very bottom of a household. Putting a captured champion on the mill was a deliberate public humiliation, not just forced labour.

Verse 5 has each of the five Philistine lords offer Delilah 1,100 pieces of silver, so 5,500 in all. Judges 17:10 hires a Levite for ten shekels of silver a year with food and clothing, which puts the offer at several lifetimes of wages. By weight, at about 0.4 ounces a shekel, it is roughly 140 pounds of silver.

direct_references: Judges 16:3: Samson carries Gaza's gates, posts, and bar to a mountain overlooking Hebron; the verse gives the landmark but no mileage or elevation gain.
Judges 16:17-22: Samson connects his hair with Nazirite dedication; after it is shaved, the narrator says the LORD has departed, and the Philistines blind and imprison him.
Judges 16:28-30: Samson asks God to strengthen him before pushing the temple's supporting pillars and dying with the Philistines, placing his plea for strength immediately before the final collapse.

rows.current_summary: Micah restores stolen silver to his mother, who uses part of it to make a silver idol for his shrine; he then hires a young Levite from Bethlehem as his priest, believing this will bring God's blessing.
rows.current_summary_original: Micah restores stolen silver to his mother, who uses part of it to make a silver idol for his shrine; he then hires a young Levite from Bethlehem as his priest, believing this will bring God's blessing.
rows.concern: Two notes assert that the divinely arranged Levite support system had stopped working, presenting an inferred motive as narrated fact and softening the private priesthood's illegality.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 17:7-12 describes a wandering Levite accepting Micah's offer of wages, clothing, and food. Verse 13 gives Micah's own expectation of the LORD's favor. Numbers 3:10 distinguishes the Aaronic priesthood from general Levite status.
rows.proposed_summary: Micah returns stolen silver to his mother, who dedicates it to the LORD but uses part to make an idol. Micah makes a private shrine and hires a wandering Levite as his priest, then assumes the LORD will prosper him. The narrator frames the period as one in which everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
cross_references: Numbers 3:5-10: The Levites are assigned to assist Aaron and his sons, while Aaron and his sons receive the priestly duties, distinguishing Levite status from appointment to the priesthood.
Deuteronomy 18:1-8: Levites receive designated support and may come to minister at the place the LORD chooses, supplying the lawful setting for their service alongside Micah's private arrangement.
Exodus 20:4-6: Making and worshiping images is forbidden, so dedicating Micah's silver to the LORD does not authorize the images made from it.
rows.translation_context_note: The shrine's dedication to the LORD does not make its image or its priesthood authorized. The text describes the Levite's decision to accept a private job; a nationwide collapse of tithes or support is a reconstruction, not the stated cause of his wandering.
rows.proposed_note: Micah's mother dedicates the silver to the LORD while using it for an image; Micah assumes that hiring a Levite guarantees the LORD's favor (17:3-5,13). The chapter reports these actions and Micah's belief without endorsing them. Levite status alone does not confer Aaronic priesthood (Numbers 3:5-10). The chapter reports the Levite accepting wages, clothing, and food; it does not identify a collapse of the national tithe system as the reason for his choice.
existing_cross_references: Exodus 20:4-6: You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness of what is in heaven or on earth, or bow down to them.
Deuteronomy 12:8: You shall not do as we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes.
Numbers 3:5-10: The Levites are given to Aaron and his sons; any outsider who comes near the priesthood is to be put to death.
Deuteronomy 18:1-8: The Levites have no allotment among their brothers, and a Levite may come to the place the LORD chooses and minister there.
Exodus 28:6-30: The ephod made for the high priest, with the breastpiece of judgment and the Urim and Thummim.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פֶּסֶל (pesel), a hewn image - מַסֵּכָה (massekah), a poured image
existing_translation_notes.note: Two different manufacturing methods, named separately because the law names both. A pesel is carved, from the verb to hew, usually in wood or stone; a massekah is cast, from the verb to pour, in molten metal over a core. Deuteronomy 27:15 puts a public curse on the man who makes either one, and Exodus 20:4 forbids them outright. Verse 3 is the sting of this chapter: the silver is dedicated to the LORD, by name, and then spent on exactly what He forbade.

Verse 5 has Micah make an ephod and teraphim for his private shrine. Teraphim are household images, kept in the home rather than at a sanctuary, and Scripture shows them used for divination (Ezekiel 21:21) and treated as valuable enough to steal: Rachel takes Laban's and hides them in a camel saddle (Genesis 31:19, 34). At least some were man-sized, since Michal lays one in David's bed to pass for a sleeping man (1 Samuel 19:13). Josiah swept them out of Judah along with the mediums and the idols (2 Kings 23:24).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מִלֵּא יַד (mille yad), to fill the hand
existing_translation_notes.note: The word translated ordained in verses 5 and 12 is literally filled his hand, and it is the fixed technical phrase for installing a priest, used of Aaron and his sons at Exodus 28:41 and 29:9. It carries the sense of putting the office, and the income, into a man's hands. Micah performs the rite on his own son, and then on a passing Levite, in a private house, with no authority to do either.

The tribe of Levi got no territory. It was given forty-eight towns scattered through the other tribes, and it lived on the tithes and the offerings brought to the sanctuary (Numbers 18:21-24, Joshua 21:41). Deuteronomy 18:6-8 gives a Levite the right to leave his town, come to the place the LORD chooses, and serve there on equal terms. Verses 7 to 13 show what happens when that system stops working: a young Levite from Bethlehem is on the road looking for somewhere to live, and takes a job as a private household priest for wages.

Verse 10 sets the Levite's terms: ten shekels of silver a year, a suit of clothes, and his food. That is about four ounces of silver annually, and it is one of the few plain wage figures in the Old Testament, useful for reading every other price in Scripture. The Levite takes a private household job because the arrangement God set up for his tribe had stopped working.

direct_references: Judges 17:3-6: Micah's mother dedicates silver to the LORD yet has images made, and Micah establishes a shrine and appoints his son as priest amid the refrain about doing right in one's own eyes.
Judges 17:7-13: The wandering Levite accepts Micah's wages, clothing, and food to become his priest, and Micah voices his own confidence that this will secure the LORD's favor.
