rows.current_summary: Five Danite spies scout Laish, approve it as a settlement, and the tribe sends six hundred armed men who seize Micah's priest and religious objects, intimidate Micah into silence, then conquer Laish and rename it Dan.
rows.current_summary_original: Five Danite spies scout Laish, approve it as a settlement, and the tribe sends six hundred armed men who seize Micah's priest and religious objects, intimidate Micah into silence, then conquer Laish and rename it Dan.
rows.concern: The summary says the Danites take Micah's priest without conveying that he willingly accepts their offer. A genealogy note treats 'Moses' and an exact grandson relationship as undisputed across editions.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 18:19-20 describes an offer to serve a tribe and the priest's glad acceptance. Verse 30 names Jonathan son/descendant of Gershom, with Moses/Manasseh readings differing among textual witnesses and editions.
rows.proposed_summary: Danite spies scout Laish, and six hundred armed Danites march there. They steal Micah's religious objects, and his priest gladly joins them after being offered a position with the tribe. They threaten Micah, destroy unsuspecting Laish, rebuild it as Dan, and establish idol worship there.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 12:5-7: Israel is to bring sacrifices and vow offerings to the place the LORD chooses, contrasting with the Danites' establishment of worship around Micah's stolen images.
Exodus 2:22: Moses names his son Gershom, supplying the family background for the Moses reading in the genealogy of the Danite priest.
rows.translation_context_note: Keep coercion of Micah separate from the priest's willing career move. Explain the Moses/Manasseh textual variant where the genealogy is discussed; follow the selected edition without treating a cross-edition rendering or exact generational interval as settled.
rows.proposed_note: The Danites steal Micah's religious objects, but the priest gladly accepts their offer to serve the tribe rather than one household (18:19-20). Verse 30 has a textual difference: some witnesses read Moses, while many Hebrew manuscripts indicate Manasseh with a raised letter nun. Editions differ accordingly. The Hebrew word translated son can also express descent, as reflected in translations using descendant. The genealogy connects the shrine's priesthood with an Israelite family; the textual and generational details require care.
existing_cross_references: Joshua 19:40-48: Dan's allotted territory on the coastal plain, and the tribe going up to fight Leshem and settling there.
Judges 1:34: The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country and would not let them come down to the plain.
Deuteronomy 12:5-7: You shall seek the place the LORD your God chooses out of all your tribes, and go there.
1 Kings 12:28-30: Jeroboam sets one golden calf at Bethel and one at Dan, and the people go as far as Dan to worship.
Jeremiah 8:16: The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan, and the whole land trembles at the sound.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: חֲגוּרִים כְּלֵי מִלְחָמָה (chagurim kele milchamah), girded with weapons of war
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 11 and 16 count the fighting men who move north as six hundred, with the families and livestock behind them and the children in front (verse 21). This is a whole clan on the move under an armed screen, not a raiding party. Six hundred is the standing size of a body of men in this period: David's band settles at six hundred (1 Samuel 23:13), and six hundred Benjaminites survive at the rock of Rimmon (20:47).

existing_translation_notes.term: Priest to a tribe rather than to one house
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אָב וְכֹהֵן (av ve-kohen), a father and a priest
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 19 offers the Levite a promotion and he takes it: be priest to a tribe and a clan in Israel instead of to one man's household. The offer is put to him with a hand over his mouth and six hundred armed men at the gate, and verse 20 says his heart was glad. Priesthood here has become a post with a salary and a career, which is the point the chapter is making about the period.

The book waits until verse 30 to name the priest, and the name lands hard: Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses. Gershom was Moses' firstborn, born in Midian (Exodus 2:22, 18:3). So the shrine at Dan, built around stolen idols, is served by Moses' own grandson and by his sons after him, and the verse says the line held the post until the captivity of the land.

The town lay at the northern springs that feed the Jordan, under Mount Hermon, isolated from Sidon and with no defence treaty (verses 7 and 28). Renamed Dan, it becomes the northern marker of the whole land in the phrase from Dan to Beersheba, and centuries later Jeroboam puts one of his golden calves there (1 Kings 12:29). An Aramaic victory inscription naming the house of David was found at the site in 1993.

direct_references: Judges 18:17-20: The Danites take Micah's religious objects and offer his priest a position with the tribe; he gladly accepts and takes the objects with him.

Judges 18:27-31: The Danites destroy unsuspecting Laish, rebuild it as Dan, and establish image worship; Jonathan is identified as a son of Gershom, son of Moses, in the account of the shrine's priesthood.

rows.current_summary: A Levite retrieves his unfaithful concubine from Bethlehem, and after lingering with her father, they travel to Gibeah where wicked men of the city gang-rape her through the night; the Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.
rows.current_summary_original: A Levite retrieves his unfaithful concubine from Bethlehem, and after lingering with her father, they travel to Gibeah where wicked men of the city gang-rape her through the night; the Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.
rows.concern: The summary leads with the woman's alleged unfaithfulness, where the textual tradition differs, but omits that she is handed to the mob. It can also imply a death sequence the narrator does not explicitly establish.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 19:2 is rendered 'unfaithful' in the selected English text; other ancient witnesses and translations read anger. Verse 25 reports the man seizing the concubine and putting her outside; she is abused all night. Verses 26-28 describe her collapsed at the doorway and unresponsive. Verse 29 describes the dismemberment; the Levite reports her death in 20:5.
rows.proposed_summary: A Levite brings his concubine back from her father's house in Bethlehem. At Gibeah, a mob demands to abuse him. The host offers the women instead, and the Levite seizes his concubine and puts her outside. The men rape and abuse her through the night. In the morning she lies unresponsive at the doorway; the Levite takes her home, cuts her into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout Israel.
cross_references: Judges 20:4-6: In his report to the assembly, the Levite says the attackers meant to kill him and that his concubine died, providing his own account to compare with chapter 19's narration.
Genesis 19:4-11: Sodom's mob demands Lot's guests, and Lot offers his daughters instead before the visitors intervene, paralleling the threat and proposed substitution at Gibeah.
Deuteronomy 22:25-27: The law condemns the man who overpowers a betrothed woman and expressly clears her of guilt, providing a legal contrast to blaming a woman for being attacked.
rows.translation_context_note: Explain 'unfaithful' versus 'angry' as a textual/lexical difference rather than silently making either reading universal. Retain the Levite's action in giving her over. Do not assert that she was killed specifically by dismemberment or at a precise point overnight; distinguish the chapter 19 narrator from the Levite's account in chapter 20.
rows.proposed_note: The Hebrew wording of 19:2 is rendered unfaithful in some editions; ancient witnesses and other translations support angry. The difference concerns how the woman came to be at her father's house. In verse 25, the Levite seizes her and puts her outside to the mob. The narrator then describes the night's abuse, her collapse at the doorway, and her failure to respond in the morning. The passage does not explicitly state the exact moment of her death. The Levite later says that she died in his account to the assembly (20:5).
existing_cross_references: Genesis 19:1-11: The men of Sodom surround Lot's house and demand the visitors, and Lot offers them his daughters.
Genesis 18:1-8: Abraham runs to meet three men, has their feet washed, and sets a meal before them under the tree.
Deuteronomy 22:25-27: The law for the man who seizes a betrothed woman in the open country and forces her.
Hosea 9:9: They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah; He will remember their iniquity.
Hosea 10:9: From the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel; there they have continued.

existing_translation_notes.note: A pilegesh was a secondary wife: a real and recognised marriage, but without the standing, the settlement or the family backing of a full wife, and her children ranked below the wife's. Verses 3 to 9 show the relationship for what it legally was, with the Levite going to her father's house and being kept there five days as a son-in-law. The law protects such a woman in Exodus 21:7-11, which requires that her food, clothing and marital rights not be reduced, and lets her go free if they are.

A Benjamite town on the central ridge road about three miles north of Jerusalem, which is why the Levite passes over Jebusite Jerusalem to reach it (verses 11 and 12). He chooses the Israelite town over the foreign one on purpose. Gibeah is later Saul's home and seat (1 Samuel 10:26, 11:4), and Hosea twice uses its name as a byword for how low Israel went.

existing_translation_notes.term: No one took them into his house
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 15 has the travellers sit in the open square of the town because nobody offers them shelter, and that is the first thing wrong in the chapter. In a country with no inns, taking in a traveller before dark was a duty every household understood; Abraham runs to do it in Genesis 18. The old man who finally takes them in is not from Gibeah at all, but from Ephraim (verse 16).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נֵתַח (netach), a piece of a butchered carcass
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 29 uses the vocabulary of butchering a sacrifice, the word for the joints an animal is cut into. What the Levite sends round the tribes is a summons that cannot be filed away or ignored, and it works: chapter 20 opens with the whole nation assembled. Saul does the same thing with a yoke of oxen when he calls out the militia for Jabesh-gilead and says this is what will be done to the oxen of any man who does not come (1 Samuel 11:7).

direct_references: Judges 19:2-3: The woman leaves for her father's house, and the Levite goes to speak kindly and bring her back, introducing the separation whose wording differs across translations.

Judges 19:22-30: The host offers women to the mob, and the Levite sends his concubine outside; after the night's abuse she is found unresponsive, and he later cuts her into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel.

rows.current_summary: Israel assembles at Mizpah, hears the Levite's account of his concubine's rape and death in Gibeah, and demands Benjamin turn over the guilty men; when Benjamin refuses, Israel fights three battles against them, using an ambush on the third day to defeat Benjamin and destroy their towns, leaving only six hundred Benjamite survivors who flee to the rock of Rimmon.
rows.current_summary_original: Israel assembles at Mizpah, hears the Levite's account of his concubine's rape and death in Gibeah, and demands Benjamin turn over the guilty men; when Benjamin refuses, Israel fights three battles against them, using an ambush on the third day to defeat Benjamin and destroy their towns, leaving only six hundred Benjamite survivors who flee to the rock of Rimmon.
rows.concern: The summary can read the Levite's self-report as the narrator's complete account of the prior atrocity, although his report omits his own part and describes the mob's intent differently.
rows.scripture_says: Judges 20:4-6 is the Levite's speech to the assembly. Compare 19:22-25: the mob demands sexual abuse, the host offers women, and the man gives the concubine to the mob. The ensuing civil war also includes violence against Benjamin's towns, animals, and those found there (20:48).
rows.proposed_summary: Israel assembles at Mizpah and hears the Levite's account of the atrocity at Gibeah. Benjamin refuses to surrender the guilty men. After two costly defeats, Israel defeats Benjamin using an ambush and burns its towns. Six hundred Benjaminite men escape to the rock of Rimmon.
cross_references: Judges 19:22-30: The narrator describes a demand to abuse the male guest and the Levite putting the woman outside, details that differ from or disappear in his later speech to the assembly.
Judges 21:16: The elders say Benjamin's women have been destroyed, explaining why the surviving Benjaminites face a separate crisis over wives.
rows.translation_context_note: Signal that the assembly hears the Levite's account and allow readers to compare it with the preceding narration. The survival count names men, not an ungendered list of all people. Preserve the devastation of the towns rather than describing only the battlefield outcome.
rows.proposed_note: Verses 4-6 record the Levite's own speech. His account omits his role in putting the woman outside and presents the mob's intent differently from 19:22-25. The assembly acts on that testimony, while the reader has also heard the preceding narrator. The war's final devastation extends to Benjamin's towns and those found there (20:48). The six hundred who escape to Rimmon are explicitly men; chapter 21 then addresses the loss of Benjamin's women.
existing_cross_references: Judges 19:29-30: The body is cut into twelve pieces and sent through all the territory of Israel to summon the tribes.
Deuteronomy 13:12-18: A town that has turned aside to serve other gods is to be struck down and its spoil burned in the open square.
Deuteronomy 17:2-7: The evil is to be purged from your midst, and the hand of the witnesses is first against the guilty.
Joshua 8:3-22: Joshua sets an ambush behind Ai and draws the defenders out with a feigned retreat.
Numbers 27:21: Israel inquires of God before the priest, the practice followed at Bethel in verses 27 and 28.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כְּאִישׁ אֶחָד (ke-ish echad), as one man
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 1 measures the muster by the two ends of the country, Dan in the far north under Hermon and Beersheba on the edge of the Negev, and adds Gilead across the Jordan. There is no king and no standing army; the tribes assemble themselves at Mizpah, a hilltop in Benjamin about eight miles north of Jerusalem, and act as one body. Samuel gathers the nation at the same place in 1 Samuel 7:5-6 and 10:17.

A sling is two cords on a leather pouch, whirled and released by letting one cord go. It was not a toy: armies fielded slingers as a standing arm, and the Assyrian relief panels of the siege of Lachish, cut for Sennacherib's palace and now in the British Museum, show them working the line alongside the archers. A stone thrown that way kills outright, which is what happens at 1 Samuel 17:49. Verse 16 says these seven hundred could sling at a hair and not miss.

Verses 27 and 28 mention almost in passing that the ark of the covenant was at Bethel and that Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, was ministering before it. That dates the whole episode. Phinehas is the man who stopped the plague at Peor in Moses' own lifetime (Numbers 25:7-8), so this atrocity belongs near the start of the period of the judges, not at its end, even though the book places it last.

Verse 47 has six hundred Benjaminites hold out four months on a rock in the wilderness east of the hill country. Sela means a crag or cliff, not a boulder, and country like that is full of limestone spurs with caves and one approach, which is why fugitives head for them all through Scripture; David does the same at Adullam and En-gedi. Those six hundred men are the entire tribe of Benjamin that survives chapter 20, which is the problem chapter 21 exists to solve.

direct_references: Judges 20:4-13: The assembly hears the Levite's account and demands that Benjamin surrender Gibeah's guilty men, but Benjamin refuses, leading into the civil war.
Judges 20:18-28: Israel consults the LORD yet suffers two costly defeats before receiving a promise of victory the next day, preserving the losses that precede Benjamin's defeat.
Judges 20:35-48: An ambush leads to Benjamin's defeat, six hundred men escape to Rimmon, and Israel burns Benjamin's towns, showing destruction beyond the battlefield alone.

existing_translation_notes.note: This chapter runs on two oaths sworn in the heat of the assembly, and Israel treats both as unbreakable. Verse 1 swears that no one will give a daughter to a Benjaminite; verse 5 swears death on any town that failed to turn up. A shevuah is a sworn oath, stronger than a vow, and Numbers 30:2 binds a man to everything that comes out of his mouth. The tribes will not simply repent of the oath, so they spend the rest of the chapter finding ways round it.

Verses 8 to 12 destroy an Israelite town under the ban for not sending men to the assembly, and spare four hundred unmarried women out of it. The town sits east of the Jordan in Gilead. Two later episodes turn on this: Saul's first act as king is to march overnight and break the Ammonite siege of Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11:1-11), and when he dies it is the men of Jabesh-gilead who travel all night to take his body off the wall of Beth-shan and bury him (1 Samuel 31:11-13).

existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 20 to 23 solve the oath by arranging an abduction: the surviving Benjaminites lie in the vineyards and each carries off a woman from the dance, and the elders undertake to square it with the fathers and brothers afterwards. The law they are working around is the one they swore themselves, since the fathers cannot be said to have given their daughters if the daughters were taken. Verse 25 closes the book on the sentence it has repeated four times: in those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

Verses 19 to 21 describe a yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh where the young women came out to dance in the vineyards, and the chapter gives directions to the place: north of Bethel, east of the road from Bethel to Shechem, south of Lebonah. Vineyard dances at a harvest feast were a normal part of the year. The chapter uses that ordinary festival as cover for carrying women off, and reports it without approving it.

rows.proposed_note: The command applies to the people and their king together. Verse 14 requires both to follow the LORD; it does not put the king beside God as a separate object of this obedience. existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 3 to 5 are a formal audit, not a burst of feeling. A judge leaving office stands in front of the people and invites any claim against him: whose ox or donkey have I taken, whom have I defrauded, from whose hand have I taken a bribe. The people are then made to answer on the record, and verse 5 seals it with the LORD as witness and the newly made king as witness, and their reply, he is witness. Samuel hands over with his accounts formally closed.

This chapter uses the phrase at both ends of its range within a few verses. In verse 18 the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel when thunder came out of a clear harvest sky, which is fright. In verse 24 Samuel tells them to fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all their heart, which is a settled way of living. Deuteronomy 10:12 puts the same word first in the list of what God requires, and Proverbs 1:7 makes it the beginning of knowledge.

Verses 9 to 11 run through the pattern of the book of Judges in three sentences: Israel forgot the LORD, He sold them into the hand of Sisera, of the Philistines and of the king of Moab, they cried out, and He sent deliverers. The men listed are Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, then Barak, then Jephthah, then Samuel himself. He puts his own name last in the list, which is how he closes the era before handing the country to a king.

Israel's rain falls from about October to April, and the wheat harvest in May and June is reliably dry; that is when threshing floors are in use and a downpour ruins the crop on the ground. Samuel calls for thunder and rain at exactly the season when nobody had ever seen it, which is why verse 18 says the people greatly feared. Proverbs 26:1 uses the same impossibility as a byword.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עֹלָה (olah), that which goes up - Greek (LXX): ὁλοκαύτωμα (holokautoma)
existing_translation_notes.note: The olah is the offering burned entire, with nothing kept back for the priest or the worshipper to eat, and the name means the thing that goes up in smoke. Before a battle it was normal to offer one, which is what Saul is waiting seven days at Gilgal to have Samuel do (10:8). Verses 9 to 12 have him call for it and offer it himself as the army melts away, and Samuel arrives as he finishes. The Greek word behind it gives English holocaust.

existing_translation_notes.term: A man after His own heart
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כִּלְבָבוֹ (kilvavo), according to his heart
existing_translation_notes.note: Samuel's sentence in verse 14 says the LORD has sought out for Himself a man according to His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people. In Hebrew the heart is where a person decides, not where he feels; it is closer to the mind and the will than to the emotions. The phrase describes a man whose choices line up with God's, and the chapter has just shown Saul making the opposite kind. Paul quotes the line at Acts 13:22.

Verses 19 to 22 report that the Philistines allowed no smith in Israel, so farmers had to go down to them to sharpen a ploughshare, mattock, axe, or sickle, and only Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear. Controlling ironworking was how the coastal cities kept the hill country disarmed; Israel could farm but could not arm. Judges 1:19 gives the other half of the picture, iron chariots the highlanders could not face.

Verse 21 gives the Philistine sharpening charge as a pim. The word appears nowhere else in Scripture and nobody knew what it meant until inscribed stone weights marked pym were dug up in Judah in the early twentieth century. A pim weighs about 7.8 grams, roughly two thirds of a shekel, so the fee for putting an edge on a farm tool was two thirds of the standard silver unit, charged per tool.

A town about seven miles northeast of Jerusalem, on the north lip of the Wadi Suweinit, a steep gorge that cuts the road running east from the central ridge. Michmash sits on one side and Geba on the other, with the ravine between them, so an army holding Michmash sealed the pass. That gorge is the ground of Jonathan's climb in the next chapter.

existing_translation_notes.note: A berit is a binding agreement sworn in public, with obligations on both sides and a penalty behind it, and Hebrew does not make one, it cuts one, from the practice of cutting animals in half and passing between the pieces (Genesis 15:9-18). Verse 3 has Jonathan cut one with David, and the covenant is renewed twice more (20:16, 23:18). Its terms are spelled out at 20:14-15, and they run past both their lifetimes: David is not to cut off Jonathan's household when he comes to power, which is the obligation he honours in 2 Samuel 9.

Verse 4 has Jonathan strip off the robe he was wearing and hand it over with his tunic, sword, bow and belt. Clothing and weapons stood for the man who wore them, and handing them across was how an agreement was made visible; that is why cutting the hem off Saul's robe is such a serious act at 24:4-5, and why Samuel reads a torn robe as a kingdom torn away at 15:27-28. What Jonathan gives away is the outfit of the king's son and heir, in front of witnesses.

Verses 6 and 7 describe a fixed custom: women coming out of the towns to meet a returning army with drums, dancing and a sung refrain. Miriam does it at the sea (Exodus 15:20-21) and Jephthah's daughter does it at Mizpah (Judges 11:34). The couplet in verse 7 is built the ordinary way for Hebrew verse, with the second line raising the number of the first, so thousands and tens of thousands is how the form works. Verse 8 has Saul refuse to hear it that way.

A marriage was arranged between households, and the groom paid the bride's father a mohar in silver, livestock, or service; Jacob worked seven years twice over for it (Genesis 29:18-27). Saul names a price of a hundred Philistines in verse 25 precisely because David is poor and the errand should kill him. David brings back two hundred.

existing_translation_notes.note: Chesed is loyalty owed under a standing obligation and kept after the obligation could safely be dropped. Verse 1 asks whether anyone of Saul's house is left, so that David may show chesed for Jonathan's sake, and verse 3 calls it the chesed of God. This is not a spontaneous kindness; it is a clause being honoured. Jonathan had made David swear it, for himself and for his descendants, at 1 Samuel 20:14-15, at a time when the odds ran the other way.

4:4 explains the injury: Mephibosheth was five years old when the news came from Jezreel, his nurse picked him up and ran, and he fell and was crippled in both feet. In a world with no wheelchairs, a man lame in both feet could not farm, could not fight and could not travel, so he depended entirely on a household that would keep him. Verse 13 notes that he lived in Jerusalem and ate at the king's table, and repeats that he was lame in both feet, which is why that arrangement was the whole of his security.

Verse 4 finds the last heir of Saul's house living at Lo-debar in Gilead, east of the Jordan, in the household of Machir son of Ammiel. Across the river was the safest place to keep him: outside the reach of the new king, in the region that had backed Ish-bosheth. Machir turns up once more, sending food and bedding to David at Mahanaim when Absalom drives him out (17:27-29), so the man sheltering Saul's grandson later supplies David's army.

Verses 7, 10, 11, and 13 repeat that Mephibosheth eats at the king's table. A place at the table was a formal grant of maintenance for life at royal expense, recorded the same way for the released Jehoiachin in Babylon (2 Kings 25:29). It also kept the last heir of the previous dynasty where the king could see him every day.

existing_translation_notes.note: Chata is the plain verb for missing a target; Judges 20:16 uses it of slingers who do not miss a hair. David's answer in verse 13 is three words in Hebrew, chatati la-YHWH, I have sinned against the LORD, and Nathan's reply comes back in the same breath. The Hebrew word behind repent is not about feeling; it is the ordinary verb for turning round and going back, used of a traveller or an army. What the prophets ask for is a change of direction that can be seen from outside. This chapter shows the difference between remorse and repentance in one man across a fortnight: verses 16 to 20 have David fasting and lying on the ground for seven days over the child, then washing, anointing himself and going in to worship the moment the child dies.

David's own sentence in verse 6, that the man must repay the lamb four times over, is a quotation of the statute. Exodus 22:1 requires four sheep for one sheep stolen and slaughtered, and five oxen for an ox. He is not inventing a penalty in anger; he is applying the law he knows, correctly, to a case he has not yet realised is his own. Nathan then answers in verse 7 with four words in Hebrew, you are the man.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: רַבָּה (Rabbah) - עִיר הַמָּיִם (ir ha-mayim), the city of waters
existing_translation_notes.note: Rabbah was the Ammonite capital, on the upper reaches of the Jabbok where modern Amman stands, and the siege that opens at 11:1 is still running here. Verse 27 explains how a siege was actually won: Joab reports that he has taken the water supply, the lower town over the springs, which means the citadel above cannot hold out and is now only waiting. He then sends for the king so the credit for the capture goes where it belongs.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

existing_translation_notes.term: Lay on the ground and fasted
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 16 to 20 set out the standard signs of mourning and pleading: fasting, sleeping on the bare ground, refusing to wash, anoint, or change clothes. Anointing with olive oil was daily grooming in a hot, dry country, so going unanointed was visible to everyone. David's servants are frightened in verse 18 because he does all of it before the death and none of it afterward.

rows.current_summary: David organizes his forces into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, then positions himself at the city gate while his troops march out; Absalom is caught by his hair in an oak tree during the battle, and Joab kills him with three javelins despite David's command to spare him. Runners bring word to David that the battle is won, but when he learns Absalom is dead, he grieves deeply in the gateway chamber, lamenting that he wishes he had died instead of his son.
rows.current_summary_original: David organizes his forces into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, then positions himself at the city gate while his troops march out; Absalom is caught by his hair in an oak tree during the battle, and Joab kills him with three javelins despite David's command to spare him. Runners bring word to David that the battle is won, but when he learns Absalom is dead, he grieves deeply in the gateway chamber, lamenting that he wishes he had died instead of his son.
rows.concern: The summary substitutes hair for head and compresses the killing into Joab's three blows.
rows.scripture_says: Absalom's head catches in the tree. Joab pierces him and ten armor-bearers strike and kill him.
rows.proposed_summary: David organizes his forces into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, then positions himself at the city gate while his troops march out; Absalom's head is caught in an oak tree during the battle; despite David's command to spare him, Joab thrusts three spears into him and ten armor-bearers kill him. Runners bring word to David that the battle is won, but when he learns Absalom is dead, he grieves deeply in the gateway chamber, lamenting that he wishes he had died instead of his son.
cross_references: 2 Samuel 14:25-26: Absalom's appearance and unusually heavy hair are described, supplying the earlier detail often connected with the later tree episode.
rows.translation_context_note: The current head-caught note already warns against adding hair, but the summary does exactly that. The hair reference explains why the familiar retelling arose.
rows.proposed_note: Verse 9 says Absalom's head was caught in the tree; it does not identify his hair as the cause. Joab thrust three spears into him, and ten armor-bearers then struck and killed him.
existing_cross_references: 2 Samuel 14:25-26: Absalom's yearly haircut, weighed at two hundred shekels by the king's weight.
Deuteronomy 21:18-21: The law for a stubborn and rebellious son who will not listen to his father or his mother.
2 Samuel 12:10-12: The word that the sword would never depart from David's house.
2 Samuel 19:1-8: Joab confronts David for shaming the men who saved his life by mourning the man who hunted him.
2 Samuel 14:27: Absalom is recorded as having three sons and a daughter, though verse 18 says he had no son to keep his name alive.

existing_translation_notes.term: The king kept out of the battle
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עֲשָׂרָה אֲלָפִים (asarah alafim), ten thousand
existing_translation_notes.note: The army refuses to let David take the field in verse 3, and their reasoning is cold arithmetic: if they run, nobody cares, and if half of them die, nobody cares, but he is worth ten thousand of them. A king in the line is the one target whose loss ends a war on the spot, which is why the enemy hunts him and why his own men would rather he sat in the gate at Mahanaim with a runner posted on the wall. His absence is also why the order about Absalom is given publicly to three commanders and then ignored.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֶלֶף כֶּסֶף (eleph kesef), a thousand of silver
existing_translation_notes.note: The soldier in verse 12 turns down a hypothetical bounty of a thousand shekels, and the figure is meant to sound enormous: a shekel weighs about two-fifths of an ounce, so this is roughly twenty-seven pounds of silver, when a Levite could be hired for ten shekels a year with board and clothing (Judges 17:10). His reason is not money but the order everyone heard the king give to Joab, Abishai and Ittai in the hearing of the whole army. Joab's answer is to take three spears and do it himself.

existing_translation_notes.term: A heap of stones over the pit
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 17 gives the king's son the burial of a condemned criminal: thrown into a large pit in the forest with a great mound of stones piled on top. The same cairn goes over Achan in the Valley of Achor (Joshua 7:26) and over the king of Ai (Joshua 8:29). It is a public marker meant to be seen from the road, and it stands directly against verse 18, where Absalom had raised a pillar in the King's Valley in his own lifetime so that his name would be remembered.

existing_translation_notes.term: His head caught fast in the oak
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֵלָה (elah), terebinth or great tree
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 9 says his head caught in the tree, not his hair; the hair is the reader's addition. He is riding a mule under a low, thick-limbed terebinth in broken forest country, and he is left hanging between the tree and the sky when the animal keeps going. Verse 8 has already noted that the forest killed more men that day than the sword.

Verses 19 to 27 turn on the two routes out of the forest of Ephraim: the Cushite goes straight over the hills, and Ahimaaz takes the longer flat road through the Jordan plain and still arrives first. News travelled at the pace of a man on foot, and a watchman on the gate tower identified runners by their gait long before they arrived (verse 27). Being first with the news was itself a position at court.

evidence.text: Now Absalom was riding on his mule when he met the servants of David, and as the mule went under the thick branches of a large oak, Absalom’s head was caught fast in the tree. The mule under him kept going, so that he was suspended in midair. (18:9).

rows.current_summary: A three-year famine leads David to execute seven descendants of Saul to satisfy the Gibeonites, whom Saul had tried to destroy; after proper burial of the remains, God ends the famine and David's forces defeat several Philistine giants in subsequent battles.
rows.current_summary_original: A three-year famine leads David to execute seven descendants of Saul to satisfy the Gibeonites, whom Saul had tried to destroy; after proper burial of the remains, God ends the famine and David's forces defeat several Philistine giants in subsequent battles.
rows.concern: The summary makes David the executioner and can obscure who demanded and carried out the killings.
rows.scripture_says: David gives the seven descendants to the Gibeonites, who execute them.
rows.proposed_summary: A three-year famine is linked to Saul's attack on the Gibeonites. David hands seven of Saul's descendants over to the Gibeonites, who execute them; after the remains are buried, God answers prayer for the land. David's forces also defeat several Philistine giants.
cross_references: Joshua 9:15-20: Israel's leaders preserve their sworn treaty with the Gibeonites after discovering the deception, establishing the oath behind the later bloodguilt dispute.
Deuteronomy 24:16: Parents and children must not be executed for one another's sins, supplying the law relevant to the execution of Saul's descendants.
rows.translation_context_note: The existing oath note explains the broken treaty but implies more about the victims' guilt than the text supplies. A proposal must avoid a dangling "whom" that attaches Saul's attack to his descendants instead of the Gibeonites.
rows.proposed_note: The famine is connected with Saul's attack on the Gibeonites, whose treaty Israel had sworn to honor. David hands over seven descendants of Saul; the Gibeonites execute them. The chapter does not identify each victim's personal involvement in Saul's attack, and Deuteronomy 24:16 prohibits executing children for their fathers' sins.
existing_cross_references: Joshua 9:3-27: The Gibeonites secure a treaty by claiming to come from a distant country, and Israel swears an oath to them.

Deuteronomy 21:22-23: A body hanged on a tree is not to be left overnight, for a hanged man is under God's curse.
1 Samuel 17:4-7: Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span, with a spear shaft like a weaver's beam.
1 Chronicles 20:4-8: The parallel roll of the Philistine giants killed by David's men.

existing_translation_notes.term: The Gibeonites and the broken oath
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 1 and 2 reach back nearly four centuries. The Gibeonites had obtained a treaty from Joshua by deception, and Israel swore to them by the LORD and kept it even after the fraud came out (Joshua 9:15-20). Saul broke that oath and tried to wipe them out, and the famine is laid at that. Verse 4 is the detail a reader should not skip: they refuse silver or gold, which is the ransom Numbers 35:31 forbids being taken for a life, and ask instead for men of the house that shed the blood.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כָּפַר (kaphar), to cover or wipe clean
existing_translation_notes.note: David's question in verse 3 is how he shall kaphar, which English renders as make atonement or make amends. The verb means to cover over or wipe away so that a debt no longer stands, and it is the technical word for what the sacrifices do (Leviticus 16:30). Behind this chapter lies the rule that bloodshed pollutes the land itself and that nothing cleanses it except the blood of the man who shed it (Numbers 35:33), which is why the famine is read as a matter still outstanding on Saul's account.

Verses 15 to 22 close with four Philistine champions, each said to be descended from Rapha, the term behind the Rephaim, the tall peoples the Bible places in the land before Israel (Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 3:11). The details are physical and specific: Ishbi-benob's bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels, about seven and a half pounds, against the fifteen pounds of Goliath's iron spearhead at 1 Samuel 17:7, and one man at Gath had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. Joshua 11:22 had already noted that the Anakim survived in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

Verses 9 and 10 set the exposure at the start of barley harvest, which is April, and say Rizpah kept the birds and the wild animals off the bodies until rain fell. The first rains come in October. She sat out on sackcloth beside her sons for something close to six months, in the open, and the law's requirement that a body be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:23) is what makes her vigil an accusation the king finally answers in verse 13.

rows.current_summary: David delivers his final words affirming God's covenant with him and promising judgment for evil men. He then catalogs his mighty warriors, listing their individual exploits and naming all thirty-seven of his chief fighters.
rows.current_summary_original: David delivers his final words affirming God's covenant with him and promising judgment for evil men. He then catalogs his mighty warriors, listing their individual exploits and naming all thirty-seven of his chief fighters.
rows.concern: "He then catalogs" attributes the narrator's warrior list to David's final oracle.
rows.scripture_says: David's oracle occupies verses 1-7. Verse 8 begins the list of mighty men in the narrative voice.
rows.proposed_summary: The chapter presents David's final oracle about just rule, God's covenant, and judgment on evil. It then lists his mighty warriors and their exploits, ending with thirty-seven men in all.
cross_references: 1 Chronicles 11:10-47: Chronicles separately lists David's mighty men and their exploits, providing the parallel catalog to the list following his last oracle.
rows.translation_context_note: The current last-words note explains the oracle but does not separate it from the following catalog. The existing Chronicles parallel supports treating the catalog as a distinct narrative section.
rows.proposed_note: Verses 1-7 present David's oracle. The list of his mighty men begins at verse 8; the chapter does not say David compiled or recited that list as part of the oracle.

2 Samuel 7:12-16: The covenant these last words call everlasting, ordered in all things and secure.
Numbers 15:5,10: The drink offering poured out to the LORD alongside the burnt offering.
Micah 5:2: Bethlehem, little among the clans of Judah, from which the ruler of Israel comes.
Psalm 72:1-7: The king who rules in the fear of God is like the light of morning and like rain on the mown grass.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נְאֻם (neum), oracle - נְעִים זְמִרוֹת (neim zemirot), the sweet singer
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 1 introduces the poem with neum, the formal word for a prophetic utterance, the same one used in the phrase declares the LORD throughout the prophets, and Balaam's oracles at Numbers 24:3. It then gives David four titles in a row: son of Jesse, the man raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet singer of Israel. Verse 2 states the claim directly, that the Spirit of the LORD spoke by him and His word was on his tongue.

Verses 8 to 39 are a formal roll of honour with two ranks in it, the Three at the top and the Thirty below, each with named captains, and it works the way a decorations list works: a man is admitted for a specific recorded action, so each entry gives the deed. It closes at verse 39 with the total, thirty-seven in all, and with one last name, Uriah the Hittite. The writer sets it there and says nothing about it.

existing_translation_notes.term: Benaiah and the lion in the pit
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 20 credits Benaiah with three things, and the middle one needs unpacking. The Hebrew says he struck down two ariels of Moab, a word built from lion and God; English versions render it champions, and what the title actually designated is not known. Then he went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion, which tells you both that cisterns were deep rock-cut shafts a man had to climb into, and that snow falls in the Judean hills in winter. Verse 23 makes him commander of David's bodyguard, and 1 Kings 2:35 makes him commander of the whole army under Solomon.

existing_translation_notes.term: Poured it out to the LORD
existing_translation_notes.note: Three men break through a Philistine garrison to fetch water from the well at Bethlehem, and David will not drink it (verses 15 to 17). Pouring a liquid out on the ground before God was the drink offering that went with the daily sacrifices (Numbers 15:5-10). He treats water bought at that risk as something only God has a right to.

rows.current_summary: The LORD incites David to take a census; after Joab completes the count of Israel's fighting men, David repents and chooses plague as his punishment, which kills seventy thousand people before stopping at Jerusalem. David buys Araunah's threshing floor, builds an altar, and offers sacrifices, and the plague ceases.
rows.current_summary_original: The LORD incites David to take a census; after Joab completes the count of Israel's fighting men, David repents and chooses plague as his punishment, which kills seventy thousand people before stopping at Jerusalem. David buys Araunah's threshing floor, builds an altar, and offers sacrifices, and the plague ceases.
rows.concern: Note-focused: the summary's divine-incitement wording is textual, but the note treats an unreported ransom failure and kingly motive as the established explanation.
rows.scripture_says: Samuel names the LORD's anger and incitement; Chronicles names Satan. David confesses sin, but this chapter does not explicitly identify omission of the ransom as the offense.
rows.proposed_summary: In anger against Israel, the LORD incites David to order a census. David later confesses sin, and a plague kills seventy thousand before the LORD stops it. David buys Araunah's threshing floor and offers sacrifices, and God answers prayer for the land.
cross_references: 1 Chronicles 21:1-8: The parallel account names Satan as the census inciter and records David's confession, preserving its different attribution from Samuel.
Exodus 30:11-16: A census requires a half-shekel ransom from each counted man to prevent plague, supplying the relevant law without proving what David omitted.
rows.translation_context_note: Both essential references are already present. The current note's claim that a military census treats people as the king's asset is an interpretation and should not be presented as the narrator's stated motive.
rows.proposed_note: Samuel opens with the LORD's anger against Israel and says He incited David; Chronicles names Satan as the inciter. David confesses that the census was sinful. Exodus 30 connects a census ransom with protection from plague, but neither account explicitly says David omitted that payment or gives that as the sole explanation.
existing_cross_references: 1 Chronicles 21:1-30: The parallel account, which opens with Satan inciting David and closes with fire falling on the altar.
Exodus 30:11-16: Every man counted must give a half shekel ransom, so that no plague breaks out among them when they are numbered.
2 Chronicles 3:1: Solomon builds the house of the LORD on Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
Genesis 22:1-14: Abraham is sent to the land of Moriah, and he names the place The LORD Will Provide.
1 Kings 8:37-40: Solomon prays that when famine, blight, or plague comes, God will hear from heaven and forgive.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כֹּפֶר נֶפֶשׁ (kopher nephesh), a ransom for a life
existing_translation_notes.note: Nothing in this chapter makes sense without Exodus 30:11-16, and no modern reader has it to hand. That law says when a census of Israel is taken, every man counted must pay half a shekel as a ransom for his life to the LORD, rich and poor alike, so that there be no plague among them when they are numbered. A count of fighting men treats the nation as an asset belonging to the king, and the half-shekel is the standing reminder that it belongs to God. Joab's objection in verse 3 is made without argument, and he is right.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד (vayyakh lev David), and David's heart struck him
existing_translation_notes.note: The Hebrew in verse 10 says David's heart struck him, using nakah, the ordinary verb for hitting or striking down. The same expression is used once before in his life, at 1 Samuel 24:5, after he cut the corner off Saul's robe in the cave. Both times it comes after the act and before anyone accuses him, and both times what follows is a confession in plain words: I have sinned greatly in what I have done.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: גֹּרֶן אֲרַוְנָה (goren Aravnah), the threshing floor of Araunah
existing_translation_notes.note: A threshing floor is a flat, hard, open circle of levelled rock, sited high and clear so the wind can carry the chaff off, and there was one on the rise just north of the old city, still owned by a Jebusite. Verse 24 has David refuse to take it as a gift, saying he will not offer to the LORD what costs him nothing, and pay for the floor and the oxen. 2 Chronicles 3:1 records what was built on that ground afterwards: Solomon's temple, on Mount Moriah, on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: חֲמִשִּׁים שְׁקָלִים כֶּסֶף (chamishim sheqalim kesef)
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 24 records the price as fifty shekels of silver, about a pound and a quarter of it, and says exactly what it bought: the threshing floor and the oxen, that is, the working surface and the animals for the sacrifice. 1 Chronicles 21:25 records a second and much larger payment, six hundred shekels of gold, and says what that bought: the site. One is the price of a floor and a pair of oxen; the other is the price of the ground the temple would stand on.

The census route in verses 2 to 8 runs from Dan at the northern springs under Mount Hermon to Beersheba in the dry south, about 150 miles apart, and it took Joab nine months and twenty days. The phrase is Israel's standard way of saying the whole country, from one end to the other. Counting fighting men over that whole span is what makes this a military census.

implemented_note_changes.original: Hebrew: כֹּפֶר נֶפֶשׁ (kopher nephesh), a ransom for a life
implemented_note_changes.note: Samuel opens with the LORD's anger against Israel and says He incited David; Chronicles names Satan as the inciter. David confesses that the census was sinful. Exodus 30 connects a census ransom with protection from plague, but neither account explicitly says David omitted that payment or gives that as the sole explanation. Exodus 30:11-16 sets the census ransom at half a shekel for each counted man, rich and poor alike, to support the Tent of Meeting.

implemented_note_changes.original: Hebrew: וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד (vayyakh lev David), and David's heart struck him
implemented_note_changes.note: The Hebrew expression behind David's conscience being stricken also appears after he cuts Saul's robe in 1 Samuel 24:5. In the census account, David immediately confesses, I have sinned greatly in what I have done (2 Samuel 24:10). In the robe episode, he tells his men he must not raise his hand against the LORD's anointed (1 Samuel 24:6). The passages share the conscience-stricken expression but record different responses.

implemented_note_changes.original: Hebrew: חֲמִשִּׁים שְׁקָלִים כֶּסֶף (chamishim sheqalim kesef)
implemented_note_changes.note: Second Samuel 24:24 records fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen; 1 Chronicles 21:25 records six hundred shekels of gold for the site. Some interpreters reconcile these figures by proposing a smaller purchase followed by a larger acquisition of the temple site. Neither account explicitly narrates two transactions or states that explanation, so it is a proposed harmonization rather than an established sequence of events.

existing_translation_notes.term: House of the Forest of Lebanon
existing_translation_notes.note: The largest building in Solomon's palace complex, a hundred cubits by fifty by thirty, roughly 150 by 75 by 45 feet, named for the four rows of cedar columns inside it that stood like a forest. It served as an armoury and treasury: 1 Kings 10:17 stores the three hundred gold shields there, and Isaiah 22:8 calls it the House of the Forest when Judah looks to its weapons.

Verse 1 notes Solomon spent seven years on the temple (1 Kings 6:38) and thirteen on his own house. The comparison is left to stand without comment. The palace complex was larger, taking in the throne hall, the hall of pillars, his own residence, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

Naboth's answer in verse 3 is not stubbornness about a price. Under the law each family's plot was permanently theirs, could not be sold outright, and returned to them in the jubilee year even if leased (Leviticus 25:23-28). Selling the vineyard would have cut his family out of the land God assigned to them, and Ahab, as king, knew the law he was asking Naboth to break.

Jezebel's letters in verses 9 and 10 call a public fast and seat Naboth at the head of the people. A town called a fast when it believed some hidden sin had brought trouble on it, and the assembly then looked for the guilty party. She sets the stage so that the two paid witnesses have a court and a crowd ready, and the sentence follows the law's own procedure exactly.

Elijah's is the object he throws over Elisha to call him from the plough (1 Kings 19:19), rolls up to strike the Jordan in verse 8, and leaves behind in verse 13. Picking it up is the visible transfer of the office.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פִּי שְׁנַיִם (pi shenayim), a mouth of two
existing_translation_notes.note: Elisha's request in verse 9 uses a legal term. The double portion is the firstborn's share of an estate, two parts where every other son gets one, guaranteed at Deuteronomy 21:17 even when the father prefers another son. He is not asking for twice Elijah's spirit; he is asking to be treated as the heir of the man's office.

Companies of prophets living together at Bethel, Jericho, and Gilgal, appearing throughout this chapter and again at 4:38 and 6:1-2. Son of in Hebrew often marks membership in a class rather than descent, so the phrase names a guild under a master. Fifty of them stand off at a distance at the Jordan in verse 7, and one of them is sent to anoint Jehu in chapter 9.

The Hebrew word naar covers anyone from a young child to a man of military age; Joseph is called a naar at seventeen and Solomon uses it of himself as king. Forty-two of them come out of Bethel, the town holding one of Jeroboam's calves, to jeer the prophet out of their territory. The number and the place mark this as a mob, not a handful of children.

The Syrian brown bear lived in the wooded hills of Israel and the Lebanon range into modern times, standing over five feet and weighing several hundred pounds. Scripture treats it as a known danger alongside the lion: David killed both (1 Samuel 17:34-36), and Amos 5:19 pictures a man escaping a lion only to meet a bear.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

Chemosh was the national god of Moab; Numbers 21:29 calls the Moabites the people of Chemosh, and Solomon built him a high place east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7). Verse 27 reports Mesha taking his oldest son, the heir to his throne, and burning him as an offering on the city wall in full view of the besieging armies. This was what Moab did when a siege went badly, and the text states it without comment.

Mesha left his own account of this war. A black basalt stone found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868, now in the Louvre, carries thirty-four lines in Moabite in which King Mesha names Omri king of Israel, describes throwing off Israel's rule, and credits Chemosh with the victory. It is the same conflict this chapter reports, told from the other side.

Verse 4 sets Moab's annual tribute at 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams. Moab's plateau east of the Dead Sea is high, dry grazing country, so the payment came in what the land produced. Withholding tribute was how a vassal declared independence, which is what verse 5 records him doing the moment Ahab died.

rows.translation_context_note: The current leprosy note already supplies the disease distinction. The proposed summary follows the stated purpose and prophetic announcement without inventing a physical act by Elisha.
rows.proposed_note: The king sends a letter on Naaman's behalf so that Naaman may be healed; Naaman is not seeking a cure for the king. existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: יַרְדֵּן (Yarden), Greek: Ἰορδάνης (Iordanēs), Aramaic: ירדנא (Yardena)
existing_translation_notes.note: River of Israel central to baptismal symbolism and repeated miracles.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

Naaman asks in verse 17 to carry Israelite soil home to Damascus. Ancient religion generally tied a god to his territory, so a foreigner who wanted to sacrifice to the God of Israel took ground from Israel to build his altar on. The request shows what he had grasped and what he had not, and the text records it without correcting him.

The temple in Damascus in verse 18 belonged to the Aramean storm god Hadad, called Rammanu, the thunderer, in Akkadian, which is where the name Rimmon comes from. Zechariah 12:11 preserves the fuller form Hadad-rimmon. As the king's chief officer, Naaman had to attend the king in that temple and support him when he bowed.

existing_translation_notes.term: Ten talents and six thousand shekels
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 5 has Naaman set out with ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten changes of clothing. A talent is about 75 pounds, so that is roughly 750 pounds of silver and, at about 0.4 ounces to the shekel, some 150 pounds of gold. It is a king's ransom for a cure, and Elisha will not take any of it.

rows.translation_context_note: French, Italian, and Russian already distinguish command from execution; the other affected versions need the same precision.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מָשַׁח (mashach), to smear with oil
existing_translation_notes.note: Olive oil poured from a flask over the head, the act that installed a man in office and made the appointment public and irreversible. Kings, priests, and on occasion prophets were anointed, and the passive participle of this verb, mashiach, is the word behind messiah. Verses 3 and 6 have it done indoors and in a hurry by a young member of a prophetic guild, because this anointing is a coup against a reigning king.

The men who throw Jezebel from the window in verses 32 and 33 are the officers of her own household. The word covers senior court servants of a royal establishment, and in the surrounding empires men in such posts, especially those with access to the women's quarters, were commonly castrated so they could found no line of their own. Isaiah 56:3-5 addresses the standing of such men in Israel directly.

A royal residence of the northern kings at the eastern end of the great valley that carries its name, the one flat corridor across northern Israel. Ahab had a palace there next to Naboth's vineyard, seized after Jezebel had the man killed by false witnesses (1 Kings 21:1-16). Verses 25 and 26 have Jehu throw Joram's body onto that same plot of ground and say why.

Verse 30 says Jezebel set her eyes in pukh and dressed her head. The paint was ground galena or antimony, black, applied around the eye with a small stick from a pot; jars and applicators turn up in graves all over the region. Doing it before appearing at an upper window is the act of a queen presenting herself in state, not a woman hiding.

Jezebel's greeting in verse 31, 'Have you come in peace, O Zimri, murderer of your master,' names a specific man. Zimri commanded half the chariots, killed King Elah while he was drinking, wiped out the royal house, and held the throne seven days before the army made Omri king and Zimri burned the palace down over himself (1 Kings 16:9-20). She is telling Jehu how long she expects his coup to last.

existing_translation_notes.note: Breach of trust against covenant obligations.

A ridge rising to about 1,700 feet on the southeast rim of the Jezreel Valley, roughly fifty miles north of Jerusalem. The valley below is the one open corridor across northern Israel, wide and flat, which is exactly the ground Philistine chariots could use and Israel could not. Saul had to fight there, and the archers on the slope broke his line (verse 3).

The chief god of the Philistine cities, whose temples stood at Ashdod, Gaza, and Beth-shan. The name is tied to dagan, grain, and his worship was a fertility cult of the harvest. Verse 10 has Saul's head fastened up in Dagon's temple, which reverses 1 Samuel 5:1-5, where Dagon's own image fell on its face before the captured ark and broke its head and hands off on the threshold.

A town east of the Jordan in Gilead, about twenty miles south of the Sea of Galilee, and a night's hard march from Beth-shan where the Philistines displayed the bodies. The men of Jabesh went because Saul's first act as king had been to march all night and break Nahash the Ammonite's siege of their town (1 Samuel 11:1-11). They buried his bones under the oak and fasted seven days.

rows.proposed_note: Joab besieges Rabbah; David takes the crown and plunder and puts the people to work. The crown is said to weigh a talent of gold and to be placed on David's head. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

The Ammonite capital, about twenty-three miles east of the Jordan on the King's Highway trade route; the site is modern Amman. It sat on a high citadel above a spring, which is why a siege rather than an assault was needed and why taking the water supply broke it (2 Samuel 12:27). Verse 1 has Joab do the work while David stays home.

Verses 4, 6, and 8 call Sippai, Lahmi, and the six-fingered man at Gath descendants of the Rapha. Israel had met unusually large men before: the spies reported them at Numbers 13:32-33, and Og king of Bashan slept in an iron bed thirteen and a half feet long (Deuteronomy 3:11). They survived in the Philistine cities of the coast after Joshua cleared them from the hill country (Joshua 11:22).

The crown in verse 2 weighs a talent, about 75 pounds. No head wears that, so it was lifted from the idol or the throne and held above David rather than worn; the text says its weight was found to be a talent and that a precious stone from it went into David's crown. As bullion that is a fortune: gold at any period is priced by the ounce, and a talent is about 1,200 troy ounces.

The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. Goliath was 'six cubits and a span' tall, about 9 feet 9 in. A 'long cubit' (Ezekiel 40:5) added a handbreadth.
The width of four fingers, about 3 inches (7.5 cm). Used for small dimensions on temple furniture and as a metaphor for the brevity of life (Psalm 39:5).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: יָם מוּצָק (yam mutsaq), the cast sea
existing_translation_notes.note: A single cast bronze basin, ten cubits across and five deep, about fifteen feet wide and seven and a half feet from brim to floor, standing on twelve bronze oxen in four groups of three facing out. Verse 6 says it was for the priests to wash in, the temple's replacement for the tabernacle's small bronze basin. At 2,000 baths, the figure given in 1 Kings 7:26, and about 5.8 gallons to a bath, that is over eleven thousand gallons of water weighing more than forty tons.

Verse 17 says the king cast the bronze work in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah. Bronze on this scale needed a place with the right casting clay for moulds, fuel, and room for furnaces, and it was done thirty-five miles from the building site, then hauled up. 1 Kings 7:47 says the bronze was never weighed because there was so much of it.

existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 12-15 record a sworn national agreement, not a private resolution: the people bind themselves by oath, with trumpets and rams' horns sounding, to seek the LORD, and verse 13 attaches the death penalty to refusal. A berit was cut, sworn aloud, and witnessed, and it carried stated penalties like any treaty of the period. The scene deliberately repeats the covenant ceremonies at Sinai and Shechem (Exodus 24:3-8, Joshua 24:22-25).

A Canaanite goddess and also the wooden object that stood for her, a pole or carved tree set beside an altar at a high place. Verse 16 says Asa's grandmother Maacah made a repulsive image for her, and Asa cut it down, crushed it, and burned it in the Kidron. Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids planting one beside the altar of the LORD, and inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai show Israelites pairing her name with the LORD's, which is exactly the mixture the reforming kings are tearing out.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֵן מוֹרֶה (kohen moreh), teaching priest
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 3 describes Israel as having gone long stretches without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without the law. Teaching was part of the priest's job description, not an extra: Deuteronomy 33:10 has Levi teach Jacob God's rules, Leviticus 10:11 makes the priests responsible for instructing Israel in the statutes, and Malachi 2:7 says the people should seek instruction from the priest's mouth.

Verse 9 has people from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon settling in Judah in large numbers. Movement ran both ways after the split, and Chronicles keeps recording it: priests and Levites came south under Rehoboam (11:13-14), and Hezekiah later sends couriers north to invite what was left of those tribes to Passover (30:10-11). The border between the two kingdoms was political, and families crossed it.

Verse 16 removes Maacah from being gevirah, a formal office at the court of Judah and not just a family relation. The king's mother held rank, sat at his right (1 Kings 2:19), and is named in the accession formula of almost every king of Judah. Stripping Maacah of the title was a public act of state, which is why it is recorded alongside the burning of her image.

The prophet Huldah tells Josiah disaster will come on Judah but he will die in peace for his repentant heart, so Josiah gathers all the people and renews the covenant to follow the LORD.
rows.concern: The eighteenth regnal year becomes age eighteen; some versions make Josiah read instead of hear. "Die in peace" also obscures the qualified promise.
rows.scripture_says: Repairs begin in the eighteenth year of the king who began at eight. Shaphan reads to Josiah. Huldah promises he will not see the coming disaster.
rows.proposed_summary: Josiah becomes king at eight, spends his youth destroying idols and high places throughout Judah and Israel, and in the eighteenth year of his reign sends officials to repair the temple; during repairs Hilkiah discovers the Book of the Law, and Josiah tears his robes in distress when he hears it read. The prophet Huldah tells Josiah disaster will come on Judah but because of his repentant heart he will not see the coming disaster, so Josiah gathers all the people and renews the covenant to follow the LORD.
cross_references: 2 Kings 22:3: The parallel account dates Josiah's commission to Shaphan to his eighteenth regnal year, confirming that the number describes his reign rather than his age.
2 Chronicles 35:20-24: Josiah is wounded in battle against Neco and dies in Jerusalem, supplying the later event to read beside Huldah's promise.
rows.translation_context_note: The secretary note already identifies Shaphan's role, but no current note addresses regnal age or the relation between the peace promise and Josiah's later death.
rows.proposed_note: The repairs begin in Josiah's eighteenth regnal year, about age twenty-six, and Shaphan reads the book to him. Huldah promises that he will be gathered to his grave in peace without seeing the coming disaster. The later account reports his death from battle wounds; the promise is not a description of an unwounded death.
existing_cross_references: 2 Kings 22:1-20: The same repair of the temple, the same book found by Hilkiah, and the same word from Huldah.
1 Kings 13:1-2: A man of God cries out against the altar at Bethel and names Josiah generations before he is born.
Deuteronomy 31:24-26: Moses puts the book of the law beside the ark of the covenant as a witness against Israel.
Deuteronomy 28:15-68: The curses read out for breaking the covenant, the words that make Josiah tear his clothes.
2 Kings 23:15-20: Josiah pulls down the altar at Bethel and burns the bones out of the tombs on it, as the man of God had said.

existing_translation_notes.note: A book at this period is a scroll of sheets sewn end to end, written on leather or papyrus and rolled, not a bound volume. Verse 15 has Hilkiah find one in the temple during the repairs and hand it to the royal secretary, who reads it aloud to the king; there was no expectation that the king read it himself. Deuteronomy 31:24-26 has Moses order the book of the law placed beside the ark, and 17:18-19 requires each king to have a copy made and read it all his life.

Verse 19 records the king's reaction to hearing the book read. Tearing the garment from the neck down was the standard public sign of grief or horror in Israel, used at news of a death (Genesis 37:34), at defeat, and at blasphemy heard in court (Matthew 26:65). It was a visible act done in front of witnesses, which is why the text records who saw it.

Verse 5 has Josiah burn the bones of the pagan priests on their own altars. Contact with a human corpse or grave made a person or place unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), so scattering the dust of the idols over the graves of their worshippers and burning bones on the altars put those sites permanently out of use. 2 Kings 23:15-18 records him doing the same at Bethel.

Shaphan in verses 8-18 is not a copyist. The sofer was a cabinet officer of the crown, listed with the army commander and the recorder among the king's chief men (2 Samuel 8:16-17), handling correspondence, records, and revenue; 2 Kings 12:10 has the king's secretary count the temple money alongside the high priest. Verse 8 sends him out with the governor of the city and the recorder, mazkir, another standing office of state.

Verse 22 sends the high priest, the king's secretary, and three other senior officials to a woman living in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem to authenticate the book. Jeremiah and Zephaniah were both prophesying at the time, and the delegation went to Huldah. She is one of a small number of women named as prophets in Scripture, with Miriam, Deborah, and Noadiah (Exodus 15:20, Judges 4:4, Nehemiah 6:14).

rows.current_summary: Enemies of Judah and Benjamin offer to help build the temple and are refused; they discourage the builders, hire counselors against them, and write letters to Persian kings accusing Jerusalem of rebellion, until Artaxerxes orders the work stopped by force and construction ceases until the second year of Darius.
rows.current_summary_original: Enemies of Judah and Benjamin offer to help build the temple and are refused; they discourage the builders, hire counselors against them, and write letters to Persian kings accusing Jerusalem of rebellion, until Artaxerxes orders the work stopped by force and construction ceases until the second year of Darius.
rows.concern: The summary turns a topical collection of later opposition letters into a chronological cause of the earlier temple halt.
rows.scripture_says: Verses 6-23 describe later city opposition under Xerxes and Artaxerxes; verse 24 resumes the temple account under Darius.
rows.proposed_summary: Enemies oppose the temple rebuilding from Cyrus to Darius. The chapter also recounts later accusations under Xerxes and Artaxerxes, including an order to halt rebuilding Jerusalem; verse 24 returns to the temple work halted until Darius's second year.
cross_references: Ezra 6:15: The temple is completed in Darius's sixth year, establishing its completion before the later Artaxerxes narrative.
Ezra 7:1: The narrative explicitly moves many years later to Artaxerxes' reign, distinguishing that setting from the temple's completion under Darius.
Nehemiah 2:1-8: Artaxerxes authorizes Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem and obtain timber for its gates and wall, supplying the later city-rebuilding setting.
rows.translation_context_note: The current kings-out-of-order note already explains this correctly. The summary contradicts it.
rows.proposed_note: The chapter groups opposition from different reigns. The letters under Xerxes and Artaxerxes concern Jerusalem and its rebuilding; verse 24 returns to the earlier temple interruption under Darius. Artaxerxes' order is not the cause of an interruption that ended before his reign.
existing_cross_references: 2 Kings 17:24-34: Assyria settles men from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim in the towns of Samaria, where they fear the LORD and serve their own gods.
Nehemiah 4:1-9: Sanballat and Tobiah jeer at the wall and then conspire to attack it.
Daniel 6:4-9: Officials who can find no fault in a man engineer a written royal decree that traps him.
Esther 3:8-11: A minister persuades a Persian king by charging that one people keeps laws unlike the king's laws.
Ezra 6:1-5: Darius orders the archives searched, and the scroll of Cyrus is found at Ecbatana.

existing_translation_notes.note: From 4:8 to 6:18, and again at 7:12-26, Ezra is written in Aramaic instead of Hebrew. Aramaic was the working language of Persian government from Egypt to India, so the letters, decrees and court records are quoted in the language they were actually filed in, while the narrative around them stays in Hebrew. The other Aramaic in Scripture is Daniel 2:4b-7:28, Jeremiah 10:11, and two words in Genesis 31:47.

existing_translation_notes.original: Aramaic: עֲבַר נַהֲרָה (avar naharah) - Hebrew: עֵבֶר הַנָּהָר (ever hannahar)
existing_translation_notes.note: The Persian satrapy west of the Euphrates, taking in Syria, Phoenicia, Cyprus and the whole land bridge down to the Egyptian frontier. The name is written from the imperial capital looking west, so 'beyond the river' means beyond the Euphrates. Judah, called Yehud, was one small province inside it, and every letter in this chapter travels up and down that chain of command.

existing_translation_notes.original: Aramaic: בְּעֵל־טְעֵם (be'el te'em, commanding officer) - סָפְרָא (safra, scribe)
existing_translation_notes.note: These are job titles, not honorifics. Be'el te'em is the provincial officer responsible for reports and decrees, and the safra is the secretary who drafted and filed the correspondence. The complaint against Jerusalem goes forward through the ordinary provincial paperwork, correctly formatted and correctly addressed.

existing_translation_notes.original: Aramaic: מִנְדָּה בְלוֹ וַהֲלָךְ (mindah, belo, va-halakh)
existing_translation_notes.note: Three separate Persian revenue streams, named again at 4:20 and 7:24. Mindah is the assessed tribute of a province, belo is a levy in kind or produce, halakh is a toll on goods in transit. The accusation in 4:13 is not religious; it is that a walled Jerusalem will stop paying all three.

existing_translation_notes.term: The kings in this chapter are out of order
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 6 names Ahasuerus (Xerxes, 486-465 BC) and verses 7-23 name Artaxerxes (465-424 BC), both of whom reigned after Darius, and then 4:24 picks the story back up in the reign of Darius (522-486 BC). The chapter gathers the whole file of opposition letters in one place before returning to the sequence of events. Read it as a dossier dropped into the narrative, not as a calendar.

The hill country north of Judah and the capital of the northern kingdom from about 880 BC until Assyria took it in 722 BC and deported the population. The men who offer to help build in 4:2 are descended from the settlers Assyria moved in afterwards, which is why they can say they have sacrificed to the God of Israel since Esarhaddon brought them up. The refusal in 4:3 is the beginning of the split that hardens into the Samaritan quarrel of the Gospels.
