rows.current_summary: Eliphaz responds by reminding Job of his past wisdom and suggesting that the innocent do not perish, implying Job must have done wrong; he then recounts a frightening nighttime vision in which a spirit told him that mortals cannot be righteous before God and are fragile creatures who perish without understanding.
rows.current_summary_original: Eliphaz responds by reminding Job of his past wisdom and suggesting that the innocent do not perish, implying Job must have done wrong; he then recounts a frightening nighttime vision in which a spirit told him that mortals cannot be righteous before God and are fragile creatures who perish without understanding.
rows.concern: The summary turns the reported spirit's comparative question into a categorical denial of human righteousness.
rows.scripture_says: In the app's text the question is whether a mortal can be more righteous than God or more pure than his Maker. Eliphaz is the speaker reporting the encounter.
rows.proposed_summary: Eliphaz implies that Job's suffering exposes wrongdoing, then describes a frightening night encounter with a spirit. In the account he reports, the spirit asks whether a mortal can be more righteous than God and stresses human frailty.
cross_references: Job 1:1: The narrator introduces Job as blameless and upright, establishing the characterization against which Eliphaz's accusations must be read.
Job 42:7-8: The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for speaking inaccurately about Him and directs them to seek Job's intercession.
rows.translation_context_note: The current speaker-warning note and Job 42 reference already protect against treating the friends' claims as God's teaching. The summary still changes the wording of the question.
rows.proposed_note: Eliphaz is reporting the spirit's words, not narrating a statement God has independently authenticated. This translation asks whether a mortal can be more righteous than God. The book introduces Job as upright and later records God's rebuke of Eliphaz and his friends.
existing_cross_references: Job 42:7-8: When the LORD finally speaks He addresses Eliphaz the Temanite by name and tells him, 'My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has.'
Galatians 6:7-8: A man reaps what he sows, the proverb Eliphaz is applying at Job 4:8.
Job 15:14-16: Eliphaz repeats the night vision's argument almost word for word in his second speech.
Genesis 15:12: A deep sleep and a dreadful great darkness fall on Abram just before God speaks to him, the same word Eliphaz uses of his night at 4:13.
1 Kings 22:21-22: A spirit comes forward and stands before the LORD in the council and offers to speak, the only other place a spirit steps out like this.

existing_translation_notes.note: A district of Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea, named for a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11,15). It had a standing reputation for wisdom, which is why Jeremiah taunts it: is there no longer any wisdom in Teman (Jeremiah 49:7)? Eliphaz is introduced by that address the way a modern speaker might be introduced by a university. Inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, written about the eighth century BC, refer to the LORD of Teman.

Not ordinary sleep. This is the heavy trance that falls on a man when God is about to act or speak: on Adam before the woman is made (Genesis 2:21), on Abram at the covenant between the pieces (Genesis 15:12), on Saul's camp when David walks through it (1 Samuel 26:12). Eliphaz uses the word to claim his night experience was a genuine revelation and not a bad dream.

An ordinary house was mud brick on a stone footing, and mud brick dissolves. A wall left unmaintained through two or three wet winters slumps back into the ground it came from, which is why ancient towns rebuilt on their own debris. Eliphaz means the human body, and the picture would land instantly on anyone who had watched an abandoned house melt.

A black goat-hair tent stands only by the tension between its poles and its guy ropes, staked into the ground. Pull the cords and the whole thing collapses at once. It was the standard picture for a life ending suddenly (Isaiah 38:12), and it fits Job, whose household lived in exactly such tents in verse 19 of chapter 1.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: five words in 4:10-11: אַרְיֵה (aryeh), שָׁחַל (shachal), כְּפִיר (kefir), לַיִשׁ (layish), לָבִיא (lavi)
existing_translation_notes.note: Two verses use five different Hebrew words for lion, and English has only the one, so the effect vanishes in translation. Lions lived in the Jordan thickets and the Syrian steppe into historical memory and were hunted by kings from Assyria to Persia; the last lions in the region were shot out during the nineteenth century. Eliphaz is piling up names for the strongest predator anyone knew, to say that even it starves.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: לֹא דִבַּרְתֶּם אֵלַי נְכוֹנָה (lo dibbartem elai nekhonah)
existing_translation_notes.note: This chapter opens the friends' speeches, which fill most of the book. At the end the LORD names Eliphaz the Temanite, the speaker here, and says 'My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has' (Job 42:7). He says it a second time in the next verse and orders seven bulls and seven rams brought so that Job can pray for them (42:8). Lines quoted out of chapters 4 through 25 are the friends talking, and the book records that verdict on them.

rows.current_summary: Job catalogs the injustices perpetrated by the wicked - stealing, exploiting the poor and vulnerable, committing murder and adultery under cover of darkness - and argues that despite their temporary success, God ultimately brings them down to death and obscurity.
rows.current_summary_original: Job catalogs the injustices perpetrated by the wicked - stealing, exploiting the poor and vulnerable, committing murder and adultery under cover of darkness - and argues that despite their temporary success, God ultimately brings them down to death and obscurity.
rows.concern: The takeaway makes the chapter sound like a settled explanation of prompt moral retribution while omitting its opening protest about delayed justice.
rows.scripture_says: Job asks why judgment is not visible, catalogs oppression, and later describes the wicked's insecurity and death.
rows.proposed_summary: Job asks why the Almighty's judgment is not visible while the vulnerable are robbed, exploited, and killed. He describes wicked people acting under darkness, then their insecurity and death, challenging anyone to refute his account.
cross_references: Job 21:7-16: Job protests that wicked people can enjoy long lives, secure homes, and prosperity, challenging a simple equation between present success and righteousness.
Job 42:7-8: The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for speaking inaccurately about Him and directs them to seek Job's intercession.
rows.translation_context_note: The current notes explain the forms of oppression but do not preserve the opening question. This is a context proposal, not a claim that the closing verses are absent.
rows.proposed_note: This remains Job's speech in a debate. His opening question and the statement that God charges no one with wrongdoing describe the apparent delay of justice. The later description of the wicked's end does not erase that protest or prove that every sufferer is being punished for personal wrongdoing.
existing_cross_references: Deuteronomy 19:14: Do not move your neighbour's boundary marker, set up by those who came before you.
Proverbs 22:28: Do not move the ancient boundary stone that your fathers set up.
Deuteronomy 24:19-21: The forgotten sheaf, the olive branch and the fallen grapes are left for the poor and the widow.
Malachi 3:5: I will be a swift witness against those who defraud labourers of their wages and oppress the widow.
Amos 8:4-6: Those who trample the needy, cheat with the ephah and the shekel, and sell the sweepings of the wheat.

existing_translation_notes.note: Fields had no fences. The line between one man's land and the next was marked by stones, and moving them by a pace at a time quietly stole a crop and could not easily be proved. The law names it three times and puts a public curse on it (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17; Proverbs 22:28). In Babylonia the same crime was blocked with carved boundary stones that recorded the grant and called down curses on anyone who shifted them.

Seizing a widow's ox or the donkey of an orphan as loan security took away the animal they ploughed and carried with, so the security destroyed the ability to repay. The law forbids taking a millstone in pledge for the same reason: it would be taking a man's livelihood as security (Deuteronomy 24:6). Job is listing lending practices that were legal in form and ruinous in fact.

existing_translation_notes.term: Glean the vineyards of the wicked
existing_translation_notes.note: Gleaning was a legal right, not charity: the harvester was forbidden to reap the field's corners, go back for a forgotten sheaf, or strip a vine or olive tree twice, and what was left belonged to the poor, the widow, the orphan and the foreigner (Leviticus 19:9-10; Deuteronomy 24:19-21). Ruth lives on it (Ruth 2). Job's protest in verses 6 to 11 is that the poor now glean for the men who are robbing them.

existing_translation_notes.term: Tread the winepresses but go thirsty
existing_translation_notes.note: A winepress was two rock-cut basins, an upper treading floor where grapes were crushed underfoot and a lower vat the juice ran into through a channel. Hundreds are still cut into the bedrock across the hill country. Treading was hot, communal work done at harvest and traditionally accompanied by singing, and the treaders drank. Job's line describes men doing that work and not being allowed a mouthful.

House walls were mud brick, so a thief did not pick a lock, he cut a hole through the wall. The law recognises the crime by that name and rules on a householder who kills a burglar found breaking in at night (Exodus 22:2-3). Jesus uses the same picture of the thief digging through (Matthew 6:19-20; 24:43). Verse 16 is a technical description of a real method.

rows.current_summary: God favors honesty, humility, and righteousness while detesting dishonesty, pride, and wickedness; the righteous find safety and prosperity while the wicked face ruin through their own actions.
rows.current_summary_original: God favors honesty, humility, and righteousness while detesting dishonesty, pride, and wickedness; the righteous find safety and prosperity while the wicked face ruin through their own actions.
rows.concern: The summary can be read as a blanket promise of wealth and physical safety for every righteous person.
rows.scripture_says: The chapter teaches the value and outcomes of integrity, generosity, and righteous conduct through wisdom sayings, not a narrated guarantee that the righteous never suffer.
rows.proposed_summary: These wisdom sayings commend honesty, humility, generosity, and righteousness, contrasting their life-giving effects with the ruin caused by deceit and greed. They warn against trusting riches and praise those who refresh others.
cross_references: Job 21:7-16: Job protests that wicked people can enjoy long lives, secure homes, and prosperity, challenging a simple equation between present success and righteousness.
Ecclesiastes 7:15: The speaker observes a righteous person dying and a wicked person living long, supplying an explicit counterexample to guaranteed earthly safety.
rows.translation_context_note: The current notes explain trade and wealth but do not identify this genre limit. The proposal removes an especially broad prosperity formulation rather than rewriting every proverb as a conditional statement.
rows.proposed_note: These are wisdom sayings about righteous and wicked ways. They are not a promise that every faithful person will become wealthy or avoid suffering. Job and Ecclesiastes explicitly describe exceptions to a simple equation between present prosperity and righteousness.
existing_cross_references: Leviticus 19:35-36: The law requires honest scales and weights, an honest ephah and an honest hin.
Deuteronomy 25:13-16: Carrying two differing weights in the bag is called detestable to the LORD.
Proverbs 6:1-5: How to escape after striking hands in pledge and putting up security for a neighbor.
1 Kings 12:6-11: Rehoboam takes the advice of his contemporaries over the elders and loses ten tribes.
Genesis 41:56-57: Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain to Egypt and to every nation during the famine.

existing_translation_notes.note: Literally balances of deceit. There were no coins in Israel in Solomon's day; silver was weighed out on a balance against stone weights carried in a pouch, so a trader who kept a light set for selling and a heavy set for buying stole from every customer. The law bans exactly that in Leviticus 19:35-36 and Deuteronomy 25:13-16. Inscribed stone weights have been dug up in Judah, including the pym, the fee the Philistines charged for sharpening tools in 1 Samuel 13:21.

existing_translation_notes.term: Gold ring in a pig's snout
existing_translation_notes.note: The nezem is a nose ring, ordinary jewelry for a woman of means; Abraham's servant puts one on Rebekah's nose in Genesis 24:22 and 24:47. The pig was an unclean animal that no Israelite household kept (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8). The proverb fastens the finest ornament a woman owned to the filthiest animal a listener could picture.

existing_translation_notes.term: Puts up security for a stranger
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עָרַב (arav) - Hebrew: תָּקַע כַּף (taqa kaf)
existing_translation_notes.note: To go surety is to make yourself liable for another man's debt, and the deal was closed by striking hands, taqa kaf (Proverbs 6:1-5; 17:18). If the debtor defaulted the creditor came after the guarantor. Proverbs 20:16 and 27:13 tell the lender to take the cloak of any man foolish enough to do this for a stranger, and 22:26-27 warns that the bed can be dragged out from under him.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מֹנֵעַ בָּר (monea bar) - Hebrew: מַשְׁבִּיר (mashbir)
existing_translation_notes.note: Grain was stored in sealed pits and jars and drawn down through the year, so in a lean season whoever held stock set the price of bread. The mashbir is the one who breaks into his store and sells; the monea bar holds it back until the price climbs. Amos 8:4-6 shows the same trade from the inside, dealers waiting for the new moon and the sabbath to be over so they can sell with a short measure and a heavy weight.

Literally takes lives. Nephesh is not an immaterial part of a person; it is the whole breathing creature, which is why Genesis 2:7 calls the man himself a living nephesh. The same two words joined together elsewhere mean to take a life away, as in Psalm 31:13, where enemies plot to take the psalmist's life.

rows.current_summary: The woman wishes her lover were her brother so she could show him affection publicly, declares that love is stronger than death and cannot be extinguished by any force, and urges him to come to her swiftly. She also reflects on protecting her younger sister and claims her vineyard as her own possession.
rows.current_summary_original: The woman wishes her lover were her brother so she could show him affection publicly, declares that love is stronger than death and cannot be extinguished by any force, and urges him to come to her swiftly. She also reflects on protecting her younger sister and claims her vineyard as her own possession.
rows.concern: "Stronger than death" changes the comparison, and the last sentence assigns the family's little-sister speech to the woman.
rows.scripture_says: Love is as strong as death. Verses 8-9 use a plural family voice, followed by the woman's reply in verse 10.
rows.proposed_summary: The woman longs for open affection and declares love as strong as death, unquenchable and beyond purchase. The poem also asks what will be done for a little sister and records the woman's reply that she is a wall. The lovers close with an invitation to come swiftly.
cross_references: Genesis 29:18-20: Jacob's love for Rachel makes seven years of service seem like a few days, providing a narrative parallel for the strength of love.
rows.translation_context_note: The current little-sister note explicitly identifies the brothers' speech and her answer. The summary contradicts it.
rows.proposed_note: Verse 6 says love is as strong as death, not stronger. The speakers are not named in the Hebrew poem; verses 8-9 are commonly read as the brothers' words, with the woman replying in verse 10. They are not safely summarized as her plan to protect a younger sister.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 38:18: Judah hands over his seal, his cord and his staff as a pledge, the seal standing for the man himself.
Haggai 2:23: I will make you like My signet ring, for I have chosen you, says the LORD of Hosts.
Deuteronomy 6:8: Tie these words as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads.
Genesis 29:18-20: Jacob serves seven years for Rachel, and they seem like a few days to him because of his love.
Matthew 21:33-41: A landowner plants a vineyard, walls it, digs a winepress and leases it to tenants for a share of the fruit.

existing_translation_notes.term: If only you were my brother
existing_translation_notes.note: 8:1 is not a wish to be related to him. A woman could greet a brother with a kiss in the street and nobody would think anything of it; showing affection to a man who was not kin in public brought contempt. She is saying she wishes she could touch him outside without paying for it, and 8:2 then takes him indoors to her mother's house.

A seal was a man's legal identity, not an ornament. It was cut from stone as a cylinder worn on a cord at the throat, or set as a stamp in a ring worn on the hand, and pressing it into clay signed a document and marked property as his. Judah hands over his seal and cord as a pledge (Genesis 38:18), Jezebel seals letters with Ahab's seal so they carry the king's authority (1 Kings 21:8), and Haggai 2:23 has the LORD make Zerubbabel like His signet ring. The heart and the arm named in 8:6 are the two places a seal was actually worn.

Sheol is the Old Testament word for the grave and the realm of the dead, where all descend (Genesis 37:35, Psalm 16:10), and the Septuagint renders it with the Greek hades. What 8:6 draws on is one property of it: Sheol does not let go and never gives anything back. Qin'ah is rendered jealousy or ardour and is the same word used for God's own zeal at Exodus 20:5.

One Hebrew word at the end of 8:6, built from shalhevet, a flame, with the ending yah, the short form of the divine name that also closes hallelujah. It is the only place in the Song where any form of the name of God appears at all. Versions render it a most vehement flame or the very flame of the LORD, depending on whether the ending is read as a superlative or as the name.

existing_translation_notes.term: All the wealth of his house
existing_translation_notes.note: Marriage in Israel was contracted with a mohar, a bride price weighed out by the groom's family to the bride's (Genesis 34:12, Exodus 22:16-17). 8:7 puts that transaction on the table and says a man offering the entire estate of his house for love would be utterly despised, which is the one thing in the book priced and then refused a price.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בַּיּוֹם שֶׁיְּדֻבַּר־בָּהּ (ba-yom she-yedubbar bah, the day she is spoken for)
existing_translation_notes.note: 8:8-9 is the brothers holding a family council. A girl's marriage was negotiated by the men of her household, and their question is what they will do when the offer comes. A wall gets battlements of silver and a door gets barred with cedar planks; either way they are deciding in advance what they will build around her. 8:10 is her answer, that she is a wall already.

A place named nowhere else in Scripture; the name reads as owner of a multitude. 8:11 has Solomon leasing the vineyard out to tenants, which is how a large holding was worked: the tenant farms it and pays the owner a fixed sum out of the crop. 8:12 then sets the arrangement aside, my own vineyard is before me.

Rent on a leased vineyard, paid in weighed silver rather than coin. A shekel ran about four tenths of an ounce, so a thousand shekels is roughly twenty-five pounds of metal. Isaiah 7:23 prices planted vines at a thousand silver shekels for a thousand vines, one shekel a vine, which puts a vineyard of that rent at about that size. The two hundred held back at 8:12 for the men who tend the fruit is a fifth of the total.

rows.current_summary: Rezin of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah march against Jerusalem, and the LORD sends Isaiah to tell the trembling Ahaz that their plot will not stand; when Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, the Lord gives one anyway, the virgin conceiving and bearing a son called Immanuel, and before the boy knows to reject evil the land of the two dreaded kings will be laid waste, yet the LORD will also bring the king of Assyria on Judah, a hired razor that leaves the land to curds and honey, briers and thorns.
rows.current_summary_original: Rezin of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah march against Jerusalem, and the LORD sends Isaiah to tell the trembling Ahaz that their plot will not stand; when Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, the Lord gives one anyway, the virgin conceiving and bearing a son called Immanuel, and before the boy knows to reject evil the land of the two dreaded kings will be laid waste, yet the LORD will also bring the king of Assyria on Judah, a hired razor that leaves the land to curds and honey, briers and thorns.
rows.concern: Note-focused: the summary follows the base translation, but the virgin/young-woman translation distinction and the two contextual horizons are not explained.
rows.scripture_says: The sign addresses Ahaz's crisis before the two threatening kings fall. Matthew later applies the Greek wording to Jesus' birth.
rows.proposed_summary: Rezin of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah march against Jerusalem, and the LORD sends Isaiah to tell the trembling Ahaz that their plot will not stand; when Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, the Lord gives one anyway, the virgin conceiving and bearing a son called Immanuel, and before the boy knows to reject evil the land of the two dreaded kings will be laid waste, yet the LORD will also bring the king of Assyria on Judah, a hired razor that leaves the land to curds and honey, briers and thorns.
cross_references: 2 Kings 16:5-9: Ahaz faces Rezin and Pekah's siege and appeals to Assyria for help, establishing the political crisis addressed by Isaiah's sign.
Matthew 1:22-23: Matthew presents Jesus' birth as fulfillment of the Immanuel prophecy, supplying the New Testament application alongside Isaiah's setting under Ahaz.
rows.translation_context_note: Both contextual references are already linked. The current Immanuel note defines the name but omits the translation issue. Preserve the app's chosen verse translation; the proposal is an added context note, not a declaration that one reading is fraudulent.
rows.proposed_note: The Hebrew word almah is translated virgin here and young woman in some other versions. Isaiah 7:16 connects the sign with the crisis facing Ahaz; Matthew 1:22-23 applies the Greek wording to Jesus' virgin birth. The immediate setting and Matthew's application are both part of the biblical context.
existing_cross_references: 2 Kings 16:5-9: Rezin and Pekah besiege Ahaz, who strips the temple and the palace treasury to hire Tiglath-pileser of Assyria against them.
2 Chronicles 28:5-8: Aram and Israel inflict heavy losses on Ahaz, killing 120,000 men of Judah in one day and carrying off 200,000 captives.
Matthew 1:22-23: Matthew cites the sign given here, the virgin who will be with child and bear a son called Immanuel, God with us.
Deuteronomy 6:16: Israel is commanded not to test the LORD as they tested Him at Massah, the rule Ahaz hides behind when he refuses a sign.
2 Kings 15:29-30: Tiglath-pileser captures Ijon, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee and deports the people, and Hoshea kills Pekah.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עִמָּנוּ אֵל (‘Immanu-El, ‘God with us’), Greek (LXX): Ἐμμανουήλ, Aramaic: עמנואל
existing_translation_notes.note: Name announced as the sign in 7:14 and echoed in 8:8-10.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עַלְמָה (‘almah, ‘young woman’), Greek (LXX): παρθένος (parthenos), Aramaic: עַלִימְתָא
existing_translation_notes.note: Word used in (7:14); Hebrew denotes a young woman of marriageable age; Greek renders with ‘virgin.’

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאָר יָשׁוּב (She’ar-yashuv, ‘a remnant shall return’)
existing_translation_notes.note: Isaiah’s son accompanying him in 7:3.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

existing_translation_notes.term: Rezin and the son of Remaliah
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֲרָם (Aram), Syria - אֶפְרַיִם (Efrayim), the northern kingdom
existing_translation_notes.note: Isaiah 7 sits inside a specific crisis. Rezin, king of Aram at Damascus, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, joined against Assyria and marched on Jerusalem to force Judah into their alliance and put their own man, the son of Tabeal, on David's throne (7:1-6). Ahaz instead bought Assyrian help; 2 Kings 16:7-9 records the payment and the result, with Tiglath-Pileser taking Damascus and killing Rezin. This is the war behind everything Isaiah says to Ahaz here.

existing_translation_notes.term: the road to the Launderer's Field
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: שְׂדֵה כוֹבֵס (sedeh khoves), the field of the fuller
existing_translation_notes.note: A fuller cleaned and finished newly woven wool by treading it in tubs, using stale urine for its ammonia and alkaline earth as a scouring agent, then bleaching and stretching it out to dry. The work needed running water and a large open drying field, and it stank, so the fuller worked outside the city walls. This spot by the upper pool's channel was the obvious place to meet a king inspecting his water supply before a siege, and Isaiah 36:2 has the Assyrian envoy stand on the same ground a generation later.

rows.current_summary: Isaiah prophesies the sudden destruction of Moab's cities, describing widespread mourning, shaved heads, sackcloth, and weeping across the land as people flee and their resources are stripped away. The waters dry up, vegetation withers, and Isaiah declares he will bring additional judgment - a lion - upon Moab's fugitives and those remaining.
rows.current_summary_original: Isaiah prophesies the sudden destruction of Moab's cities, describing widespread mourning, shaved heads, sackcloth, and weeping across the land as people flee and their resources are stripped away. The waters dry up, vegetation withers, and Isaiah declares he will bring additional judgment - a lion - upon Moab's fugitives and those remaining.
rows.concern: The summary makes Isaiah personally the bringer of the final judgment.
rows.scripture_says: The prophetic oracle announces added judgment in the first person; Isaiah is its messenger, not the one personally inflicting it.
rows.proposed_summary: Isaiah announces Moab's devastation, mourning, fleeing populations, and ruined water and vegetation. The oracle ends with a threat of further judgment, pictured as a lion against Moab's fugitives and survivors.
cross_references: Jeremiah 48:1-5: The LORD announces Moab's devastation and the mourning of its towns, providing a parallel divine oracle rather than an action personally inflicted by Isaiah.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Moab notes give history and geography but do not distinguish the prophet's delivery of the oracle from the threatened action.
rows.proposed_note: The first-person threat belongs to the prophetic announcement of judgment. The chapter does not depict Isaiah personally attacking Moab or bringing a lion against its refugees.
existing_cross_references: Numbers 21:27-30: The ballad of Heshbon names Ar of Moab, Dibon, Nophah, and Medeba, the same towns Isaiah lists in ruins.
Jeremiah 48:1-3: Jeremiah's oracle against Moab opens with Nebo devastated, Kiriathaim captured, and a cry from Horonaim.
Genesis 19:36-37: Lot's older daughter bears a son named Moab, the father of the Moabites.
Deuteronomy 2:9: Israel is told not to harass Moab, because the LORD has given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.
Deuteronomy 14:1: Israel is forbidden to cut themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead, the mourning rites Isaiah 15:2 describes in Moab.

existing_translation_notes.note: Moab held the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, good sheep country, and it was a relative: Genesis 19:37 traces the nation to Lot. Its god was Chemosh, which is why Numbers 21:29 calls Moabites the people of Chemosh and 1 Kings 11:7 has Solomon building him a high place outside Jerusalem. What that worship could involve is recorded at 2 Kings 3:27, where the king of Moab, losing a siege, offered his own eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite victory inscription of the ninth century BC found at Dhiban in 1868, has that same king credit Chemosh with his wars against Israel.
Variant forms in (15:9) and (15:2) place associated with bloodshed imagery.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

existing_translation_notes.term: The towns of the Moab oracle
existing_translation_notes.note: 15:1-9 names about a dozen real towns on the plateau east of the Dead Sea and expects the reader to know the map. Several of them appear on a stone found in 1868 at Dhiban, the biblical Dibon: an inscription set up by Mesha king of Moab in the ninth century BC, which names Chemosh over and over, names Omri king of Israel, and names Nebo and Medeba as towns Mesha took back. The names in this chapter are places that were still standing when it was written.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: קָרְחָה (qorchah, baldness) - גְּרוּעָה (geru'ah, cut off)
existing_translation_notes.note: 15:2-3 has Moab mourning with every head shaved, every beard cut, sackcloth in the streets and weeping on the housetops. Roofs were flat and were living space, so grief went on in public view. Israel was forbidden this particular form of it: Leviticus 19:27-28 and Deuteronomy 14:1 bar shaving the head and gashing the body for the dead, which is why the description reads as foreign practice.

rows.current_summary: Moab is urged to send tribute and shelter fugitives, but Isaiah laments Moab's pride and her coming destruction - her vineyards will wither, her joy will cease, and within three years her splendor and people will be greatly diminished. A future ruler from David's house will establish a throne of justice and faithfulness.

A future ruler from David's house will establish a throne of justice and faithfulness.
rows.concern: The summary gives the sheltering request to Moab as its duty, although the app's wording asks for refuge for Moab.
rows.scripture_says: The appeal asks that fugitives stay with the addressee and that refuge be given to Moab from the destroyer.
rows.proposed_summary: The oracle calls for tribute to Zion and voices an appeal for shelter for Moab's fugitives. It anticipates a faithful ruler in David's house, then laments Moab's pride and ruined vineyards and announces that its glory will fade within three years.
cross_references: Jeremiah 48:29-33: The oracle condemns Moab's pride and laments ruined vineyards and lost harvest joy, paralleling Isaiah 16's judgment and mourning.
rows.translation_context_note: The current hesed note addresses the throne in verse 5, not the dialogue in verses 3-4. The proposal names the displayed reading while leaving room for the known translation ambiguity.
rows.proposed_note: In the wording used here, the appeal asks that Moab's fugitives receive refuge. English versions differ over the speakers and the relationship of Moab to the fugitives, so the summary needs to follow the displayed translation without reversing who seeks shelter.
existing_cross_references: 2 Kings 3:4-5: Mesha king of Moab, a sheep breeder, pays Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams, then rebels after Ahab dies.
Jeremiah 48:29-33: Jeremiah repeats the charge of Moab's pride and mourns the vine of Sibmah and the winepresses that no longer run.
Numbers 32:37-38: Reuben rebuilds Heshbon, Nebo, Baal-meon, and Sibmah, towns that later pass into Moabite hands.
Ruth 4:13-17: Ruth the Moabite bears Obed, who becomes the father of Jesse, the father of David, whose tent Isaiah 16:5 names.
Amos 2:1-3: Moab is judged for burning to lime the bones of Edom's king, and fire consumes the citadels of Kerioth.

existing_translation_notes.note: Location in 16:1 on the route mentioned.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: כִּשְׁנֵי שָׂכִיר (kishnei sakir); Greek (LXX): ὡς ἔτη μισθωτοῦ
existing_translation_notes.note: Precise time reckoning for three years (16:14).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek (LXX): ἔλεος, Aramaic: חסדא
existing_translation_notes.note: Term in 16:5 describing the established throne; listed without interpretation.

existing_translation_notes.term: Send the lamb to the ruler
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: שִׁלְחוּ־כַר (shilchu khar, send a lamb)
existing_translation_notes.note: 16:1 is tribute, paid the way a herding country pays it. 2 Kings 3:4 gives the figures for the same arrangement: Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder and delivered a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams to the king of Israel every year, and stopped when Ahab died. Sending the lamb from Sela to Zion is Moab asking for shelter with the payment in front.

existing_translation_notes.term: The vines of Sibmah and the shout in the presses
existing_translation_notes.note: 16:8-10 is Moab's wine country going silent. Grapes were trodden barefoot in a rock-cut vat with the juice running through a channel into a lower basin, and the treaders sang and called in rhythm to keep time; hedad is the word for that shout. 16:10 says the treader treads out no wine and the shout has been stopped, and Jeremiah 48:32-33 repeats the same lines about the same vineyards.

rows.current_summary: Isaiah pronounces judgment on Egypt: the Lord will cause internal strife, dry up the Nile, devastate crops and livelihoods, and confound Egypt's leaders; yet he also promises that future Egyptian cities will speak Canaan's language, build altars to the Lord, and worship alongside Assyria and Israel.
rows.current_summary_original: Isaiah pronounces judgment on Egypt: the Lord will cause internal strife, dry up the Nile, devastate crops and livelihoods, and confound Egypt's leaders; yet he also promises that future Egyptian cities will speak Canaan's language, build altars to the Lord, and worship alongside Assyria and Israel.
rows.concern: The summary turns the chapter's singular altar into multiple altars built by the cities.
rows.scripture_says: Five cities speak the language of Canaan; an altar stands in Egypt's center and a pillar near its border.
rows.proposed_summary: Isaiah announces judgment on Egypt's society, river, livelihoods, and leaders. He also pictures five cities turning to the LORD, an altar and boundary pillar as witnesses, and Egypt, Assyria, and Israel worshiping under God's blessing.
cross_references: Zephaniah 3:9-10: God promises purified speech and worshipers bringing offerings from beyond Cush, paralleling the vision of nations turning to His worship.
rows.translation_context_note: The current altar/pillar note already gives the singular pair and its purpose. The summary should retain that distinction.
rows.proposed_note: Verse 18 names five cities speaking Canaan's language. Verse 19 then describes one altar in Egypt's center and one pillar near its border, rather than a separate altar in every city.
existing_cross_references: Exodus 7:20-21: Aaron strikes the water of the Nile, it turns to blood, the fish die, and the Egyptians cannot drink from the river.
Exodus 12:12: The LORD declares He will execute judgment on all the gods of Egypt on the night of the Passover.
Psalm 78:43: God performed His signs in Egypt and His wonders in the fields of Zoan, the city whose princes Isaiah calls fools.

existing_translation_notes.term: The flax workers and the weavers
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פִּשְׁתִּים שְׂרִיקוֹת (pishtim seriqoth, combed flax)
existing_translation_notes.note: 19:9 names the trade Egypt was known for across the ancient world. Flax was grown on the flooded fields, retted in water, combed out and spun into linen so fine that Egyptian linen was a luxury export everywhere, and it was the cloth Egyptian priests were required to wear. The whole industry depended on the Nile rising, which is why 19:5-10 runs from the water failing to the fishermen mourning to the weavers ruined, in that order.

existing_translation_notes.note: Fixed resolve amid abuse (50:7).

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר כְּרִיתוּת (sepher kerithuth, a document of cutting off)
existing_translation_notes.note: 50:1 names two legal instruments and asks to see the paperwork for either. A husband who divorced his wife had to put it in writing and hand it to her, which is the requirement at Deuteronomy 24:1-3, and the document was her protection. A man in debt could sell his children into service to clear it, which 2 Kings 4:1 and Nehemiah 5:5 show happening. The verse asks where the writ is and which creditor was paid, and answers that there was neither.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: לְמֹרְטִים (le-morettim, to those who pluck out)
existing_translation_notes.note: The three things listed at 50:6 are not random violence, they are calculated humiliations. Beards were a mark of standing, so pulling one out was a public unmaking; when Hanun shaved off half the beards of David's envoys at 2 Samuel 10:4-5 it was an act of war and the men were kept away until they grew back. Spitting in the face carried disgrace in law as well, at Numbers 12:14 and Deuteronomy 25:9.

existing_translation_notes.term: Morning by morning he awakens my ear
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: לְשׁוֹן לִמּוּדִים (leshon limmudim, the tongue of the taught)
existing_translation_notes.note: 50:4 uses the vocabulary of a pupil, not a master. Limmudim are those under instruction, the same word for disciples at 8:16. The verse has the ear woken each morning to listen like one being taught, and the purpose given is to know how to sustain with a word the one who is weary. 50:5 then says the ear was opened and he was not rebellious.

rows.current_summary_original: The LORD declares that true worship requires humility and obedience rather than ritual sacrifices, and promises that those who tremble at his word will see Jerusalem restored and all nations gathered to his holy mountain. He will judge the rebellious with fire while the faithful enjoy his comfort and peace.
rows.concern: "Rather than ritual sacrifices" can make the chapter abolish all sacrificial worship instead of condemning rebellious worship.
rows.scripture_says: The LORD esteems humility and condemns offerings from people choosing abominations; the same chapter still describes offerings and worship.
rows.proposed_summary: The LORD esteems those who are humble and tremble at His word, and rejects worship joined to rebellion. He promises Jerusalem's restoration and the gathering of nations, while announcing judgment on the rebellious and comfort for His people.
cross_references: Isaiah 1:11-17: The LORD rejects offerings joined to bloodshed and demands justice, identifying the rebellious conduct behind the condemnation of worship.

rows.translation_context_note: The current contrition note identifies the desired posture but does not address this overstatement. Malachi's flawed-offering rebuke supplies the closest existing context.
rows.proposed_note: The contrast is with worshipers who choose their own ways and delight in abominations. The chapter later still describes offerings, priests, and worship, so it does not simply say that every ritual offering is rejected.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נֶכֶה־רוּחַ / חָרֵד עַל דְּבָרִי, Greek (LXX): ταπεινὸς τῷ πνεύματι / τρέμων τοὺς λόγους, Aramaic: מְכִיךְ רוּחָא / דְּחֵיל מִן פִּתְגָמִי
existing_translation_notes.note: God’s chosen worship posture (66:2-5).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: תּוֹלָעָתָם לֹא תָמוּת… אֵשָׁם לֹא תִכְבֶּה, Greek (LXX): ὁ σκώληξ οὐ τελευτᾷ… τὸ πῦρ οὐ σβέννυται, Aramaic: תַּלְעָא לָא מֵית… נוּרָא לָא דָעֵךְ
existing_translation_notes.note: Unending sign of judgment against persistent rebellion (66:24).
To bow down or prostrate oneself in humility. Used for reverence toward God (Genesis 22:5; Exodus 4:31; Psalm 95:6; Isaiah 66:23) but also for kings or angels. Very physical and posture-centered.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

A milky-white resin from the Boswellia tree of southern Arabia. Burned as incense in the temple (Exodus 30:34); offered with every grain offering. The magi's second gift, traditionally read as signaling priesthood.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עֹרֵף כֶּלֶב (oreph kelev, breaking a dog's neck) - דַּם־חֲזִיר (dam chazir, pig's blood)
existing_translation_notes.note: 66:3 pairs each lawful offering with something unthinkable: the ox with killing a man, the lamb with breaking a dog's neck, the grain offering with pig's blood, the incense with blessing an idol. Dogs were unclean scavengers, not pets, and breaking an animal's neck was how a firstborn donkey was destroyed if nobody redeemed it (Exodus 13:13). The verse does not say the offerings stopped; it says what they had become.

existing_translation_notes.term: Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal and Javan
existing_translation_notes.note: 66:19 sends survivors to named nations at the far edge of the known world. Javan is Greece, the name used for the Greeks at Genesis 10:2 and Daniel 8:21. Tubal lay in Anatolia, Lud in Asia Minor, and Tarshish was the far western port the long-haul ships sailed for, the direction Jonah ran. The point of the list is distance: these are the places that have never heard the report or seen the glory.

rows.current_summary: Jeremiah declares Judah's sin is permanent and warns that those who trust in flesh rather than the LORD will wither like desert shrubs, while those who trust in him will flourish like trees by water. He then receives instruction to stand at Jerusalem's gates and tell the people to keep the Sabbath holy, promising that obedience will bring prosperity and continued rulership, while disobedience will result in fire consuming the city's fortresses.

He then receives instruction to stand at Jerusalem's gates and tell the people to keep the Sabbath holy, promising that obedience will bring prosperity and continued rulership, while disobedience will result in fire consuming the city's fortresses.
rows.concern: "Sin is permanent" turns deeply engraved guilt into a claim that repentance or healing is impossible.
rows.scripture_says: Sin is pictured as engraved on hearts and altars. The chapter also asks for healing and gives a conditional call to obey.
rows.proposed_summary: Judah's sin is pictured as engraved on its heart and altars. Jeremiah contrasts trust in people with trust in the LORD, prays for healing, and delivers a Sabbath warning: obedience brings continued life in the city, while refusal brings consuming fire.
cross_references: Jeremiah 31:31-34: The LORD promises a new covenant with law written on hearts and sins forgiven, providing context against reading engraved guilt as beyond forgiveness.
Ezekiel 36:26-27: The LORD promises a new heart and His Spirit enabling obedience, supplying the restoration counterpart to a deeply corrupted heart.
rows.translation_context_note: The current altar-horns note explains the location of the inscription but not the summary's stronger permanence claim. The later heart-writing promise is essential context.
rows.proposed_note: The engraved writing pictures guilt deeply embedded in the people and their worship. It does not state that God cannot forgive or change them: verse 14 asks for healing, and Jeremiah 31 promises God's law written on the heart and sins forgiven.
existing_cross_references: Exodus 32:15-16: Tablets written by the finger of God, the opposite of the iron pen and diamond point of 17:1.
Psalm 1:1-3: The man who delights in the law is a tree planted by streams of water whose leaf does not wither.
Exodus 20:8-11: The Sabbath command, the statute the gate sermon of 17:19-27 prosecutes.
Nehemiah 13:15-22: Nehemiah shuts Jerusalem's gates before the Sabbath to stop the trade, the enforcement Jeremiah called for.
Deuteronomy 30:15-20: Life and death set before the people, with the charge to choose life.

existing_translation_notes.term: Iron pen with a diamond point
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עֵט בַּרְזֶל (et barzel) - Hebrew: שָׁמִיר (shamir)
existing_translation_notes.note: Two tools from stone-cutting. An iron stylus scratched soft surfaces; a harder tip, shamir, was needed to cut stone or gemstone, and the same word is used in Ezekiel 3:9 and Zechariah 7:12 for the hardest thing there is. Verse 1 says the sin is engraved this way on the tablet of the heart and on the horns of the altar, meaning it is cut in, not written on.

Four projections rising from the corners of the altar. Blood from a sin offering was smeared on them, as in Leviticus 4:7, and a man in danger of his life could seize them for sanctuary, as Adonijah and Joab do in 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28. Verse 1 says the guilt is carved into the very place where guilt was supposed to be dealt with.

Verses 5-8 set two plants side by side. One is a scrub bush in the salt flats and the parched wilderness, which sees no rain and cannot tell when good comes. The other is a tree with roots run out to a watercourse; it does not notice the heat and keeps bearing in a drought year. In a country where the difference between the two is a matter of where the roots reach, the picture needs no explanation.

existing_translation_notes.term: A partridge hatching eggs it did not lay
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 11 draws on a piece of country lore about the partridge sitting on another bird's clutch and losing the brood when they hatch and go. It is applied to a man who gets rich by injustice and finds it gone by mid-life.

existing_translation_notes.term: Bearing a burden through the gates
existing_translation_notes.note: The Sabbath sermon in 17:19-27 targets one specific act: carrying goods in and out of the city gates on the seventh day. Gates were where markets were held and where produce entered, so a load coming through the gate on the Sabbath means business was open. Nehemiah 13:15-22 later shuts the gates from dusk on the sixth day for exactly this reason.

rows.current_summary_original: Jeremiah delivers judgment against the Judean royal palace and successive kings, warning that disobedience will bring ruin, exile, and disgrace, with specific condemnation of Jehoiakim's oppression and Jehoiachin's removal from power. The palace will become a wasteland, the kings will lose their thrones, and none of Jehoiachin's descendants will rule Judah again.
rows.concern: "None ... will rule Judah again" can erase the text's Davidic-throne scope and imply that no descendant can ever hold any office.
rows.scripture_says: The judgment says none of Coniah's offspring will prosper sitting on David's throne and ruling in Judah; later Zerubbabel is a governor and receives signet language.
rows.proposed_summary: Jeremiah denounces royal injustice and announces disgrace and exile for Judah's kings. Jehoiachin is judged as a failed royal line: none of his offspring will prosper on David's throne in Judah.
cross_references: Haggai 1:1: Zerubbabel is identified as governor of Judah under Darius, establishing his office in the later setting alongside the judgment on Jehoiachin's royal line.
Haggai 2:23: The LORD calls Zerubbabel His chosen servant and likens him to a signet ring, supplying the later signet image alongside Jeremiah's rejection of Coniah.

rows.translation_context_note: The existing signet note already links Zerubbabel and the reversal of signet imagery, and Matthew is already linked. The summary should preserve the royal scope instead of broadening it to every kind of rule.
rows.proposed_note: The judgment concerns prosperity on David's throne in Judah. Zerubbabel, a later descendant, appears as governor rather than king, and Haggai calls him God's chosen signet. Matthew still includes Jeconiah in the genealogy; the passage cannot be reduced to a claim that he had no biological children.
existing_cross_references: Deuteronomy 24:14-15: A hired worker must be paid before sundown on the day he works, the statute Jehoiakim breaks in 22:13.
2 Kings 23:31-34: Jehoahaz reigns three months, is deposed by Pharaoh Neco and dies in Egypt; the Shallum of 22:11-12.
2 Kings 24:1-6: Jehoiakim's reign, rebellion and death, the king condemned in 22:13-19.
2 Kings 24:8-16: Jehoiachin surrenders and is carried to Babylon with his mother, the Coniah of 22:24-30.
Matthew 1:11-12: Jeconiah stands in the line from David to Joseph, between Josiah and Shealtiel.

existing_translation_notes.note: Judah's last kings each carry more than one name, which makes the chapter hard to follow. Shallum in 22:11 is Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, deposed after three months. Coniah in 22:24 is Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah in Matthew 1:11. Throne names were assigned at accession, sometimes by the foreign king doing the appointing, as 2 Kings 23:34 and 24:17 both record.

Cedar came by sea from Lebanon and was the most expensive building timber in the region, used for Solomon's temple and palace. Vermilion is a red pigment from mercury ore, used to paint panelling. Verse 14 lists them as the marks of a palace built with unpaid labour, which is why the next verse asks whether cedar makes a king.

Verse 19 says Jehoiakim will be dragged out and thrown beyond the gates of Jerusalem. A dead pack animal was hauled outside the walls and left. For a king of Judah, who expected a tomb among his fathers in the city of David, this is the announcement that there will be no tomb and no mourning.

A carved seal, worn on the hand or on a cord, pressed into wet clay to seal documents and jars. It was the owner's legal signature and never left him. Verse 24 says that even if Coniah were the signet on God's right hand, He would pull it off. Haggai 2:23 later says the opposite of Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin's grandson.

existing_translation_notes.term: Write this man down as childless
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 30 explains its own terms in the same breath: none of his offspring will prosper, sitting on David's throne and ruling in Judah. Jehoiachin had sons, listed in 1 Chronicles 3:17-18, and 52:31-34 has him alive and eating at the Babylonian king's table. The sentence is about the throne, not about descendants.

rows.current_summary_original: The LORD promises to restore Israel from exile, gathering them from distant lands and establishing a new covenant where his law is written on their hearts and all people know him directly; Jerusalem will be rebuilt and made holy.
rows.concern: "All people know him directly" loses the covenant-membership scope and can sound like an unconditional statement about everyone.
rows.scripture_says: The new covenant is named with Israel and Judah; all within that covenant know the LORD.
rows.proposed_summary: The LORD promises to gather and restore His people and make a new covenant with Israel and Judah, writing His law on their hearts and forgiving their sins. All His covenant people will know Him, and Jerusalem will be rebuilt and made holy.
cross_references: Hebrews 8:8-12: Hebrews quotes the covenant promise to Israel and Judah, including shared knowledge of the Lord and forgiveness, preserving the promise's covenant setting.
Hebrews 10:16-17: Hebrews repeats the promises of law on hearts and sins remembered no more, linking the heart-writing language with covenant forgiveness.
rows.translation_context_note: The current new-covenant note names everyone knowing Him but does not restate the antecedent. Both Hebrews references are already present.
rows.proposed_note: The promise that all will know the LORD belongs to the new covenant announced with Israel and Judah. It is not phrased as a statement that every person already knows God regardless of that covenant. Hebrews quotes this promise in its account of Christ's covenant.
existing_cross_references: Hebrews 8:8-12: The new covenant of 31:31-34 quoted in full and applied.
Hebrews 10:16-17: The same passage quoted a second time, for laws on the heart and sins remembered no more.
Matthew 2:16-18: Rachel weeping for her children applied when Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem.
Genesis 35:16-20: Rachel dies in childbirth and is buried on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem, the grave 31:15 speaks from.
Ezekiel 36:26-27: A new heart and God's Spirit put within His people, the same promise in different words.

existing_translation_notes.note: Jacob's wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, buried on the road near Bethlehem according to Genesis 35:19. Ramah in 31:15 is a town in Benjamin about five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem, and 40:1 records it as the staging camp where prisoners were chained before the march to Babylon. The verse puts the mother of the northern tribes at a deportation depot, hearing her descendants pass.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה (berith chadashah) - Greek: διαθήκη καινή (diatheke kaine)
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 31-34 are the only place in the Old Testament where the phrase new covenant appears. Four things are named: God's instruction written on the heart rather than on stone, the relationship formula I will be their God and they will be My people, everyone knowing Him without needing to be taught, and sins forgiven and not remembered. Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes the whole passage.

Verse 21 tells the exiles going out to plant markers and guideposts along the way, and to note the highway they are travelling. Caravan routes were marked with cairns and pillars so a traveller could find the road back across country with no landmarks. The instruction assumes the return trip before the outward journey is finished.

Verse 29 quotes a saying doing the rounds in Judah: the fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. It is a complaint about inherited punishment. Verse 30 cancels it, and Ezekiel 18:1-4 takes the same saying and answers it at chapter length.

existing_translation_notes.term: The fixed order of sun, moon and stars
existing_translation_notes.note: Verses 35-37 stake the promise on two things nobody can move: the daily and nightly order of the lights, and the unmeasured size of the heavens and the foundations of the earth. The argument is a wager. If the first can be broken, the second falls too.

existing_translation_notes.term: The valley of the dead bodies and the ashes
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 40 names the Hinnom ravine and the ash dumps south of Jerusalem, the ground where children had been burned at Topheth in 7:31 and 19:5. The chapter ends by declaring that ground holy to the LORD and inside the rebuilt city.

rows.current_summary: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that Babylon will capture Jerusalem and burn it, though Zedekiah himself will die peacefully; later, God condemns the people for freeing their Hebrew slaves and then re-enslaving them, promising them death by sword, plague, and famine instead.
rows.current_summary_original: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that Babylon will capture Jerusalem and burn it, though Zedekiah himself will die peacefully; later, God condemns the people for freeing their Hebrew slaves and then re-enslaving them, promising them death by sword, plague, and famine instead.
rows.concern: "Die peacefully" can imply escape or a comfortable end, although the oracle first promises captivity and the later narrative records imprisonment.
rows.scripture_says: Zedekiah will be captured and taken to Babylon but will not die by the sword; later he is blinded and imprisoned until death.
rows.proposed_summary: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that Jerusalem will burn and he will be taken to Babylon, though he will not die by the sword. God then condemns the people for freeing Hebrew slaves and taking them back, announcing judgment for the broken covenant.
cross_references: Jeremiah 39:6-7: Zedekiah sees his sons killed, is blinded, and is taken in chains toward Babylon, showing that the peace promise did not mean escape from capture.
Jeremiah 52:11: Zedekiah is taken to Babylon and kept in custody until death, specifying his captive end alongside the promise that he would not die by the sword.
rows.translation_context_note: The current peace note already explains this exactly. The summary should agree with its narrower explanation.
rows.proposed_note: Death in peace is set against death by the sword, not against captivity. The oracle says Zedekiah will be taken to Babylon; the later account says he was blinded and remained imprisoned until death.
existing_cross_references: Exodus 21:2-6: A Hebrew slave serves six years and goes free in the seventh, the law 34:14 cites.
Deuteronomy 15:12-18: The same release law, with the added command not to send him away empty-handed.
Leviticus 25:39-43: An Israelite in debt is not to be worked as a slave but as a hired man, and goes free at the Jubilee.
Genesis 15:9-18: Animals cut in two and a flame passing between the pieces, the oath ritual behind 34:18-20.
2 Kings 25:1-7: The siege, the night flight and Zedekiah's capture, the end 34:2-5 announces.

existing_translation_notes.note: Hebrew does not make a covenant, it cuts one, and 34:18 shows why. The parties cut an animal in two and walked between the halves. The unspoken sentence was let this be done to me if I break my word, which is why God says the men who passed between the calf's pieces and then broke the oath will be handed over and become food for birds.

Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 require a Hebrew bought as a slave to be freed after six years of service. Verse 14 says the fathers did not listen and the law had been ignored for generations. Under siege the owners suddenly kept it, and 34:11 records that as soon as the Babylonian army withdrew they took their freed people back. The word deror is the same one used for the Jubilee proclamation in Leviticus 25:10.

Verse 7 says these two were the last fortified cities of Judah still holding out besides Jerusalem. Lachish guarded the approach from the coastal plain about twenty-five miles (40 km) southwest of Jerusalem; Azekah sat between them in the Elah valley. A group of inscribed potsherds found in the gate of Lachish, written during this war, includes a soldier reporting that he is watching for the fire signals of Lachish because he can no longer see Azekah.

Verse 5 promises Zedekiah death in peace with the customary funeral fire and the lament Alas, lord. It is not a promise of escape. 39:7 and 52:11 record that he was blinded and taken to Babylon in bronze fetters, and 52:11 adds that he stayed in prison there until the day of his death, dying a captive rather than by the sword.

existing_translation_notes.term: Spices burned at a royal funeral
existing_translation_notes.note: The burning promised in 34:5 is not cremation, which Israel did not practise. It is a fire of aromatics kindled in the king's honour, recorded for Asa in 2 Chronicles 16:14 and denied to Jehoram in 2 Chronicles 21:19. Withholding it was an insult; granting it, as here, is the promise of a proper burial.

rows.current_summary: Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on clay and acts out its siege with an iron pan as a wall; he then lies on his left side for 390 days bearing Israel's sin, then on his right side for 40 days bearing Judah's sin, eating rationed bread baked over cow dung to symbolize how Jerusalem will face famine and defilement.
rows.current_summary_original: Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on clay and acts out its siege with an iron pan as a wall; he then lies on his left side for 390 days bearing Israel's sin, then on his right side for 40 days bearing Judah's sin, eating rationed bread baked over cow dung to symbolize how Jerusalem will face famine and defilement.
rows.concern: Commands for a symbolic action are narrated as a fully documented uninterrupted performance with an explained historical timetable.
rows.scripture_says: God commands the enacted siege and assigns days for years. The chapter records the command and Ezekiel's fuel objection, not a diary of every day's performance.
rows.proposed_summary: The LORD commands Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem's siege, lie on his sides for days assigned to Israel's and Judah's guilt, and eat measured food and water. After Ezekiel objects to human excrement as fuel, God permits cow dung; the sign depicts siege scarcity and exile defilement.
cross_references: Numbers 14:34: Forty days of spying correspond to forty years of bearing guilt, supplying another explicit prophetic day-for-year reckoning.
Exodus 12:40: The text gives 430 years for Israel's stay in Egypt, supplying the numerical comparison made with Ezekiel's assigned days.
2 Kings 25:1-4: Jerusalem endures a Babylonian siege and severe famine before its defenses are breached, supplying the historical siege context for Ezekiel's sign.
rows.translation_context_note: The current days note supplies the numerical comparison with Egypt but states the performance directly. The proposal separates the text's command from an unrecorded daily reconstruction without denying that Ezekiel obeyed.
rows.proposed_note: The 390 and 40 days are explained as days for years, but the chapter does not identify a calendar start and end for those years. It gives prophetic instructions and the exchange about fuel; further reconstructions of how the daily sign was performed remain interpretations.
existing_cross_references: 2 Kings 25:1-4: The siege of Jerusalem as it happened, with the famine and the breach of the wall.
Leviticus 26:26-29: Bread rationed out by weight and eaten without satisfaction, in the covenant curses.
Deuteronomy 28:52-57: Siege pressed against the high fortified walls until people eat their own children.
Numbers 14:34: A year for each day, forty years for the forty days of spying out the land.
Deuteronomy 23:12-14: The law requiring human waste to be buried outside the camp, the uncleanness 4:12-15 turns on.

existing_translation_notes.note: A sun-dried mud brick, the standard building block of Mesopotamia and also its writing surface: scribes drew and wrote on damp clay. Verse 1 has Ezekiel scratch a plan of Jerusalem onto one, which is a Babylonian mapmaker's act. Clay tablets carrying city plans have been recovered from Mesopotamia, so the sign uses the local medium.

Verse 2 names the whole kit in order. The siege wall is a wall of circumvallation thrown up around the city so nothing gets in or out. The ramp is a packed earth and rubble slope built up against the wall to bring men and machines level with the top; the Assyrian assault ramp at Lachish still stands. The camps are the troop enclosures, and the battering rams are timber frames on wheels housing an iron-headed beam.

A flat iron griddle, ordinary kitchen equipment used for baking flatbread over a fire; the same word appears in Leviticus 2:5. Verse 3 has him stand it on edge between himself and the model city as an iron wall. A cooking plate becomes a barrier, in the chapter that is about to ration his food.

existing_translation_notes.term: Twenty shekels of food a day
existing_translation_notes.note: A shekel weighed about two fifths of an ounce (11.4 grams), so twenty shekels is roughly eight ounces (230 grams) of bread for a whole day, weighed out and eaten at set times. That is a starvation ration, and it is measured rather than served because under siege food stopped being a meal and became an allowance.

existing_translation_notes.term: A sixth of a hin of water
existing_translation_notes.note: A hin is about a gallon (3.8 litres), so a sixth of a hin is roughly two thirds of a quart, about 21 fluid ounces (0.6 litre), for a day. A working adult needs several times that in a hot climate. The measured water in 4:11 is the same message as the weighed bread: the city's cisterns are being counted out cup by cup.

Dried animal dung was the ordinary cooking fuel in a land short of firewood, and still is in parts of the region. What God first commands in 4:12 is human excrement, which Deuteronomy 23:12-14 requires to be buried outside the camp. Ezekiel protests in 4:14 that he has never eaten anything unclean, and the fuel is changed to cow dung. The horror is the point: under siege even the fire is defiled.

Verses 4-6 assign a day for each year, the same reckoning Numbers 14:34 uses. He lies 390 days on his left side for the northern kingdom and 40 on his right for Judah, 430 in all, which is the number of years Exodus 12:40 gives for Israel in Egypt. The bread of 4:9 is a famine loaf of six mixed grains and pulses, wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt, thrown together because no one ingredient is left in quantity.

rows.current_summary_original: A man in linen takes burning coals from among the cherubim and scatters them over the city as the LORD's glory rises from above the cherubim and moves toward the temple threshold. The cherubim, each with four faces and accompanied by four wheels covered in eyes, rise upward with the LORD's glory and move toward the east gate of the temple.
rows.concern: The summary and coal note narrate the actual scattering as observed, though the chapter records the order, receipt of coals, and departure.
rows.scripture_says: The man is commanded to scatter coals, receives them, and goes out. The scattering itself is not separately narrated.
rows.proposed_summary: The LORD orders the man in linen to scatter burning coals over Jerusalem; he receives the coals and goes out. The glory of the LORD moves from the temple threshold to the cherubim and the east gate as Ezekiel sees their faces and wheels.
cross_references: 2 Kings 25:9: The Babylonian destruction burns the temple, palace, and Jerusalem's major buildings, supplying the later historical fire associated with Ezekiel's judgment vision.
Ezekiel 43:1-5: The LORD's glory returns through the east gate and fills the temple, reversing the departure described in Ezekiel 10.
rows.translation_context_note: The current coal note blends the vision with the later historical fire. Keep the symbolic connection but label what is commanded and what is actually narrated.
rows.proposed_note: Verse 2 commands scattering coals over the city, and verse 7 records the man receiving them and going out. The chapter does not separately describe the scattering. The vision signifies judgment as the LORD's glory departs; the later burning of Jerusalem is a related event, not another detail Ezekiel reports seeing here.
existing_cross_references: Ezekiel 1:4-28: The same throne, living creatures and wheels, described at the Kebar canal.
Exodus 25:18-22: Cherubim of hammered gold over the ark, where God says He will meet with Moses and speak.
1 Kings 8:10-11: The cloud fills the house so the priests cannot stand to minister, the arrival that 10:18 reverses.
Isaiah 6:6-7: A live coal taken from the altar with tongs and carried to the prophet's mouth.
Ezekiel 43:1-5: The glory returns to the temple by the east gate, the road it leaves by here.

existing_translation_notes.note: Not infants with wings. They are the guardian figures of God's throne: stationed at Eden's gate with a flaming sword in Genesis 3:24, worked in gold over the ark in Exodus 25:18-22, carved into the temple walls and doors in 1 Kings 6:29-35, and here bearing the throne itself. Composite winged guardian creatures flanking thrones and doorways are standard in the art of the whole region.

The departure is deliberately slow and is tracked step by step: from above the cherubim to the threshold in 10:4, back over the cherubim in 10:18, out to the east gate in 10:19, up from the middle of the city in 11:23, and finally to the hill east of Jerusalem. Nothing is destroyed until it has gone. The same route runs in reverse in 43:1-5.

Verse 2 sends the man in linen in among the wheels to take fire from between the cherubim and throw it over Jerusalem. The fire comes from the throne itself. Verse 7 has a cherub hand it to him, so the burning of the city in 2 Kings 25:9 is shown here as beginning with fire carried out of the sanctuary.

Verse 12 says the whole bodies of the cherubim, their backs, hands, wings and the wheels, were covered with eyes all around. It follows chapter 8, where the elders in the hidden room say the LORD does not see us. The vision answers that in the plainest way available.

In 1:10 the four faces are man, lion, ox and eagle. In 10:14 the ox has been replaced by the face of a cherub, and 10:20 states that Ezekiel now recognises the creatures from the Kebar as cherubim. The book records the identification changing as he understands what he saw the first time.

He then measures the entire temple complex and finds it forms a perfect square, five hundred cubits on each side, with a wall separating the holy from the common.
rows.concern: Note-focused: five hundred cubits follows this translation, but readers comparing the Hebrew or other versions encounter reeds/rods and a materially different scale.
rows.scripture_says: The app prints five hundred cubits. The Hebrew and ancient-version handling of the measurement has produced differing English renderings.

He then measures the entire temple complex and finds it forms a perfect square, five hundred cubits on each side, with a wall separating the holy from the common.
cross_references: Ezekiel 40:5: The measuring rod is defined as six long cubits, establishing why a measurement in reeds or rods differs in scale from cubits.
Ezekiel 45:2: The sanctuary's section is described as five hundred cubits square with surrounding open land, providing a related dimension for comparison.
rows.translation_context_note: The current walkway note does not address the unit issue. This is a comparison note, not a proposed change to the displayed Bible translation or a claim that the chosen number is certainly wrong.
rows.proposed_note: This translation gives the enclosure as five hundred cubits on each side. Other versions render the measurement in reeds or rods, reflecting a textual and unit question. Ezekiel 40:5 defines a measuring reed as six long cubits, so the two renderings do not represent the same physical size.
existing_cross_references: Leviticus 6:14-18: The grain offering eaten by the priests in a holy place, the meals the chambers of 42:13 are for.
Leviticus 10:10: Distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean.
Exodus 28:40-43: The garments made for the priests to serve in, which 42:14 says must be left behind.
Numbers 18:8-10: The most holy offerings given to the priests, to be eaten by the males in a most holy place.
Ezekiel 44:17-19: The same rule about changing out of the linen garments before going out to the people.

existing_translation_notes.note: Rooms built into the temple courts, used as offices, stores and dining rooms. Verse 13 says the priests eat the most holy offerings there and lay up the grain, sin and guilt offerings. Under Leviticus 6:16 and Numbers 18:9-10 the priests' portion had to be eaten inside the sanctuary precinct, so the building is a purpose-made refectory and strongroom.

existing_translation_notes.term: Changing out of the holy garments
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 14 makes it a rule of movement: a priest who has been serving may not walk out into the outer court until he has taken off the clothes he ministered in, because those garments are holy. 44:19 repeats it and adds the reason, so that he does not transmit holiness to the people by touching them with the cloth. Holiness in these chapters behaves like something that can be carried on fabric.

Verses 15-20 close the survey by measuring the outer boundary on all four sides: five hundred cubits each way, a perfect square, with a wall around it. Verse 20 states the wall's whole purpose in one line, to separate the holy from the common. In long cubits that is roughly 875 feet (267 m) on a side, about seventeen acres.

Verse 4 puts a passage in front of the chamber blocks, ten cubits wide and a hundred long, with the doors opening onto it from the north. The vision keeps describing circulation, where a person walks and which way a door faces, because the whole point of the layout is controlling who goes where.

rows.concern: "The city with the LORD's sanctuary" can place the sanctuary inside the city instead of its separate priestly district.
rows.scripture_says: The holy district contains separate priestly and Levitical allocations; the sanctuary is in the priestly portion and the city occupies the remaining strip.
rows.proposed_summary: The tribes receive their allotments from north to south. The central district has separate priestly land containing the sanctuary, Levitical land, and city land, with the prince's land beside it. The city's gates bear the tribes' names, and its name is The LORD Is There.
cross_references: Ezekiel 45:1-6: The sanctuary stands within the priests' portion, with adjacent Levitical and city allocations, confirming the separation of sanctuary land and city land.
Revelation 21:12-13: The city has twelve gates named for Israel's tribes, three on each side, providing the later parallel to Ezekiel's tribal gates.
rows.translation_context_note: The current sacred-square note already distinguishes the three strips. The summary should preserve that spatial distinction and the chapter's concluding name.
rows.proposed_note: The sanctuary stands in the priestly allotment. The city and its common-use land form a separate strip within the larger district; the sanctuary is not placed inside the city. The chapter ends with the city's name, The LORD Is There.
existing_cross_references: Joshua 13:1-19:51: The first division of the land by lot, tribe by tribe, that this chapter redraws.
Numbers 34:13-29: A leader named from each tribe to apportion the land as an inheritance.
Revelation 21:12-13: A city with twelve gates, three on each side, named for the twelve tribes of Israel.
Ezekiel 47:13-23: The outer borders of the land and the rule for allotting it, immediately before this list.
Genesis 49:1-28: Jacob blesses his twelve sons, the tribes whose names run down this map.

existing_translation_notes.note: The old allotments in Joshua 13 to 19 followed terrain and were unequal, and Judah's portion dwarfed some others. This map ignores geography: thirteen parallel bands running east to west across the whole country, seven tribes north of the sacred district and five south, each the same width. Nobody gets the better hills, and the tribes descended from the slave-born sons, Dan, Asher, Naphtali and Gad, are no worse placed than the rest.

Verses 8-20 set aside a block 25,000 cubits on each side in the middle of the country: 25,000 by 10,000 for the priests with the sanctuary in it, the same for the Levites, and 25,000 by 5,000 for the city and its farmland. At the long cubit of 40:5 that square runs roughly eight miles (13 km) a side. The prince gets the land on either side of it, so he is next to the sanctuary and not in it.

Verses 30-34 give the city three gates on each of its four sides, each named for a tribe. Levi gets a gate, and Joseph is one gate instead of two, so Ephraim and Manasseh are counted together and the twelve comes out even. Revelation 21:12-13 describes the same arrangement, twelve gates with the names of the twelve tribes, three to a side.

The last line of the book, 48:35, gives the city a new name meaning The LORD Is There. Everything from chapter 8 onward has turned on presence: the glory leaving the temple, the exiles told in 11:16 that God had been a sanctuary to them in small measure, and the glory returning in 43:1-5. The book closes by naming the city after the one thing it had lost.

Verse 35 gives the city's perimeter as 18,000 cubits, four sides of 4,500 each, which at the long cubit is roughly one and a half miles (2.4 km) a side. That is a planned square, not the ridge-and-valley shape of the real Jerusalem. The name in the same verse, and not the dimensions, is what the chapter ends on.
