rows.current_summary: God commands Hosea to buy back his unfaithful wife for silver and barley, requiring her to live with him in separation; the passage compares this to how Israel will eventually return to seek the LORD after a long period without king, sacrifice, or idols.
rows.current_summary_original: God commands Hosea to buy back his unfaithful wife for silver and barley, requiring her to live with him in separation; the passage compares this to how Israel will eventually return to seek the LORD after a long period without king, sacrifice, or idols.
rows.concern: The summary states a buy-back of Gomer as certain, while the woman's identification depends on translation; a current cross-reference also calls thirty shekels twice the total price despite the barley.
rows.scripture_says: Hosea pays fifteen shekels plus barley for the woman. The app reads "your wife again"; the Hebrew wording is rendered differently in other versions and does not repeat Gomer's name.
rows.proposed_summary: At the LORD's command, Hosea shows love again to an adulterous woman, paying silver and barley and requiring a period of sexual restraint. The sign depicts Israel's time without its institutions and its later return to the LORD and David its king.
cross_references: Hosea 1:2-3: Hosea marries the specifically named Gomer after the LORD's command, supplying the earlier identification considered when reading the unnamed woman in chapter 3.
Exodus 21:32: Thirty shekels compensate the master of a servant gored by an ox, providing a legal comparison rather than a stated total value for Hosea's silver and barley.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Exodus reference says thirty shekels is twice what Hosea pays, ignoring the barley. The proposed wording distinguishes the chosen translation and common identification from what is named explicitly.
rows.proposed_note: This translation identifies the woman as Hosea's wife again, commonly understood as Gomer, but the chapter does not repeat her name and other versions say a woman. Verse 2 gives fifteen shekels plus barley; comparing only the silver with the thirty-shekel payment in Exodus 21:32 does not establish the total value of the purchase.
existing_cross_references: Exodus 21:32: Thirty shekels of silver is the fixed payment for a slave killed by an ox, twice what Hosea pays here.
Leviticus 27:1-4: The sanctuary valuation of persons, fifty shekels for a man and thirty for a woman.
2 Samuel 6:19: David hands out a loaf, a date cake and a raisin cake to the whole crowd at the ark's return.
Exodus 28:6-14: The ephod worn by the high priest, worked in gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarn.
Ezekiel 37:24-25: My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי (va-ekkereha li, and I bought her for myself)
existing_translation_notes.note: 3:2 pays fifteen shekels of silver plus a homer and a lethech of barley. The verb is karah, to purchase or acquire, and it is not the ordinary word for buying goods. This is a woman already his wife being paid for a second time, out of whatever hand held her.

existing_translation_notes.term: What the buy-back price was worth
existing_translation_notes.note: Half the payment at 3:2 is metal and half is grain. Silver was weighed out, not counted; a shekel ran about four tenths of an ounce, roughly eleven grams, so fifteen shekels is close to six ounces of silver. Thirty shekels was the fixed compensation for a slave killed by an ox (Exodus 21:32) and the sanctuary valuation of a woman (Leviticus 27:4), so this is exactly half the standard figure. A homer is ten ephahs, a little over six bushels, and a lethech is half a homer, which puts the barley at roughly nine bushels.

Barley was the cheap grain, poor man's bread and animal feed, harvested weeks before the wheat. The law prices a barley field accordingly (Leviticus 27:16), and the jealousy offering at Numbers 5:15 is barley flour with no oil and no incense on it, the plainest offering in the system. Paying half of 3:2 in barley says what kind of transaction this was.

Pressed cakes of dried grapes, festival food handed out at public celebrations (2 Samuel 6:19). At 3:1 they are what Israel loves while turning to other gods, because the harvest feasts at the Baal shrines ran on the same food and drink. Jeremiah 7:18 shows the same pattern in Judah, whole households baking cakes for the queen of heaven.

3:4 lists what Israel will go without, and every item is a physical object. A matsevah is a standing stone erected at a shrine, which Deuteronomy 16:22 forbids outright. The ephod is the priestly vestment used to seek an answer from God (1 Samuel 23:9-12). Teraphim are household gods, the figures Rachel stole from her father (Genesis 31:19) and the one Michal put in a bed to fake a sleeping man (1 Samuel 19:13), and Ezekiel 21:21 shows them used for divination.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֵין מֶלֶךְ וְאֵין שָׂר (en melekh ve-en sar)
existing_translation_notes.note: 3:4 strips out two systems at once: the state, king and officer, and the whole apparatus of worship, sacrifice and pillar and ephod and household gods. What is left is many days of neither. 3:5 then says afterward they will seek the LORD and David their king, so the sentence is bounded and the text says so.

implemented_note_changes.original: Hebrew: וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי (va-ekkereha li, and I bought her for myself)
implemented_note_changes.note: This translation identifies the woman as Hosea's wife again, commonly understood as Gomer, but the chapter does not repeat her name and other versions say a woman. Verse 2 gives fifteen shekels plus barley; comparing only the silver with the thirty-shekel payment in Exodus 21:32 does not establish the total value of the purchase.

implemented_note_changes.term: What the buy-back price was worth
implemented_note_changes.note: Verse 3:2 names fifteen shekels of silver plus a homer and a lethech of barley. Silver was weighed rather than counted; at roughly eleven grams per shekel, the silver alone is about six ounces. A homer is ten ephahs and a lethech is half a homer, so the grain amounts to one and a half homers. The text does not assign that barley a silver value, so the total cannot be identified as exactly half the thirty-shekel compensation in Exodus 21:32.

Barley was the cheap grain, poor man's bread and animal feed, harvested weeks before the wheat. The law prices a barley field accordingly (Leviticus 27:16), and the jealousy offering at Numbers 5:15 is barley flour with no oil and no incense on it, the plainest offering in the system. Barley forms part of the payment in 3:2, alongside fifteen shekels of silver.

implemented_reference_changes: Exodus 21:32: Thirty shekels compensate the master of a servant gored by an ox, providing a legal comparison rather than a stated total value for Hosea's silver and barley.
Hosea 1:2-3: Hosea marries the specifically named Gomer after the LORD's command, supplying the earlier identification considered when reading the unnamed woman in chapter 3.

rows.current_summary: Edom's pride in its rock-cleft heights will not save it: allies will betray it and its treasures will be pillaged, because Esau did violence to his brother Jacob, gloating, looting, and cutting off fugitives on the day strangers cast lots for Jerusalem. The Day of the LORD is near for all nations, but on Mount Zion there will be deliverance; the house of Jacob will be a blazing fire and the house of Esau stubble, and the kingdom will belong to the LORD.
rows.current_summary_original: Edom’s pride in its rock-cleft heights will not save it: allies will betray it and its treasures will be pillaged, because Esau did violence to his brother Jacob, gloating, looting, and cutting off fugitives on the day strangers cast lots for Jerusalem. The Day of the LORD is near for all nations, but on Mount Zion there will be deliverance; the house of Jacob will be a blazing fire and the house of Esau stubble, and the kingdom will belong to the LORD.
rows.concern: The summary can make the individual Esau attack the individual Jacob during Jerusalem's fall.
rows.scripture_says: The oracle addresses Edom and Judah through their ancestral names; it concerns nations descended from the brothers.
rows.proposed_summary: Edom's pride and defenses will fail because Esau's descendants betrayed their kin, the people of Judah, during Jerusalem's disaster. They gloated, looted, and intercepted fugitives. The Day of the LORD brings judgment, deliverance on Zion, and the LORD's kingdom.
cross_references: Genesis 36:1-8: Esau is identified with Edom and settles his household in Seir, supplying the ancestral basis for the national names in Obadiah.
Numbers 20:14-21: Israel addresses Edom as a brother, but Edom refuses passage and threatens force, supplying an earlier example of conflict between the related peoples.
Psalm 137:7: The psalm recalls Edom urging Jerusalem's destruction, paralleling Obadiah's charge against the later nation rather than the patriarch personally.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Edom/Esau note defines the relationship, but the summary switches from Edom to an unqualified personal Esau. Existing references already include the descendants and earlier national hostility.
rows.proposed_note: Esau and Jacob function here as ancestral names for Edom and Israel or Judah. The oracle is about later peoples and Jerusalem's disaster, not an account of the two patriarchs personally taking part in that event.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 25:29-34; Genesis 36:1-8: Esau/Edom background.
Jeremiah 49:7-16: Parallel oracle against Edom.
Numbers 20:14-21: Edom’s refusal to Israel (hostility roots).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֱדוֹם (ʾEdom), עֵשָׂו (ʿEsav), שֵׂעִיר (Seʿir), Greek (LXX): Ἐδώμ, Ἠσαῦ, Σηείρ, Aramaic: אדום, עשו, שעיר
existing_translation_notes.note: People/land descended from Esau dwelling in Mount Seir (the rugged highlands south of Judah).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: צִיר (tsir, ‘envoy/messenger’), Greek (LXX): ἄγγελος, Aramaic: שליחא (shliḥa)
existing_translation_notes.note: The report/mission that calls nations against Edom (1:1).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: חַגְוֵי־סֶלַע (ḥagvê-selaʿ), Greek (LXX): τὰς ὀπὰς τοῦ πέτρας, Aramaic: נקיקי טורא
existing_translation_notes.note: High rock dwellings (cf. Sela/Petra) Edom trusted for safety (1:3).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: נֶשֶׁר (nesher), Greek (LXX): ἀετός, Aramaic: נשרא
existing_translation_notes.note: Image of height/speed; even there God says He will bring Edom down (1:4).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

rows.current_summary: Micah declares God's judgment against Samaria and Jerusalem for their idolatry and sin; God will destroy Samaria and the plague of her wickedness will spread to Judah, causing mourning across the towns of Judah as the people go into exile.
rows.current_summary_original: Micah declares God's judgment against Samaria and Jerusalem for their idolatry and sin; God will destroy Samaria and the plague of her wickedness will spread to Judah, causing mourning across the towns of Judah as the people go into exile.
rows.concern: "Plague of her wickedness" turns the wound of judgment into wickedness spreading from Samaria.
rows.scripture_says: Micah mourns Samaria's incurable wound reaching Judah and Jerusalem in the context of coming destruction.
rows.proposed_summary: Micah announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem for idolatry. Samaria's devastation is pictured as an incurable wound reaching Judah and Jerusalem, and Micah laments the towns facing disaster and exile.
cross_references: 2 Kings 17:5-6: Assyria captures Samaria after a three-year siege and deports Israelites, supplying the destruction setting behind Micah's wound imagery.
2 Kings 18:13-17: Assyria captures Judah's fortified cities and sends a force to Jerusalem, paralleling Micah's image of devastation reaching Judah's gate.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Assyrian conquest references already provide the relevant historical setting, but no note explains the wound image.
rows.proposed_note: The wound reaching Judah is part of the oracle's picture of devastation and judgment. The verse does not call it a contagious spread of Samaria's wickedness into Judah.
existing_cross_references: 2 Kings 17:5-6: Assyria besieges Samaria for three years, captures it, and deports Israel to Halah, Gozan and the cities of the Medes.
2 Samuel 1:20: David's lament opens with the line Micah reuses, tell it not in Gath, proclaim it not in Ashkelon.
2 Kings 18:13-17: Sennacherib takes the fortified cities of Judah and sends his commanders from Lachish up to Jerusalem.
1 Samuel 22:1-2: David takes refuge in the cave of Adullam and four hundred distressed and indebted men gather to him.
Isaiah 20:2-4: Isaiah walks stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Cush.

existing_translation_notes.note: 'Etnan is the specific word for a prostitute's fee, and it is used here for the income of Samaria's idol shrines (1:7). Deuteronomy 23:18 bars that money from ever being brought into the house of the LORD. Micah says the silver Samaria collected as a harlot's hire will be stripped off her images and end up paying harlots again.

The capital of the northern kingdom, built by Omri around 880 BC on a hill he bought for two talents of silver (1 Kings 16:24). It stood alone above the valley, which is why 1:6 pictures its stones poured down the slope and its foundations laid bare. Assyria besieged it three years and deported its people in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5-6), inside Micah's own lifetime.

Judah's second city, about 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem, guarding the road up from the coastal plain, and a chariot base, which is why 1:13 tells it to harness the team. Sennacherib stormed it in 701 BC and covered a room of his palace at Nineveh with carved reliefs of the siege, now in the British Museum. The earthen assault ramp his army raised against the southwest corner is still on the site.

Micah's own town (1:1), in the Shephelah, the low chalk hills between the coastal plain and the Judean highlands, near Gath and roughly 25 miles southwest of Jerusalem. Its neighbours in this same list, Lachish, Mareshah and Adullam, all sit in that corridor, which is the ground an army coming up from the coast has to cross. Micah is naming the towns of his own district as the invasion route.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית לְעַפְרָה (Beth le-Aphrah) - שָׁפִיר (Shaphir) - צַאֲנָן (Tsa'anan) - מָרוֹת (Maroth) - לָכִישׁ (Lakhish) - אַכְזִיב (Akhziv) - מָרֵשָׁה (Mareshah)
existing_translation_notes.note: Every town in this list is punned on its own name, and English can carry none of it. Beth-leaphrah means house of dust, so roll in the dust. Shaphir means fair, and its people go by stripped. Tsa'anan sounds like the verb to go out, and its people do not come out. Maroth sounds like bitter, and it waits for good. Lachish sounds like rekhesh, the word for the chariot team it is told to harness. Achzib sounds like akhzav, a wadi that runs dry when you need it. Mareshah sounds like yoresh, the conqueror who takes possession.

Nesher covers both the eagle and the griffon vulture, and the vulture is the bird in view at 1:16 because its head and neck are bare of feathers. Shaving the head was a mourning rite (Job 1:20, Amos 8:10). Walking barefoot and stripped at 1:8 is the same language of grief, and Isaiah 20:2-4 has a prophet doing it as a public sign.

rows.current_summary: Leaders who hate good and love evil tear the skin and flesh of the people, and prophets proclaim peace for whoever feeds them, so God will hide his face and leave the seers without answer; Micah, filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, declares that because rulers judge for bribes, priests teach for a price, and prophets divine for money while leaning on the LORD's presence, Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become a heap of rubble.
rows.current_summary_original: Leaders who hate good and love evil tear the skin and flesh of the people, and prophets proclaim peace for whoever feeds them, so God will hide his face and leave the seers without answer; Micah, filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, declares that because rulers judge for bribes, priests teach for a price, and prophets divine for money while leaning on the LORD’s presence, Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become a heap of rubble.
rows.concern: The summary repeats butchery imagery as a bare historical action without identifying the metaphor for exploitation.
rows.scripture_says: Micah describes predatory rulers through skinning, chopping, and cooking imagery, then explicitly condemns bribery and paid prophecy.
rows.proposed_summary: Micah depicts corrupt rulers as butchers devouring the people and condemns prophets who promise peace for payment. Filled with the LORD's Spirit, he exposes injustice and announces that Zion and Jerusalem will be ruined despite the leaders' false confidence.
cross_references: Ezekiel 22:27-29: Officials are likened to wolves while extortion and oppression are explicitly named, supplying a parallel for Micah's predatory imagery.
Jeremiah 26:18-19: Judah's elders quote Micah's warning about Jerusalem and recall Hezekiah seeking God, preserving the prophecy's later reception.
rows.translation_context_note: The current references already include Ezekiel's parallel devouring imagery, but there is no explanatory note. The proposal makes the poetic image visible without softening the abuse.
rows.proposed_note: The skinning and cooking language portrays the rulers' predatory treatment of the people. The chapter identifies their concrete corruption as bribery, paid teaching, and paid prophecy; the imagery is not a separate historical report that those rulers literally ate their subjects.
existing_cross_references: Jeremiah 26:18: Micah 3:12 quoted in Hezekiah’s time.
Ezekiel 22:27-29: Princes, priests, and prophets devour and extort.
Matthew 23:23: Justice, mercy, and faithfulness neglected (later rebuke).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: קָסַם (qāsam), Greek (LXX): μαντεύομαι, Aramaic: קְסָם
existing_translation_notes.note: Forbidden practice tied to paid oracles (3:11). Micah contrasts this with true word from God.

A payment to a judge to bend a verdict. The law bans it in the same words twice, that a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19), and Deuteronomy 27:25 puts a public curse on anyone who takes one to kill an innocent man. Micah 3:11 says Jerusalem's judges took bribes openly and still said the LORD was among them.

existing_translation_notes.term: Priests who teach for a price
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בִּמְחִיר יוֹרוּ (bimchir yoru, they teach for a price)
existing_translation_notes.note: Teaching the law was part of a priest's job, not a service for sale (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10). Priests were given no tribal land and lived on the tithes and assigned portions of the offerings instead (Numbers 18:20-21), so they were already provided for. Charging for a ruling meant the ruling went to whoever paid.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: צִיּוֹן שָׂדֶה תֵחָרֵשׁ (tsiyyon sadeh techaresh)
existing_translation_notes.note: This sentence was still being quoted roughly a century later. In Jeremiah 26:17-19 the elders of Judah name Micah the Moreshite, repeat this verse word for word, and point out that Hezekiah did not put him to death for saying it. The quotation is what kept Jeremiah from being executed.

rows.current_summary: The LORD calls the mountains to witness his accusation against Israel, reminding them of his past acts and asking what offering they think will satisfy him; he tells them he requires justice, mercy, and humility, then pronounces judgment on their dishonest dealings and empty harvests because they have followed the evil ways of Omri and Ahab.
rows.current_summary_original: The LORD calls the mountains to witness his accusation against Israel, reminding them of his past acts and asking what offering they think will satisfy him; he tells them he requires justice, mercy, and humility, then pronounces judgment on their dishonest dealings and empty harvests because they have followed the evil ways of Omri and Ahab.
rows.concern: The summary makes the LORD ask what offering would satisfy Him; the offering questions are spoken by a worshiper facing the LORD.
rows.scripture_says: The LORD recounts His faithfulness, then a human voice asks about offerings, including a firstborn; verse 8 answers with justice, covenant love, and humble walking.
rows.proposed_summary: The LORD calls creation to hear His case and recalls His saving acts. A worshiper asks what offering could answer the charge, even imagining a firstborn; the answer is justice, mercy, and humble walking with God. The chapter then condemns fraudulent trade and the ways of Omri and Ahab.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.
1 Samuel 15:22: Samuel declares obedience better than sacrifice, supplying a parallel to Micah's answer about what the LORD requires.
Hosea 6:6: The LORD calls for mercy and knowledge of God above sacrifice, paralleling Micah's correction of an escalating focus on offerings.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Ahaz reference mentions child sacrifice, but neither the cross-references nor a note explicitly separates the human question from divine instruction. This is especially relevant to the Jephthah discussion.
rows.proposed_note: The questions in verses 6-7 come from the one asking how to approach the LORD, not from God requesting ever larger sacrifices. The firstborn question is part of that escalating rhetoric; it is not a command to sacrifice a child. Verse 8 states the answer.
existing_cross_references: Numbers 22:1-6: Balak king of Moab sends to Pethor for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel.
Joshua 4:19-20: Israel crosses the Jordan and camps at Gilgal, where Joshua sets up the twelve stones.
Amos 8:4-6: Traders shrink the ephah, inflate the shekel, rig the scales, and buy the poor for silver.
1 Kings 16:23-33: Omri buys the hill of Samaria and his son Ahab builds a temple of Baal and sets up an Asherah pole.
2 Kings 16:3: Ahaz king of Judah sacrificed his own son in the fire, following the practice of the nations.

existing_translation_notes.term: Balak and Balaam, Shittim to Gilgal
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מִן־הַשִּׁטִּים עַד־הַגִּלְגָּל (min ha-Shittim ad ha-Gilgal)
existing_translation_notes.note: At 6:5 the LORD's case points to two things the reader is expected already to know. Balak king of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel and the curse kept coming out as blessing (Numbers 22-24). Shittim was the last camp east of the Jordan (Numbers 25:1) and Gilgal the first camp west of it (Joshua 4:19), so the two names are the start and the end of the crossing into the land.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בְּכוֹרִי (bekhori, my firstborn) - פְּרִי בִטְנִי (peri vitni, the fruit of my body)
existing_translation_notes.note: 6:7 climbs a ladder of offerings, calves, then thousands of rams, then ten thousand rivers of oil, and ends at burning a child. That was a live practice in the region and not a figure of speech: 2 Kings 3:27 has the king of Moab offer his eldest son on the wall, and 2 Kings 16:3 and 21:6 record kings of Judah passing their own sons through the fire. The law bans it outright at Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5.

existing_translation_notes.term: Ten thousands of rivers of oil
existing_translation_notes.note: Revavah is the Hebrew for ten thousand and stands for any uncountable amount. Olive oil was pressed by the jar and stored by the jar, never by the streambed, so 6:7 is offering a physical impossibility on purpose. Each rung of the ladder costs more, and the answer at 6:8 costs nothing and is the one thing not offered.

existing_translation_notes.term: Do justice, love loyal love, walk humbly
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט (asot mishpat) - אַהֲבַת חֶסֶד (ahavat chesed) - הַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת (hatsnea lekhet)
existing_translation_notes.note: Mishpat is the court's verdict, what a judge is supposed to hand down. Chesed is loyalty inside a covenant, the faithfulness owed to someone you are bound to, which is why both mercy and steadfast love render it. Hatsnea lekhet is to walk close in, without display. The three answer the sacrifices piled up in 6:6-7.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אֵיפַת רָזוֹן (eiphat razon, a wasted ephah)
existing_translation_notes.note: The ephah was the standard dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts, the amount Ruth carried home after a day of gleaning (Ruth 2:17). A short ephah is a scoop cut down so the seller hands over less than he charges for (6:10). Leviticus 19:35-36 and Deuteronomy 25:14-15 require a full measure by name, and Amos 8:5 catches merchants at the same trick.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: מֹאזְנֵי רֶשַׁע (mozne resha) - אַבְנֵי מִרְמָה (avne mirmah, stones of deceit)
existing_translation_notes.note: Weights were cut stones carried in a pouch, and 6:11 pictures a bag of them. The fraud was simple: keep two sets, a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling. Deuteronomy 25:13 forbids exactly that, two kinds of weight in your bag, a large and a small, and Proverbs 20:23 calls a false balance no good thing.

existing_translation_notes.term: Statutes of Omri, works of the house of Ahab
existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: חֻקּוֹת עָמְרִי (chuqqot Omri) - מַעֲשֵׂה בֵית־אַחְאָב (ma'aseh veth Achav)
existing_translation_notes.note: Omri founded Samaria, and his son Ahab married Jezebel of Sidon and built a temple of Baal in it (1 Kings 16:23-33). Their policy is the standard 6:16 measures Judah against, a century later and in the southern kingdom, which is the sting. Omri was known outside Israel too; Assyrian records went on calling the northern kingdom the house of Omri for generations after his line ended.

rows.current_summary: Priests who refuse to honor God's name fall under a curse, for the covenant with Levi called for reverence and true instruction, but their teaching makes many stumble; Judah profanes the sanctuary by marrying the daughter of a foreign god, men break faith with the wife of their youth though God hates divorce and seeks godly offspring, and the people weary the LORD by asking, 'Where is the God of justice?'
rows.current_summary_original: Priests who refuse to honor God’s name fall under a curse, for the covenant with Levi called for reverence and true instruction, but their teaching makes many stumble; Judah profanes the sanctuary by marrying the daughter of a foreign god, men break faith with the wife of their youth though God hates divorce and seeks godly offspring, and the people weary the LORD by asking, ’Where is the God of justice?’
rows.concern: The summary makes one difficult rendering of 2:16 appear uncontested, and the current references largely miss the marriage context.
rows.scripture_says: The passage condemns betrayal of a covenant wife. English translations differ over the subject and wording of verse 16.
rows.proposed_summary: Malachi condemns priests who corrupt their calling and men who betray their covenant wives. He calls the people to faithfulness in worship and marriage, warns against violence, and rebukes their claim that God approves evildoers or neglects justice.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 24:1-4: The law describes divorce certificates and prohibits a first husband reclaiming his former wife after another marriage, supplying the legal background to divorce language.
Matthew 19:3-9: Jesus answers a divorce dispute by citing creation, explaining Moses' concession, and stating an exception for sexual immorality, supplying further marriage context.

1 Corinthians 7:10-15: Paul discusses separation, reconciliation, mixed-belief marriages, and an unbelieving spouse's departure, supplying the distinct circumstances addressed in later divorce teaching.
rows.translation_context_note: Current cross-references concern priestly worship and omit the marriage passages. This proposal identifies a real translation difference without settling every theological question about divorce.
rows.proposed_note: The Hebrew of verse 16 is difficult. This translation reads God as saying He hates divorce; others refer to the man who hates and divorces his wife. Both readings occur in a passage condemning marital betrayal and violence. Other biblical discussions of divorce belong alongside this verse rather than being replaced by a slogan.
existing_cross_references: Leviticus 22:17-25: Defects make offerings unacceptable.
Deuteronomy 33:8-11: Blessing on Levi for teaching and guarding.
Ezekiel 44:15-23: Priests to teach the holy vs. the common.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: עִוֵּר / פִּסֵּחַ / חוֹלֶה (ʿivver / pisseaḥ / ḥoleh), Greek (LXX): τυφλόν / χωλόν / νοσοῦν, Aramaic: סַמֵּא / חִגֵּר / כֵהֵא
existing_translation_notes.note: Blind, lame, or sick animals were forbidden as sacrifices (1:8).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית לֵוִי (berit Levi), Greek (LXX): διαθήκη Λευΐ, Aramaic: קְיָמָא דְלֵוִי
existing_translation_notes.note: A ministry covenant marked by fear of God, true teaching, and turning many from sin (2:4-8).

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: פֶּרֶשׁ (peresh, the stomach contents and dung of a sacrificial animal)

A Greek silver coin roughly equivalent to a Roman denarius; one day's wage. The lost coin of Luke 15:8 is a drachma; a woman's dowry might be ten drachmas worn as a headpiece, which is why losing one is so distressing.
A silver coin worth four drachmas; exactly the temple tax for two people. The coin Peter finds in the fish's mouth (Matthew 17:27) is a stater, paying the tax for both Jesus and Peter.

The seed of the black mustard plant (Sinapis nigra); proverbially the smallest seed a Galilean farmer planted (about 1 mm across), growing into a 10-foot shrub. Jesus uses it as His image for faith (Matthew 17:20) and for the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:31-32).
Two drachmas; the annual half-shekel temple-tax amount (Matthew 17:24). Each adult Jewish male was assessed this amount.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

rows.concern: The takeaway joins verses 1-8 to the longer ending without disclosing the manuscript variation, although the added material supplies most of its appearance, commission, and ascension claims.
rows.scripture_says: Mark 16:1-8 records the empty tomb and the women's flight. Verses 9-20 form the longer ending; the Berean Standard Bible footnote records manuscripts ending at verse 8 or having a shorter ending.
rows.proposed_summary: Women find the stone rolled away and hear that the crucified Jesus has risen, with word for his disciples and Peter, and they flee trembling; the risen Lord then appears to Mary Magdalene, to two walkers, and to the Eleven, rebukes their unbelief, sends them into all the world to preach the gospel to every creature with signs following, and is taken up into heaven to sit at the right hand of God.
cross_references: Matthew 28:16-20: The risen Jesus sends the Eleven to make disciples of all nations, baptize, and teach obedience, giving another Gospel's commission account alongside Mark's longer ending.
Luke 24:50-53: Jesus blesses his disciples near Bethany and is carried into heaven, giving Luke's account of the ascension also reported in Mark's longer ending.
rows.translation_context_note: Add the textual note missing from current chapter notes; retain the included passage without claiming that the manuscript tradition is uniform.
rows.proposed_note: Verses 9-20 are commonly called Mark's longer ending. Some early manuscripts end after verse 8, and others contain a shorter ending, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote records. The longer ending is included in this edition; the manuscript variation concerns this ending rather than the empty-tomb report in verses 1-8.

rows.current_summary: The word of God comes to John, who preaches repentance, answers crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers, and points to One mightier who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, until Herod locks him up; at Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends like a dove as heaven calls him beloved Son, and his line is traced from Joseph back through David and Abraham to Adam, the son of God.
rows.current_summary_original: The word of God comes to John, who preaches repentance, answers crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers, and points to One mightier who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, until Herod locks him up; at Jesus’ baptism the Spirit descends like a dove as heaven calls him beloved Son, and his line is traced from Joseph back through David and Abraham to Adam, the son of God.
rows.concern: The imprisonment clause immediately before Jesus' baptism can imply that John was already imprisoned when Jesus was baptized.
rows.scripture_says: Luke 3:19-20 closes the section on John with his imprisonment before returning to Jesus' baptism in 3:21-22. Mark 1:9-14 narrates Jesus' baptism before John is imprisoned.
rows.proposed_summary: John preaches repentance, answers the crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers, and points to one mightier who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends like a dove and a voice from heaven calls him the beloved Son; his genealogy runs through Joseph, David, and Abraham to Adam. Luke also reports Herod's imprisonment of John after John rebukes his conduct.
cross_references: Mark 1:9-14: Jesus' baptism precedes John's arrest in Mark's sequence.
John 3:22-24: John is still baptizing before his imprisonment.
rows.translation_context_note: Distinguish Luke's arrangement of the material from the chronology inferred by reading adjacent summary clauses as successive events.
rows.proposed_note: Luke closes his account of John's public ministry with the imprisonment report (3:19-20), then returns to Jesus' baptism (3:21-22). The placement of the report is not a statement that John was imprisoned before that baptism; Mark 1:9-14 gives the order explicitly.

existing_translation_notes.note: Harvest imagery for sorting wheat and chaff (3:17).

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

Literally 'ruler of a fourth'; a Roman client-ruler over a portion of a former kingdom. Herod the Great's territory was divided after his death among three of his sons; Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, is the Herod who executes John the Baptist (Matthew 14:1) and mocks Jesus before His crucifixion (Luke 23:7-11).

rows.current_summary: Jesus defends his grain-picking disciples as the Son of Man, Lord of the Sabbath, and restores a withered hand; after a night of prayer he chooses the twelve apostles, and on a level place he blesses the poor, pronounces woes on the rich, commands love of enemies and mercy like the Father's, forbids judging, says each tree is known by its fruit, and ends with the houses built on rock and on ground without foundation.
rows.current_summary_original: Jesus defends his grain-picking disciples as the Son of Man, Lord of the Sabbath, and restores a withered hand; after a night of prayer he chooses the twelve apostles, and on a level place he blesses the poor, pronounces woes on the rich, commands love of enemies and mercy like the Father’s, forbids judging, says each tree is known by its fruit, and ends with the houses built on rock and on ground without foundation.
rows.concern: Forbids judging can be read as a blanket ban on all moral discernment while dropping the same passage's beam-and-speck instruction.
rows.scripture_says: Luke 6:37-42 joins judging and condemning with mercy and forgiveness, then commands removing one's own beam before helping a brother; 6:43-45 calls for recognition of fruit.
rows.proposed_summary: Jesus defends his grain-picking disciples as the Son of Man, Lord of the Sabbath, and restores a withered hand; after a night of prayer he chooses the twelve apostles, and on a level place he blesses the poor, pronounces woes on the rich, commands love of enemies and mercy like the Father's, warns against condemning others while ignoring one's own faults, says each tree is known by its fruit, and ends with the houses built on rock and on ground without foundation.
cross_references: Matthew 7:1-5: Jesus says the measure used to judge will be used in return and tells the hearer to remove his own beam before helping with his brother's speck, matching Luke's warning against hypocrisy.
John 7:24: Jesus calls for judging justly rather than by appearances.
rows.translation_context_note: Add the judgment passage's own context without turning the command into a new exhaustive theory of judgment.
rows.proposed_note: The command about judging stands beside commands not to condemn and to forgive (6:37). Jesus then warns against trying to remove another person's speck while ignoring one's own beam, and says to remove the beam first so one can see clearly to help (6:41-42).
existing_cross_references: 1 Samuel 21:1-6: David and the bread of the Presence.
Exodus 20:8-11: Sabbath command.
Matthew 12:1-14; Mark 2:23-3:6: Parallels.

A lay reform movement emphasizing strict observance of the written Torah PLUS an oral tradition (the 'tradition of the elders'). Believed in bodily resurrection, angels, and a coming Messiah. Paul was a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5); Jesus' sharpest disputes were typically with this group, though He shared many of their core beliefs.

rows.current_summary_original: Supported by women he healed, Jesus tells the sower parable, explains the soils as ways of hearing the word, and calls those who hear and do God’s word his mother and brothers; he stills a storm with a word, frees the Gerasene man from Legion into the drowned pigs, heals the woman who touches his fringe after twelve years of bleeding, and raises Jairus’s daughter with ‘Child, get up!’
rows.concern: The demons leave the man and enter pigs; the pigs drown. Distinguish the actors and their fate.
rows.scripture_says: Luke 8:30-33 identifies many demons by the name Legion. Jesus permits them to enter the pigs; the pigs rush into the lake and drown, while the man is restored.
rows.proposed_summary: Supported by women he healed, Jesus tells the sower parable, explains the soils as ways of hearing the word, and calls those who hear and do God's word his mother and brothers; he stills a storm with a word, frees the Gerasene man from the demons called Legion, permitting them to enter pigs that then drown, heals the woman who touches his fringe after twelve years of bleeding, and raises Jairus's daughter with 'Child, get up!'
cross_references: Mark 5:9-15: Jesus permits the demons to enter the pigs; the pigs drown, while the man is later found clothed and in his right mind, clarifying the different actors and outcomes.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Legion note does not correct the summary wording that appears to put the man into the pigs. Some translations additionally say the demons drown.

rows.concern: The plow is an illustration in a warning about following Jesus, not an action he performs on people.
rows.scripture_says: Luke 9:62 is a spoken comparison about commitment to following Jesus. It does not narrate Jesus removing people from a plow.
rows.proposed_summary: Jesus sends the Twelve to preach and heal, perplexing Herod, and feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish; Peter confesses him the Christ of God, Jesus foretells his suffering and calls for daily cross-bearing, is transfigured in glory speaking with Moses and Elijah of his departure at Jerusalem, frees a convulsing boy, again predicts his betrayal, sets a child as the measure of greatness, refuses fire on a Samaritan village, and warns that anyone who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is unfit for the kingdom of God.
cross_references: 1 Kings 19:19-21: Elisha leaves his plowing, asks to say goodbye to his parents, and then follows Elijah, connecting a prophetic call with both the farewell request and the plow image in Luke.

rows.current_summary: The seventy-two go out two by two and return rejoicing that demons submit, though Jesus points them to names written in heaven and blesses what they see; a law expert's test draws out love of God and neighbor, answered by the Samaritan who showed mercy to the robbers' victim, and busy Martha hears that Mary, listening at the Lord's feet, has chosen the good portion.
rows.current_summary_original: The seventy-two go out two by two and return rejoicing that demons submit, though Jesus points them to names written in heaven and blesses what they see; a law expert’s test draws out love of God and neighbor, answered by the Samaritan who showed mercy to the robbers’ victim, and busy Martha hears that Mary, listening at the Lord’s feet, has chosen the good portion.
rows.concern: Answered by the Samaritan can make the Samaritan sound like a participant answering the law expert rather than a figure in Jesus' story.
rows.scripture_says: Luke 10:25-29 records the law expert's questions; Jesus tells the story in 10:30-35 and asks which person acted as a neighbor in 10:36-37.
rows.proposed_summary: The seventy-two go out two by two and return rejoicing that demons submit, though Jesus points them to names written in heaven and blesses what they see; a law expert's test draws out love of God and neighbor, and Jesus answers his question with the story of a Samaritan showing mercy to a robbers' victim, and busy Martha hears that Mary, listening at the Lord's feet, has chosen the good portion.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 6:5: The command to love the LORD with all one's heart, soul, and strength is one of the Torah texts the law expert quotes before Jesus tells the Samaritan story.
Leviticus 19:18: The command to love one's neighbor accompanies a ban on revenge and grudges; the law expert quotes it before asking Jesus to define neighbor.
rows.translation_context_note: The existing Levite note already calls this a parable; align the summary and add the two Torah commandments explicitly quoted in the scene.
rows.proposed_note: Jesus tells the Samaritan story in response to the law expert's question, 'Who is my neighbor?' (10:29-30). At its end Jesus asks which person became a neighbor to the injured man, and the expert answers, 'The one who showed him mercy' (10:36-37).
existing_cross_references: Isaiah 52:7: Peace proclaimed to households (good news theme).
Matthew 11:20-27: Woes and thanksgiving parallel.
Revelation 20:12: Names in heaven/book imagery (later context).

existing_translation_notes.note: Jesus’ statement as the messengers report back (10:18).

A Roman silver coin equal to one day's wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2). 100 denarii were 3 to 4 months of wages. Bore the image of the emperor (Mark 12:16), making it the focus of the 'render to Caesar' tax question.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

The Greek-language counterpart to Hebrew Sheol used in the Septuagint and New Testament; the general realm of the dead, not specifically a place of punishment. Revelation 1:18 has Christ holding 'the keys of Death and Hades.' Distinct from Gehenna.

From the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where child sacrifice to Molech was once practiced (2 Kings 23:10) and where the city refuse was later burned. The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: πρὸς τοὺς πεπιστευκότας αὐτῷ Ἰουδαίους (pros tous pepisteukotas auto Ioudaious)
existing_translation_notes.note: The exchange that runs from 8:31 to the end of the chapter is introduced as words spoken 'to the Jews who had believed Him', straight after 8:30 says many believed in Him. Inside that exchange Jesus grants their descent outright, 'I know you are Abraham's descendants' (8:37), and then puts the question on conduct: 'If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham' (8:39). Everyone in the room is Jewish, the speaker included, and John has already recorded Jesus saying 'salvation is from the Jews' (4:22).

John uses this one word more than sixty times, and it does not always cover the same people. At 4:9 it marks a Judean over against a Samaritan; at 6:41 it is a grumbling crowd in Galilee; at 11:19 and 11:31 it is the neighbours who came to console Martha and Mary, many of whom then believe (11:45); at 19:3 it is the title Roman soldiers use to mock Him, 'King of the Jews'. Inside this chapter alone it covers a group that had just believed Him (8:31) and, by 8:59, a group picking up stones.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί (prin Abraam genesthai ego eimi)
existing_translation_notes.note: The Greek changes tense mid-sentence: Abraham 'came into being', a past event, and then 'I am', present. That is the wording God gives Moses at the bush, 'I AM WHO I AM' (Exodus 3:14), which the Greek Old Testament renders ego eimi ho on. The reaction in 8:59 is immediate; they pick up stones, the penalty Leviticus 24:16 sets for blaspheming the Name.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

A lay reform movement emphasizing strict observance of the written Torah PLUS an oral tradition (the 'tradition of the elders'). Believed in bodily resurrection, angels, and a coming Messiah. Paul was a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5); Jesus' sharpest disputes were typically with this group, though He shared many of their core beliefs.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

rows.concern: A single warning about bonds merges the Tyre disciples' instruction not to go with Agabus' prediction; it can silently decide the tension over whether Paul should continue.
rows.scripture_says: Acts 21:4 says the disciples through the Spirit told Paul not to go. Agabus predicts binding and delivery to Gentiles in 21:11; companions urge Paul not to go in 21:12; Paul remains resolved in 21:13-14.
rows.proposed_summary: Disciples at Tyre urge Paul through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem; later Agabus predicts his arrest, and his companions plead with him not to go, but Paul remains resolved and ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus; while he purifies himself at James's counsel, Jews from Asia incite the crowd, which beats him until Roman soldiers arrest him, and he gains leave to address the people.
cross_references: Acts 20:22-24: Paul says the Spirit compels him toward Jerusalem while the Holy Spirit repeatedly warns of imprisonment and hardship; these statements provide the earlier setting for the warnings in Acts 21.
rows.translation_context_note: The current Agabus sign-act note is accurate but does not address the distinct Tyre instruction or the tension with Acts 20.
rows.proposed_note: Luke distinguishes the messages: the Tyre disciples tell Paul through the Spirit not to go (21:4), while Agabus predicts what will happen to him there (21:11). Paul continues despite his companions' pleas. In Acts 20:22-24, Paul also describes himself as compelled by the Spirit to go and says that the Holy Spirit warns him of imprisonment and hardships. These statements should be preserved without turning the summary into a verdict on Paul's obedience.

Paul worked at the tent trade in Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla, cutting and stitching cloth or leather panels (Acts 18:1-3). In 5:1-4 he uses the trade for the body: a tent that gets struck and folded away, set against a building from God not made with hands. The same word group names the tabernacle, the tent Israel carried through the wilderness.

The verb first meant to exchange one thing for another, including changing money into other coin, and from that to change enmity into friendship. It was ordinary language for ending a quarrel between two men or two cities. The word group appears five times in 5:18-20, and the accounting sense stays live: 5:19 says God was not reckoning their trespasses to their account.

existing_translation_notes.note: For an Israelite this was done on the eighth day of life as the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:9-14, Leviticus 12:3). What the agitators were asking of grown gentile men in Galatia was surgery without anaesthetic, weeks of recovery, and real risk of infection, and Paul adds in 5:3 that it obligated the man to keep the whole law. It also marked him permanently in a world where men exercised and bathed naked: 1 Maccabees 1:14-15 records Jewish men in Jerusalem building a gymnasium and having the mark surgically undone to pass as Greeks.

Leaven was not a packet of yeast. It was a lump of dough held back from the last baking and left to sour, then worked into the new batch, so one handful carried through everything it touched. At Passover the law required every trace of it out of the house and out of Israel's whole territory for seven days, and eating it cut a man off from the people (Exodus 12:15, 19, 13:7). The Mishnah describes searching the house for it by lamplight the night before (Pesachim 1:1). That is the picture behind 5:9.

The word in the list at 5:20 is the drug word, the root behind English pharmacy. It covers the mixing of potions, spells, and poisons together, since the same practitioner supplied all three. The Greek Old Testament uses the related word for the magicians who matched Moses in Pharaoh's court (Exodus 7:11, 22) and for the sorceries Babylon trusted in (Isaiah 47:9, 12). Revelation puts it in the same kind of list at 9:21, 18:23, and 21:8.

The word in 2:7 is doulos, slave, and the ancient reader pictured a sale. Slaves were displayed on a raised platform in the market, often stripped so buyers could examine them, with a placard hung round the neck stating origin, skills, and defects; the aediles' edict required a seller to declare a slave's illnesses and faults, and imported slaves had their feet chalked white. A slave had no legal standing, no claim on his own body, and no right to refuse. That is the position 2:7 says was taken up deliberately, and 2:8 carries it to a death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: κύριος (kyrios) - Hebrew: יהוה (the divine name)
existing_translation_notes.note: Philippians 2:10-11 quotes Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD swears by Himself that every knee will bow to Him and every tongue swear allegiance; Paul quotes the same verse again at Romans 14:11. The Greek Old Testament renders the divine name of the Hebrew text, the four letters YHWH, with kyrios, Lord, and kyrios is the word standing at the end of 2:11. The reader of an English Bible sees Lord in both places without seeing that the quotation and the confession use the same word.

Philippi to Rome was something over seven hundred miles: the Egnatian Way west across Macedonia, a sea crossing of the Adriatic, then the Appian Way up to Rome, six weeks or more each way in good conditions and not attempted in winter. Epaphroditus made that trip carrying the congregation's gift, fell ill on the work and nearly died, and the news of his illness had time to reach Philippi and the news of their worry to get back to him (2:25-30). The word Paul uses of him in 2:30 is a gambler's word: he staked his life on the throw.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων (basileus tōn basileuontōn)
existing_translation_notes.note: This was a real imperial title before it was a hymn line. Great kings who ruled over lesser kings used it: Nebuchadnezzar is called king of kings in Daniel 2:37 and Ezekiel 26:7, and Artaxerxes signs himself that way in Ezra 7:12. Deuteronomy 10:17 had already applied the pattern to God, 'God of gods and Lord of lords'. Paul is putting the highest title a man could claim where it belongs.

The name means Useful, and it was a common slave name; owners named slaves for what they wanted out of them. Paul plays on it three times and English can only show one. In verse 11 he is achrestos, useless, and now euchrestos, useful. In verse 20, 'let me have some benefit from you', the verb is onaimen, built on the same root as the man's name. Paul is punning on a slave's name while asking his owner to take him back as a brother.

Under Roman law a slave who left remained his owner's property wherever he went, and the law was built to get him back. Owners advertised, and professional slave-catchers, fugitivarii, worked for a fee. A recovered runaway could be flogged, branded on the forehead, or fitted with an iron collar; collars survive with the message cast into them telling the finder to return the wearer to his master. Anyone who sheltered another man's slave was liable to the owner for the loss. Sending Onesimus back was the legally safe act; the letter he carried was not.

existing_translation_notes.term: No longer as a slave, but a beloved brother
existing_translation_notes.note: Rome had a formal route out of slavery: an owner could free a slave before a magistrate, by entering him on the census, or by will, and a slave freed that way by a Roman citizen became a citizen himself, still owing his former owner deference and set days of work as a patron. Paul does not name that procedure. He asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul (verse 17), says he will do more than is asked (verse 21), and leaves it there. The letter is also addressed to Apphia, Archippus, and the assembly meeting in the house (verses 1-2), so the request was read out in front of everyone who would see the answer.

existing_translation_notes.term: I write this with my own hand
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: τῇ ἐμῇ χειρί (tē emē cheiri)
existing_translation_notes.note: Letters were normally dictated to a trained secretary, and the sender then wrote the last lines himself as a signature. The secretary of Romans names himself in the text: 'I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter' (Romans 16:22). Paul flags his own hand in 1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11, Colossians 4:18, and calls it the mark in every letter in 2 Thessalonians 3:17. Here that hand signs a debt: charge whatever he owes to my account, I will repay it. It is written in the shape of a promissory note.

Xenia is both the guest quarters and the bond itself. Guest-friendship in that world was a formal, binding, reciprocal obligation, not a courtesy: the host owed a guest food, lodging, and protection, and the tie passed down to the children of both houses. In the Iliad two warriors find mid-fight that their grandfathers were guest-friends, and they refuse to fight each other and swap armour instead (Iliad 6.212-231). Paul asks for a room in the house of the man he is asking to take back a runaway.

Jewish tradition attached this line to Isaiah. The Martyrdom of Isaiah, a Second Temple Jewish work, says King Manasseh had him sawn in half with a wooden saw, and the Babylonian Talmud records the same execution at Yevamot 49b. Manasseh's reign is the one 2 Kings 21:16 describes as filling Jerusalem with innocent blood from end to end.

Rahab kept a house built into the wall of Jericho, which is how she could let the spies down on a rope through her window after the city gate was shut behind the search party (Joshua 2:15). The scarlet cord she left hanging there marked the house to be spared, and Joshua 6:22-25 says she and her whole family were brought out alive and settled among Israel. Matthew 1:5 lists her in the line of David.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: אָוֶן / עַוְלָה (ʾāwen / ʿawlāh, sense), Greek: ἀνομία (anomía, NT), Aramaic: עולא (ʿawlâ)
existing_translation_notes.note: Means deliberate violation of God’s law; used here to equate sin with rebellion against God’s standard.

The firstborn son of Adam and Eve, who killed his brother Abel in a field after God accepted Abel's offering and not his own (Genesis 4:1-16). John does not use the ordinary word for murder here. The Greek verb is sphazo, to cut the throat, the butcher's word for slaughtering a sacrificial animal, used again of the Lamb in Revelation 5:6.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: τίθημι τὴν ψυχήν (tithēmi tēn psychēn)
existing_translation_notes.note: The wording is lifted straight out of the Good Shepherd passage, where Jesus says it of Himself in John 10:11, 10:15, and 10:17-18. John then applies the same phrase, word for word, to what believers owe one another.

Splanchna are the inward organs, the heart and liver and lungs. Greek and Hebrew both located strong feeling in the gut where English puts it in the heart, so the literal sense of 3:17 is 'shuts his inward parts against him'. The same word stands behind 'tender mercy' in Luke 1:78 and 'affection' in Philippians 1:8. The 'earthly possessions' of that verse is bios, a man's means of living.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: הָאִשָּׁה הַנִּבְחֶרֶת (hāʾiššāh hannibḥéreṯ, sense), Greek: ἐκλεκτῇ κυρίᾳ (eklektē kyría, NT), Aramaic: אתתא בחירתא (ʾettatā baḥīrtā)
existing_translation_notes.note: Likely refers to a specific woman believer and her household, though some interpret it figuratively of a church; literally means 'chosen lady.'

The Greek has the definite article: not an elder, but the elder. He gives no name, which tells you the people receiving this letter needed none. The same word names an office held in every assembly, with elders appointed city by city (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5), and Peter uses it of himself in 1 Peter 5:1. Third John opens with the identical two words.

existing_translation_notes.term: Do not receive him into your home
existing_translation_notes.note: Travelling teachers had nowhere else to go. Inns were few, rough, and had a bad name, so a man arriving in a town went to a believer's house, ate at that table, slept under that roof, and was sent on with supplies for the next stage; 3 John 1:5-8 shows the same arrangement working properly. Taking a teacher in was therefore a public endorsement of him, and the household's own standing went behind whatever he then taught. Shutting the door was the only lever an ordinary family had.

A chartes is a sheet of papyrus, made by laying strips cut from the pith of the papyrus reed crosswise, then pressing and drying them into a single page. Melan is literally 'the black', ink mixed from soot or lampblack with gum and water, laid on with a cut reed. A letter this short is one sheet. In 3 John 1:13 he names the pen as well, the kalamos, a reed cut to a point and split at the tip.

rows.current_summary_original: Christ addresses three churches: Sardis is spiritually dead despite its reputation and must repent or face sudden judgment, though a few remain faithful; Philadelphia is weak but obedient and will be protected from coming trials; Laodicea is lukewarm and self-deceived about its poverty, and Christ calls it to buy spiritual refinement and repent.
rows.concern: Will be protected from coming trials expands a specific promise about the hour of testing into a general promise of protection from future trials.
rows.scripture_says: Revelation 3:10 promises Philadelphia keeping from the hour of testing coming on the whole world, alongside a call to perseverance and holding fast in 3:8,10-11.

rows.translation_context_note: Narrow the promise to its stated object and avoid deciding a disputed mechanism or end-times scheme through the summary.
rows.proposed_note: The promise to Philadelphia concerns the coming 'hour of testing' (3:10), and the letter also calls for perseverance and holding fast (3:10-11). The verse does not name how this keeping will occur. It should not be expanded into a promise that this church will experience no further suffering.

existing_translation_notes.note: The old capital of Lydia and of Croesus, set on a spur of Mount Tmolus so steep the garrison thought one side needed no watch. It was taken that way twice. Cyrus captured it about 546 BC after a soldier watched a Lydian climb down the cliff for a dropped helmet and led a party up the same route (Herodotus 1.84), and Antiochus III took it the same way in 214 BC. Verse 3 tells the church that if it does not wake, He will come like a thief and it will not know what hour.

Founded by Attalus II Philadelphus and named for his loyalty to his brother. It sat on a fault line: the earthquake of AD 17 flattened twelve cities of the province in one night (Tacitus, Annals 2.47), and Strabo writes that its walls were constantly cracking and much of the population lived outside in the fields. Verse 12 promises the one who conquers that he will be made a pillar in the temple of God and will never go out.

Laodicea had no spring of its own. Water was piped in by aqueduct from springs about five miles off, and the stone pipe blocks recovered on the site are thick with mineral scale from it. Hierapolis, whose hot mineral springs are visible across the valley about six miles north, and Colossae with its cold water ten miles east, both had what Laodicea did not. The word in 3:16 for what will be done with the lukewarm mouthful is emeo, to vomit.

existing_translation_notes.term: Gold, white garments and eye salve
existing_translation_notes.note: The letter offers the city three things it was famous for producing. Laodicea was a banking centre so rich that after the earthquake of about AD 60 it rebuilt itself and refused imperial help (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). Its district was known for glossy black wool. It lay in Phrygia, the source of the powder used in ancient eye ointments, and had a medical school. Verse 18 tells it to buy gold, white clothes and eye salve from Christ instead.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ἡ κλεὶς Δαυίδ (he kleis Dauid)
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 7 takes the wording from Isaiah 22:22, where the LORD strips the palace steward Shebna of his office and gives the key of the house of David to Eliakim, who opens and none shuts. A royal steward's key was a physical badge of office, carried on the shoulder, controlling access to the king. The image is authority over admission.

Solomon's temple had two free-standing bronze pillars at its porch, each with a name of its own, Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:15-22). Greek temples carried the names of benefactors and priests carved on their columns. In an earthquake city, a pillar that never goes out is a promise with weight.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ἡ βίβλος τῆς ζωῆς (he biblos tes zoes)
existing_translation_notes.note: Cities kept a citizen register, and a name struck off it ended a man's legal standing. The image is older than that: Moses asks to be blotted out of the book God has written (Exodus 32:32-33), and the psalmist speaks of the book of the living (Psalm 69:28). Verse 5 promises the opposite, that the name will not be erased and will be acknowledged before the Father.

existing_translation_notes.term: A quart of wheat for a denarius
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: χοῖνιξ σίτου δηναρίου (choinix sitou denariou)
existing_translation_notes.note: A choinix is about a quart, and it was reckoned as one man's grain ration for one day; Herodotus (7.187) uses exactly that figure to calculate the supply of Xerxes' army. So the cry in 6:6 prices a single day's bread for a single man at a full day's wage, with nothing left for a family or for anything else. In ordinary times a denarius bought something like eight to sixteen quarts of wheat. This is famine pricing, roughly ten times normal, announced as a market rate.

A Roman silver coin, the standard day's wage for a labourer, which is the going rate Jesus names in the parable of the vineyard (Matthew 20:2). It carried the emperor's head, which is why it was the coin produced in the tax question (Mark 12:16). Two denarii covered the injured man's care at the inn (Luke 10:35).

Grain was normally sold by the sack and eaten without counting. Weighing it out on a balance is itself a sign of scarcity, and the Law uses that image for judgment: they shall deliver your bread again by weight, and you shall eat and not be satisfied (Leviticus 26:26; Ezekiel 4:16). The rider holds the balance, and the price is called out from the middle of the living creatures.

existing_translation_notes.term: Do not harm the oil and the wine
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: τὸ ἔλαιον καὶ τὸν οἶνον μὴ ἀδικήσῃς (to elaion kai ton oinon me adikeses)
existing_translation_notes.note: Olives and vines are deep-rooted perennials that survive a dry year which destroys a grain crop, and both were the region's cash exports rather than its daily food. The limit set in 6:6 spares the two things a poor man cannot eat and leaves the grain ruined. Grain, oil and wine are the standard triad for a land's produce (Deuteronomy 7:13; Joel 2:19).

Chloros is the ordinary word for the green of growing things; Mark 6:39 uses it of green grass, and it is the root of English chlorophyll. Applied to a face or a body it means the greenish grey of sickness and death. The colour is the point of the rider's name.

existing_translation_notes.term: Sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ῥομφαίᾳ καὶ ἐν λιμῷ καὶ ἐν θανάτῳ καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν θηρίων (rhomphaia, limos, thanatos, theria)
existing_translation_notes.note: The four instruments listed in 6:8 are the same four the LORD names in Ezekiel 14:21 as His four disastrous acts of judgment against Jerusalem: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. The word rendered pestilence here is thanatos, death, which is how the Septuagint often translates the Hebrew for plague. The list is a quotation, not a new inventory.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: σάκκος τρίχινος (sakkos trichinos, sackcloth of hair)
existing_translation_notes.note: Sackcloth was woven from black goat hair, coarse and dark, and worn against the skin as a sign of mourning. Verse 12 does not just say the sun went dark; it says it went the colour of mourning cloth, and the moon the colour of blood. Joel 2:31 and Acts 2:20 use the same pair of images.

Hades is not hell. It is the term the Septuagint uses to render Hebrew Sheol, the common realm of the dead. In 6:8 Hades follows the fourth rider as a named figure, the way a burial detail follows an army. It is distinct from Gehenna and from the lake of fire, into which 20:14 says Death and Hades are themselves thrown.

rows.current_summary: The seventh seal opens to silence; seven angels receive trumpets and an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the altar. rows.current_summary_original: The seventh seal opens to silence; seven angels receive trumpets and an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the altar. As the first four angels sound their trumpets, devastating plagues strike the earth - hail and fire burn vegetation, a burning mountain poisons the sea, the star Wormwood contaminates water supplies, and darkness covers a third of the sky; an eagle warns of three more woes to come.
rows.concern: The mountain-like object turns a third of the sea to blood; Wormwood makes freshwater bitter. Do not conflate the two trumpet judgments.
rows.scripture_says: Revelation 8:8-9 describes something like a burning mountain and a third of the sea becoming blood. In 8:10-11 Wormwood affects freshwater, making it bitter.
rows.proposed_summary: The seventh seal opens to silence; seven angels receive trumpets and an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the altar. As the first four angels sound their trumpets, devastating plagues strike the earth - hail and fire burn vegetation, something like a burning mountain is thrown into the sea, turning a third of it to blood, the star Wormwood contaminates water supplies, and darkness covers a third of the sky; an eagle warns of three more woes to come.

Jeremiah 9:15: The LORD threatens to give his people wormwood and poisoned water, a prophetic use of bitter, deadly drink echoed by the Wormwood star's effect on rivers and springs.
rows.translation_context_note: Separate sea-to-blood imagery from bitter freshwater; poisoned sea conflates the two trumpets.
rows.proposed_note: The second trumpet brings something like a burning mountain into the sea, and a third of the sea becomes blood (8:8-9). The third trumpet brings the star Wormwood onto rivers and springs, making their waters bitter (8:10-11). These are distinct visions.

existing_translation_notes.term: Silence for about half an hour
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: σιγὴ ὡς ἡμιώριον (sige hos hemiorion)
existing_translation_notes.note: The only measured stretch of silence in Scripture, and it follows six seals of noise. In the temple the moment of incense was the quiet one, with the crowd outside praying and no sound from within (Luke 1:10). Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7 both call for silence before the LORD when judgment is at hand.

A fire pan for carrying live coals from the altar and burning incense on them. The high priest carried one behind the veil on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12-13), and the daily incense went up on the golden altar morning and evening. In 8:5 the angel fills the same censer with fire from the altar and throws it to the earth, so the vessel that carried up the prayers brings down the answer.

Not a musical instrument but a signal. Numbers 10:1-10 gives the priests two silver trumpets for summoning the assembly, breaking camp, going to war and sounding over the offerings. Seven trumpets circled Jericho for seven days (Joshua 6). A trumpet in this book is an announcement everyone hears at once.

A shrub of the Artemisia family, grey-leaved and intensely bitter, common in dry country. Scripture uses it as the standard image for what is bitter and poisonous to drink: a root bearing poisonous fruit and wormwood (Deuteronomy 29:18), justice turned to wormwood (Amos 5:7), and the LORD feeding a rebellious people wormwood and poisoned water (Jeremiah 9:15). In 8:11 the star is given the name.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: τὸ τρίτον (to triton, the third)
existing_translation_notes.note: The fraction runs through the whole chapter: a third of the earth, the trees, the sea, the creatures, the ships, the rivers, the sun, the moon, the stars, the day and the night. It is a limited stroke, larger than the fourth given to the horsemen in 6:8 and short of the whole. Ezekiel 5:1-4 divides the prophet's shorn hair into thirds for three different judgments.

rows.current_summary: John sees a beast from sea and another from earth empowered by dragon, demanding worship, persecuting saints, and marking followers with 666.
rows.current_summary_original: John sees a beast from sea and another from earth empowered by dragon, demanding worship, persecuting saints, and marking followers with 666.
rows.concern: Distinguish the two beasts and the coerced mark; the mark is the name or number of the name, not exclusively the printed numeral 666.
rows.scripture_says: Revelation 13:2 gives the sea beast authority from the dragon. The earth beast enforces worship and the mark in 13:12-17; the mark is the beast's name or number of its name, not exclusively a printed 666.
rows.proposed_summary: John sees a beast from the sea empowered by the dragon, blaspheming God and waging war against the saints. A second beast from the earth promotes worship of the first and requires a mark for buying and selling: the beast's name or the number of its name, given as 666.
cross_references: Daniel 3:4-6: An image is worshiped under threat of death.
Revelation 14:9-12: Beast worship and its mark are contrasted with the saints' endurance.
rows.translation_context_note: Differentiate the beasts' actions and coerced economic allegiance. The existing number note also needs the attested 616 variant rather than implying every manuscript simply has the same three letters.
rows.proposed_note: The second beast makes people worship the first and enforces the mark needed for buying and selling (13:12,16-17). The mark is described as the beast's name or the number of its name; verse 18 gives the number as 666. Some manuscripts read 616, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote records. The passage does not name a modern person or technology.
existing_cross_references: Daniel 7:3-8: Four beasts rising from sea.
Daniel 3:5-6: Image to be worshiped under threat of death.
2 Thessalonians 2:9: Signs and wonders of lawless one.

existing_translation_notes.note: Charagma is not a vague sign. It is the technical word for something stamped or engraved: the imprint of a die on a coin, the official stamp certifying a document, a brand burned into a slave or an animal. It is placed on the right hand or the forehead (13:16), the two places nobody can hide, and 13:17 ties it to the right to buy or sell. Acts 17:29 uses the same word for the engraved work of an idol.

Greek had no separate digits. The alphabet did double duty, so the number in 13:18 stands in the manuscripts as three letters, chi xi stigma. Because every name was therefore also a sum, people played with it: a wall at Pompeii carries the line 'I love her whose number is 545'. That letter arithmetic is what 'let the one who has understanding calculate' refers to, and the text supplies the total rather than the name.

existing_translation_notes.term: The image that was given breath
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: εἰκών τοῦ θηρίου (eikon tou theriou, image of the beast)
existing_translation_notes.note: An eikon is a statue or portrait, and compulsory reverence toward one was a real civic instrument in the province these letters go to. Pergamum built the first temple in Asia to Rome and Augustus in 29 BC, Smyrna won one for Tiberius in AD 26, and refusing the required gesture at such a temple was treated as disloyalty rather than as a private belief. Daniel 3:5-6 is the older version of the same demand: bow at the sound of the music or go into the furnace.

existing_translation_notes.term: Two beasts, and what the second is called later
existing_translation_notes.note: Verse 1 has a beast come up out of the sea; verse 11 has a second come up out of the earth, with two horns like a lamb and the voice of a dragon. This second one is the one that makes the image, works signs, and enforces the mark. Later in the book it is called by a different name, the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), which is the text's own identification.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: μῆνας τεσσεράκοντα δύο (menas tesserakonta dyo)
existing_translation_notes.note: Three and a half years, expressed three different ways across these chapters: forty-two months here and at 11:2, 1,260 days at 11:3 and 12:6, and a time, times and half a time at 12:14. Daniel uses the same span (Daniel 7:25; 12:7). It is a period with a stated limit, counted from its start.

implemented_note_changes.note: Greek letters could serve as numerals, so 666 could be written as chi xi stigma. Some manuscripts instead read 616, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote records. Because every name was therefore also a sum, people played with it: a wall at Pompeii carries the line 'I love her whose number is 545'. That letter arithmetic is what 'let the one who has understanding calculate' refers to, and the text supplies the total rather than the name.

The second beast makes people worship the first and enforces the mark needed for buying and selling (13:12,16-17). The mark is described as the beast's name or the number of its name; verse 18 gives the number as 666. Some manuscripts read 616, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote records. The passage does not name a modern person or technology.

implemented_reference_changes: Daniel 3:4-6: An image is worshiped under threat of death.
