rows.current_summary: Heaven erupts in praise as God judges the great prostitute, and a wedding supper for the Lamb is announced; then a rider on a white horse called Faithful and True wages war against the beast and kings of the earth, capturing the beast and false prophet while his armies are defeated by the sword from his mouth.
rows.current_summary_original: Heaven erupts in praise as God judges the great prostitute, and a wedding supper for the Lamb is announced; then a rider on a white horse called Faithful and True wages war against the beast and kings of the earth, capturing the beast and false prophet while his armies are defeated by the sword from his mouth.
rows.concern: The beast and kings lose their armies; the rider does not defeat his own heavenly army.
rows.scripture_says: Revelation 19:14 places heaven's armies with the rider. Verses 19-21 place the beast and earthly kings' armies against him, with those opposing forces defeated.
rows.proposed_summary: Heaven erupts in praise as God judges the great prostitute, and a wedding supper for the Lamb is announced; then a rider on a white horse called Faithful and True wages war against the beast and kings of the earth, capturing the beast and false prophet while the beast's and kings' armies are defeated by the sword from the rider's mouth.
cross_references: Isaiah 11:4: The ruler strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth and slays the wicked with his breath, a prophetic comparison for the sword from the rider's mouth.
Ezekiel 39:17-20: The LORD summons birds and beasts to eat fallen warriors and drink their blood, the feast image echoed by Revelation's summons to birds and defeat of the rider's enemies.
rows.translation_context_note: Replace his armies with the beast's and kings' armies, so the rider is not depicted defeating his own followers.
rows.proposed_note: The armies of heaven follow the rider (19:14). The beast and the kings of the earth gather their armies to oppose him (19:19). Those opposing forces are defeated by the sword from the rider's mouth (19:20-21).
existing_cross_references: Psalm 45:3-5: Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, and ride out victoriously for truth and righteousness.
Isaiah 11:4: He shall strike the earth with the rod of His mouth, and with the breath of His lips slay the wicked.
Deuteronomy 10:17: The LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty and the awesome.
Ezekiel 39:17-20: Birds and beasts are summoned to a sacrificial feast to eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of princes.
Matthew 22:1-14: A king gives a wedding feast for his son, sends out his servants, and inspects the guests' clothing.

existing_translation_notes.original: Hebrew: הַלְלוּ־יָהּ (hallelu-Yah, praise Yah) - Greek: Ἁλληλουϊά (Hallelouia)
existing_translation_notes.note: A Hebrew imperative, praise, joined to the shortened form of the divine name. It opens and closes many psalms, especially the block of Psalms 146 to 150 where it stands at both ends of every one. Revelation 19:1, 3, 4 and 6 are the only four occurrences of the word in the New Testament, and they all fall in these six verses.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: βύσσινον λαμπρὸν καθαρόν (byssinon lampron katharon)
existing_translation_notes.note: Byssos is the expensive bleached linen of Egypt, the cloth used for priestly garments and for the rich man's clothing in Luke 16:19. It appears twice in this chapter, on the bride (19:8) and on the armies following the rider (19:14). Verse 8 states what it stands for and leaves nothing to guess: the righteous deeds of the saints.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ἱμάτιον βεβαμμένον αἵματι (himation bebammenon haimati)
existing_translation_notes.note: The robe is already stained when the rider appears, before any battle in the chapter is fought. Isaiah 63:1-3 is the passage in view: someone comes from Edom with crimson garments because he has trodden the winepress alone and their lifeblood spattered his clothes. Verse 15 names the same winepress.

Two Greek words are translated sword. The machaira is the short blade a soldier or a butcher carried; the rhomphaia is a long broad Thracian sword, the one used in this book (1:16; 2:12; 19:15, 21). It comes out of His mouth, not His hand, which matches Isaiah 11:4, where He strikes the earth with the rod of His mouth.

existing_translation_notes.term: King of kings and Lord of lords
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: βασιλεὺς βασιλέων καὶ κύριος κυρίων (basileus basileon kai kyrios kyrion)
existing_translation_notes.note: King of kings was the formal title of the great kings of the East, claimed by Babylonian and Persian monarchs; Ezra 7:12 has Artaxerxes use it of himself and Daniel 2:37 applies it to Nebuchadnezzar. Deuteronomy 10:17 and Psalm 136:2-3 give the corresponding title to God. Verse 16 has it written on the robe and on the thigh, the place a rider's name would be visible to anyone standing beside the horse.

existing_translation_notes.term: The marriage supper of the Lamb
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: τὸ δεῖπνον τοῦ γάμου τοῦ ἀρνίου (to deipnon tou gamou tou arniou)
existing_translation_notes.note: A Jewish wedding ran in two stages: the betrothal, legally binding from the day it was made, and later the procession that brought the bride to the groom's house for a feast lasting days. Verse 9 pronounces a blessing on those invited to that supper. Verses 17-18 immediately set a second supper against it, the one the birds are called to.

rows.current_summary: The angel shows John the river of life, tree of life, and throne of God in the holy city where God's servants will serve him and see his face; Jesus declares he is coming soon and warns against adding to or removing words from this prophecy.
rows.current_summary_original: The angel shows John the river of life, tree of life, and throne of God in the holy city where God's servants will serve him and see his face; Jesus declares he is coming soon and warns against adding to or removing words from this prophecy.
rows.concern: The summary assigns the adding-and-taking-away warning directly to Jesus, although verses 18-19 do not explicitly reidentify their first-person speaker.
rows.scripture_says: Revelation 22:16 explicitly names Jesus, 22:17 names Spirit and bride, 22:18 begins I testify without naming the speaker again, and 22:20 distinguishes the testimony and the response Come, Lord Jesus.
rows.proposed_summary: The angel shows John the river of life, tree of life, and throne of God in the holy city where God's servants will serve him and see his face; Jesus declares he is coming soon, and the book closes with a warning against adding to or removing words from this prophecy.
cross_references: Deuteronomy 4:2: A parallel warning prohibits adding to or subtracting from the commanded word.
Deuteronomy 12:32: Israel is told to obey the commands without adding to or subtracting from them, a further parallel to Revelation's warning against changing the words of its prophecy.
rows.translation_context_note: Use a neutral attribution rather than silently deciding the speaker at a transition. The existing adding-and-taking-away note already limits the warning to this prophecy.
rows.proposed_note: The conclusion contains successive voices: Jesus speaks in 22:16, the Spirit and bride in 22:17, a first-person testimony in 22:18-19, and the response to Jesus' promise in 22:20. The warning belongs explicitly to the words of prophecy in this book; its speaker is not named again in verses 18-19.
existing_cross_references: Genesis 3:22-24: The way to the tree of life is guarded by cherubim and a flaming sword turning every way.
Ezekiel 47:1-12: Water flows from under the temple threshold, and trees on both banks bear fruit every month, their leaves for healing.
Zechariah 14:8-11: Living waters flow out from Jerusalem summer and winter, and there shall be no more curse.
Daniel 12:4-10: Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end.
Deuteronomy 4:1-2: Do not add to the word I command you, and do not take anything from it.

existing_translation_notes.term: The river and the tree of life
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ξύλον ζωῆς (xylon zoes, tree of life)
existing_translation_notes.note: A river flows from the throne down the middle of the street, with the tree on both sides bearing twelve crops, one each month, its leaves for the healing of the nations (22:1-2). Ezekiel 47:1-12 describes water from under the temple threshold with trees on both banks fruiting monthly and leaves for healing. The tree first appears in Genesis 2:9 and was closed off in Genesis 3:22-24; here the guard is gone.

existing_translation_notes.term: Do not seal up the words
existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: μὴ σφραγίσῃς τοὺς λόγους (me sphragises tous logous)
existing_translation_notes.note: Daniel was told the opposite: shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). Sealing a document kept it closed and unread until the right moment. The instruction in 22:10 is that this scroll is not to be sealed, because the time is near.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ἐπιθῇ ἐπ' αὐτά (epithe ep' auta, if anyone adds to them)
existing_translation_notes.note: The warning in 22:18-19 is the same formula Moses uses twice, do not add to the word and do not take from it (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). Ancient treaties and public documents commonly carried a clause of this kind to stop copyists and officials from altering the text. Here it closes the book it belongs to.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ἔρχου κύριε Ἰησοῦ (erchou kyrie Iesou) - Aramaic: מרנא תא (marana tha, our Lord, come)
existing_translation_notes.note: The prayer in 22:20 is preserved in its Aramaic form by Paul at the end of 1 Corinthians, marana tha (1 Corinthians 16:22), and the Didache, an early church manual, uses the same Aramaic word in a communion prayer. Aramaic was the everyday language of Judea, so this is one of the few places where the actual sound of the earliest believers' prayer survives in the text.

existing_translation_notes.original: Greek: ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς ὁ πρωϊνός (ho aster ho lampros ho proinos)
existing_translation_notes.note: The morning star is the planet Venus, the last light still visible as the sky goes grey, the sign that night is ending. Balaam's oracle says a star shall come out of Jacob and a sceptre rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17), and 2 Peter 1:19 speaks of the morning star rising in your hearts. In 22:16 Jesus applies the title to Himself, along with the root and the offspring of David.

Latreuo means to serve or minister, especially in priestly duty, and it is the word behind English liturgy's companion term latria. Luke 1:74-75 uses it of serving God in holiness all our days, and Paul applies it in Romans 12:1 to presenting your body as a living sacrifice. Revelation 22:3 says His servants will latreuo Him and see His face, which is temple language for work, not for a posture.
